sens: Temporary dwelling made of canvas or branches
Pavilion or structure set up for a particular occasion
Dwelling, in the figurative sense of a place of residence
H7900.detail:
1. A tent is a lightweight and portable dwelling, set up with canvas or branches, used by nomads and travelers for shelter. It is an impermanent structure, suited for life on the move. In Lamentations 2:6, God "devastates" the tent of the people as one destroys a fragile shelter: the image expresses total ruin and the profanation of the sanctuary.
2. A tent can also refer to a structure temporarily erected for a specific use, such as a pavilion or shelter set up for a feast or religious assembly. It is a lightweight building that is assembled and disassembled as needed.
3. Figuratively, the word can mean "dwelling" or "place of habitation": the tent becomes a poetic image of a person's house, home, or refuge.
H7900.origine: The Hebrew word שֹׂךְ (sokh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or setting up a temporary protection. It literally designates a nomadic dwelling, characteristic of life in the desert and countryside in antiquity. In Lamentations 2:6, it metaphorically represents the temple of Jerusalem itself, destroyed during the devastation of the city.
H7900.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 2:6. In this context of lamentation over the destruction of Jerusalem, the prophet compares the sanctuary of the Lord to a tent that God would have destroyed "like a garden." This image emphasizes the profanation and complete ruin of the holy place, evoking the collapse of a fragile and temporary structure. The word reinforces the feeling of abandonment and desolation that overwhelms the people after the siege of Babylon.
H7900.portee: This image of the destroyed tent reminds the Christian reader that even sacred places and sanctuaries that seem permanent are fragile before the judgment of God. It also teaches that the true dwelling of God's people is not a stone edifice, but a living relationship with the Lord that can be restored through grace and repentance.

sens: To go to bed or lie down on a bed to sleep or rest
To remain lying in a fixed position (an object, a corpse)
To have sexual relations with someone
To be laid down after death, to rest in the tomb
To remain inactive or unvigilant, to give in to rest
H7901G.detail:
1. To go to bed or lie down to sleep or rest: this is the simplest and most common meaning. Samuel lies down in his bed in the temple (1 Samuel 3:2-6), and Naomi asks Ruth to observe where Boaz will lie down to sleep, then to go lie down near him (Ruth 3:4, 3:7-8).

2. To remain lying or to be placed in a stationary position: this is the image of a person or object that remains on the ground or a bed without moving. A dead child is laid on the bed of the prophet Elisha (1 Kings 4:21, 4:32), and David lays the Moabites down on the ground by measuring them with a cord (2 Samuel 8:2).

3. To have sexual relations with someone: the verb expresses the carnal act through the image of two people lying together. Nathan tells David: "The Lord's women will lie with another" (2 Samuel 12:11), and Amnon lies with his sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13:11, 13:14).

4. To be laid down after death, to rest in the tomb: this is lying down in the sense of eternity. All the kings of the nations rest in their tombs (Isaiah 14:18), and David himself lies down with his ancestors (2 Samuel 7:12).
H7901G.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the image of lying down on the ground or a bed: it is a simple and very ancient verb that has changed little throughout the history of the language. The word can take many forms (simple, passive, causative verbs) that affect its meaning: "to lie down oneself," "to be laid down by someone else," "to make lie down." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the same verb: the idea of physical extension and rest is central there.
H7901G.emploi: The verb "lie down" is one of the most frequent in biblical vocabulary, with 91 occurrences in the Septuagint. It appears in almost all historical and wisdom books. In the sense of "sleeping," it paints domestic scenes: David sleeps in his camp (1 Samuel 26:5-7), a sick man "lies down" in bed (1 Kings 17:19). In the sense of "remaining lying" or "resting immobile," it describes both death (Job 14:12: "man lies down") and the rest of the righteous (Proverbs 3:24: "I will lie down"). In the sexual sense, the text is more discreet but clear: Ruth "lies down" near Boaz (Ruth 3:14), and the account of Lot in Sodom uses the word to speak of imposed homosexual relations (Genesis 19:4). In the Psalms and Job, the word takes on a spiritual significance: being laid down also means knowing peace or suffering abandonment.
H7901G.portee: This word reminds us that rest and sleep are gifts from God, not a shame: this is why the Psalmist says, "I will lie down and sleep" as an expression of trust. But it also emphasizes that our bodies are fragile and mortal: all kings lie down in the dust. Finally, the use of the verb for sexual relations shows that Scripture speaks openly about the body and intimacy, integrating them into its moral teaching.

sens: To be lying down, to lie on the ground or a bed
To sleep, to take rest at night or at noon
To spend the night somewhere, to lodge there
To have a sexual relationship with someone
To be laid down in death, to be buried
To rest, to find peace (in a figurative sense)
H7901H.detail:
1. The simplest and most common meaning: to be extended horizontally on something. Jacob "lay down" in a place after putting a stone under his head (Genesis 28:11). This is the basic physical image: the body lying down.
2. To sleep or take rest, especially during the night or in the hot hours of the day. The servant of Ish-bosheth was "lying down for his midday rest" (2 Samuel 4:5), meaning extended to rest during the scorching hours.
3. To settle for the night somewhere, to lodge: one who "lies down in the house" of a contaminated person must wash his clothes (Leviticus 14:47). The word designates both the act and the place.
4. To lie with someone in the sense of intimate relations. The Hebrew text expresses this discreetly but clearly through the same word.
5. To die and be buried, to rest in the tomb. When it is said of a king that he will be "laid down with his fathers" (1 Kings 1:21), it means he will join his ancestors in death.
6. Figuratively, to find peace, tranquility, or trust. "You will lie down" in safety (Job 11:18) means you will live in peace and serenity, without fear.
H7901H.origine: The verb comes from an ancient Hebrew root describing the simple and primary action: to extend oneself on the ground. In Hebrew, the "lying down" body is the basic image of one who rests, sleeps, or dies. The root appears in various contexts: the rest of the weary body, sleep, death that returns the body to the earth. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this verb is often rendered by words expressing the state of being extended or lying down.
H7901H.emploi: This verb appears about fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used first in a physical and concrete sense: lying down to sleep, for a nap (2 Samuel 4:5), to spend the night (Genesis 28:11, Leviticus 14:47). It also designates the act of taking rest while keeping one's clothes (Deuteronomy 24:13). Gradually, the meaning broadens: lying down in terms of intimate relations (a discreet but clear allusion), lying with the fathers (to die and be buried) in 1 Kings 1:21, and figuratively the rest of the soul in Job 11:18. In Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, the word designates sleep and rest that man cannot escape, or that he seeks.
H7901H.portee: This word reminds the believer that rest is a deep human need and that God intended it for daily life. Sleep and rest are not a weakness, but a gift. On a more serious note, "lying down with one's fathers" reminds us that death is common to all and that everyone will one day join their own. It is a sober and dignified word that speaks of the mortal condition without dramatizing it.

sens: To lie down on a bed or on the ground to rest
To spend the night somewhere, to lodge
To have sexual relations with someone
To be lying down after death, to rest
To relax, to cease acting (figurative sense)
H7901I.detail:
1. To lie down to rest: this simply means to get into bed or lie down on the ground. It is the basic physical act of lying down (Genesis 34:2 says that Shechem "lay with her").
2. To lodge somewhere, to spend the night: when one lies down elsewhere than at home, one stays there for the night. It is to welcome someone or to be welcomed.
3. To have sexual relations: this is the most common meaning in the Bible, particularly in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. Genesis 19:32 shows daughters saying, "Let us lie with our father" to have children.
4. To be laid to rest forever after dying: this is the image of one who will not rise again.
5. Figuratively, to relax or cease being active: when the threat "lies down" somewhere (Ezekiel 23:8), it is as if it settles and stretches out lazily.
H7901I.origine: The Hebrew verb שכב (shakav) comes from a very ancient root meaning simply "to be stretched out, to rest." The basic image is that of horizontal rest, of the body lying down. From this naturally flow all the meanings: resting from fatigue, lodging a guest, and by extension, sexual intimacy (often described in the Bible simply as "lying together"). The word belongs to the basic vocabulary of daily life.
H7901I.emploi: This verb appears 43 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the first five books (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Numbers). Its most frequent use concerns sexual relations, lawful or unlawful: Genesis 34:2 (Shechem and Dinah), Exodus 22:16 (seduction of a virgin), Leviticus 20 (forbidden relations). The word is also used for simple rest (Genesis 26:10) or lodging (Genesis 19:32). Sometimes it also describes what happens at death. The Law often uses it to state prohibitions against certain unions, showing the importance that Scripture attached to sexual purity.
H7901I.portee: This word reminds the believer that the body and sexuality are not neutral in God's eyes: biblical Law clearly establishes which relations are lawful and which are abominations. Recognizing the moral weight of this verb in legislative passages helps to understand that the Bible is not silent on sexual ethics, but provides a divine foundation for it. It is an invitation to take seriously God's design for the body and human relationships.

sens: To lie down horizontally to sleep or rest
To spend a night somewhere, to lodge
Intimate relations between man and woman
To die and be buried alongside one's ancestors
To be dead, to remain in death
H7901J.detail:
1. To lie down horizontally to sleep or rest: the verb describes the physical action of lying down to take a rest. This is the concrete and basic meaning of the word.

2. To spend a night somewhere, to lodge: when one lies down somewhere, one spends the night there. This is the natural extension of the previous meaning.

3. Intimate relations between man and woman: the verb is used to refer to the marital act, particularly in the Old Testament when intimacy must be respected ("to lie with a woman").

4. To die and be buried alongside one's ancestors: this is the major meaning in the accounts of kings. "To lie with one's fathers" means to die and receive burial among one's predecessors. Example: "David lay with his fathers, and he was buried in the city of David" (1 Kings 2:10).

5. To be dead, to remain in death: in prophetic passages (Ezekiel), the verb expresses the state of the dead in the realm of the dead. Example: "Ezekiel sees the dead lying together" (Ezekiel 32:27-32).
H7901J.origine: The Hebrew verb "shakav" paints the image of someone who stretches out, lies down. Its root evokes horizontal rest. The word belongs to the family of positional verbs: like "yashuv" (to sit) or "amad" (to stand), it describes a posture of the body. In Hebrew, the same verb serves for all these contexts: to rest, to lodge, the marital act, or death viewed as a final rest alongside the fathers. This richness comes from the fundamental image: the state of one who lies down, passive and motionless.
H7901J.emploi: The verb appears 45 times in the Hebrew Bible. Its most frequent use is in the stereotypical formula of the Kings and Chronicles: "So-and-so lay with his fathers" or "lay with his fathers and was buried." This formula recurs dozens of times (1 Kings 2:10; 11:43; 14:20; 16:6; 2 Kings 8:24; 13:13; 16:20; 2 Chronicles 16:13; 33:20, etc.), describing the death and burial of the kings of Israel and Judah. It marks a natural and honorable death, followed by a dignified burial. In Job and the Psalms (Job 7:21; Psalm 88:6), the verb takes on a tone of rest or torpor. In Ezekiel (32:19-32), it designates the dead lying together in sheol, the realm of the dead. The context changes the emphasis: from the peaceful death of the just king to the state of the defeated or the wicked in the afterlife.
H7901J.portee: This word reminds us that death in the Bible is not a brutal annihilation, but a rest with the ancestors. The formula "to lie with one's fathers" confers a certain dignity to the deceased king: he joins the lineage of his own. It also states that death is inevitable and natural for every man, even the most powerful. For today's believer, it opens reflection on eternal rest with the Lord and the importance of continuity between generations in the people of God.

sens: Emission of male seed
Layer, deposit that covers a surface
State of ritual impurity related to the emission of seed
H7902.detail:
1. The word designates the involuntary or voluntary emission of male seed. It is a natural physical phenomenon, but the Law connects it to a ritual impurity that requires purification by washing (Leviticus 15:16).
2. By extension, the word also means a layer or deposit that covers a surface — like the layer of dew in the desert in the morning (Exodus 16:13), or the frost that dissipates this layer in the morning (Exodus 16:14).
3. The word can finally designate the state of impurity itself caused by this emission: the garment or skin affected by it becomes impure until evening and must be washed (Leviticus 15:17).
H7902.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to lie down, to rest" — the image of what rests on a surface or the act of lying down. The seed is understood as what "rests" or "flows" from the body and contaminates. This is why the word expresses both the physical deposit (the layer of dew) and the sexual emission.
H7902.emploi: The word appears 9 times, concentrated in the purity code of Leviticus (chapters 15, 19, 22) and in the laws of Numbers. It always describes either a physical layer (dew, Exodus 16:13-14) or the emission of seed and its ritual consequences. In Leviticus 15:16-18, it concerns impurity contracted at night (involuntary) or during sexual relations, which requires washing and isolation until evening. The context shows that it is not about moral guilt, but a temporary ritual impurity: purification by water is always possible.
H7902.portee: This word reminds us that the Israelite Law governed even the most intimate areas of life, not out of prudery, but to teach that the whole body belongs to God and must be treated with respect. Impurity is never permanent — it can be washed away — which shows God's tenderness: He does not reject those who contract it, but brings them back to purity through simple acts. It is an image of grace, long before Christ.

sens: sexual act, carnal relationship between a man and a woman
forbidden or immoral sexual relationship
unnatural act
H7903.detail:
1. The word designates the sexual act itself, the carnal union between a man and a woman. It is a neutral term, purely descriptive, that appears in the laws of Moses: "If a man lies with a beast, he shall be put to death" (Leviticus 20:15) where it refers to the condemned act.
2. It can specifically denote a forbidden, immoral, or illegitimate sexual relationship — one that breaks a marriage or commitment. In Numbers 5:20, it refers to marital infidelity: "If another man besides your husband has lain with you."
3. Finally, it designates unnatural acts, such as relations with a beast (Leviticus 18:23, 20:15), which violate the created order.
H7903.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root שׁכב (shakhab), which means "to lie down, to be stretched out." The image is that of a body lying down, in a horizontal position of rest or sleep — from which the sense of intimate union has developed. It is the same root that produces "bed" and "to lie down" in the sense of resting.
H7903.emploi: The word appears four times in the Torah, always in the context of sexual law. It denotes the act itself, without judgment of form, but always within a normative framework: Leviticus 18:20 and 18:23 prohibit it (with another man's wife, with a beast), Leviticus 20:15 and Numbers 5:20 state it as a reason for condemnation or defilement. The Bible uses this blunt term to clarify the prohibition unequivocally.
H7903.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that sexuality is not a neutral zone: it is framed by divine law and marital commitment. The repetition of this prohibition teaches that physical union has moral dignity, that it is not free from all ties, and that it is profaned by infidelity or perversion. It is an invitation to respect the created order.

sens: To move quickly from one place to another
To wander aimlessly, caught in excessive agitation
To be carried away by a consuming passion
H7904.detail:
1. The verb describes a rapid and repeated movement: in the text of Jeremiah, well-fed horses "run" to and fro, going back and forth with agitation (Jeremiah 5:8). It is the image of a frantic race, of a restless coming and going.
2. This running can evoke wandering, a state of trouble or excitement: the animal does not settle down, it is in constant motion. The context of spirited horses suggests a loss of control.
3. Applied to men (as is the case in Jeremiah), this verb describes a state of desire: men run after carnal desires, carried away by a craving that dominates them, just like a horse excited by instinct.
H7904.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁכָה (sha.khah) has an uncertain meaning in biblical Hebrew; it appears mainly in the intensive form (Hiphil). Its basic image seems to be that of rapid and agitated movement, perhaps related to the idea of a disorderly race. The translation "to run" captures its essence: a movement without restraint, given over to an impulse.
H7904.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 5:8. Moses denounces the people of Israel with a blunt image: like well-fed horses, too fat and vigorous, who run to and fro neighing after their neighbors' women. This passage associates running with unbridled carnal desire, with a lack of moral restraint. The image is that of a creature given over to its basest instincts, without modesty or restraint.
H7904.portee: This word paints a picture of spiritual degradation: when man abandons the fear of God, he becomes like a beast in heat, given over to his cravings. Jeremiah reminds us of this to show us the infamy of carnal sin. For the Christian reader, it is a call to vigilance: not to let the desires of the flesh carry us away like a senseless beast, but to maintain control over our instincts by grace.

sens: Barbed pointed weapon thrown by hand or with a weapon
Projectile for hunting or fishing designed to pierce and hold its prey
H7905.detail:
1. The harpoon is a weapon composed of a barbed point attached to a shaft, designed to penetrate deeply into the body of its target and not detach. In Job 40:26, God asks Job if he can cover the skin of the Leviathan with harpoons: it is the image of weapons that penetrate and remain lodged in the thick flesh of the sea monster, showing the invulnerability of this creature against human projectiles.
2. By extension, the harpoon denotes any pointed weapon thrown for hunting or fishing, especially those equipped with barbs that prevent the prey from escaping once pierced. This weapon underscores the power and resilience of the Leviathan: if even human harpoons cannot pierce it, it possesses a superhuman nature that escapes human control.
H7905.origine: The Hebrew word sukkah (סכה) is related to the notion of piercing, penetration, and pointed weapon. The root evokes what penetrates or pierces. The biblical context associates this word with weapons of war and hunting, particularly those that wound by piercing. The harpoon, with its characteristic barb, embodies the idea of a weapon that does not let go once it has reached its target.
H7905.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 40:26, at the heart of God's discourse about the Leviathan. This unique usage emphasizes the exceptional and superhuman power of the described creature: harpoons, these fearsome weapons intended to pierce the toughest prey, are powerless against the Leviathan. This mention isolates the word in a poetic and theophanic context, where God highlights the invulnerability of His monstrous creation to humble Job and remind him that there are forces in the universe that exceed human understanding and power.
H7905.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to contemplate the power of God, who created beings and forces beyond what human weapons can conquer. It relativizes human capabilities: our best weapons, our most strenuous efforts, remain vain in the face of divine sovereignty. It is a lesson in humility and trust in the Creator rather than in one's own strength.

sens: Place near Rama in Israel
Site characterized by a large cistern
H7906.detail:
1. Sécou is a location situated near the city of Rama, in the region of the territory of Israel. It is a sufficiently precise place-name for King Saul to know it and go there during his pursuit of David (1 Samuel 19:22).
2. The site is particularly marked by the presence of a large cistern — a well or water reservoir dug into the ground — suggesting an important water point in this region.
H7906.origine: The Hebrew name שֵׂכוּ (Sécou) literally means "the watch" or "the watchtower," evoking a lookout post. This etymology may reflect the strategic function of the place or its topographical situation. The word comes from a root that refers to the idea of looking, observing, or watching.
H7906.emploi: Sécou appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 19:22, in the account where King Saul pursues the prophet Samuel and David. Saul goes to Sécou, where there is a large cistern, to ask the inhabitants if they have seen Samuel and David pass by. It is a concrete topographical detail that anchors the action of the narrative in real places known to the readers of the time.

sens: The inner part of the being, the seat of thought and understanding
The entirety of mental and intellectual faculties
H7907.detail:
1. This word designates the invisible inner part of a person, the heart in a deep sense — not the physical organ, but the seat where thought, discernment, and will arise. In Job 38:36, God asks: "Who has put wisdom in the heart, or who has given understanding to the spirit?" — He speaks of this hidden region where intelligence and understanding reside.
2. More broadly, it refers to the mental faculty itself, this power to understand and know that is given to us. That is why "wisdom" and "understanding" are placed here: this word names the seat and instrument of human thought.
H7907.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning to look or observe; it may have originally designated what one perceives or sees, before shifting to the sense of what is perceived internally — the spirit, the understanding. The English gloss "heart" confirms its role as the seat of mental and emotional life.
H7907.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 38:36, in a speech by God. There, it is associated with wisdom and understanding, the most precious divine gifts. This rare context makes it an emphatic term: God raises the question of the source of our abilities to understand. The parallelism with "heart" (the previous word) shows that "spirit" here aims at the intellectual and conscious dimension of being.
H7907.portee: This verse invites the believer to recognize that their intelligence, their ability to think and understand the things of God, does not come from themselves — it is a divine gift. It is an invitation to humility and gratitude towards the one who has placed in us this power of discernment. It also reminds us that our spirit is meant to receive divine wisdom.

sens: Loss, death, or absence of a person's children
Grief, sorrow caused by this loss
State of solitude and abandonment resulting from it
H7908.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the concrete loss of children: their death or absence. In Isaiah 47:8-9, Babylon, proud, believes it is safe and says, "I shall never be a widow, nor shall I know the loss of children" — it is a threat that this misfortune will happen to her, meaning she will lose those who ensure her lineage and protection.
2. The word also carries the emotional weight of this misfortune: the mourning, the sorrow, the affliction felt by one who has lost their children. In Psalms 35:12, when the psalmist says, "my soul is in abandonment," he evokes this solitude and distress caused by childlessness — or more broadly, the absence of support and consolation.
3. By extension, the term can express any state of abandonment or desolation, where one feels alone, devoid of help, as if they have lost what gave meaning to life.
H7908.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁכוֹל comes from a root that expresses the idea of dispossession or emptiness. In biblical Hebrew, it is mainly used to describe the condition of women who have lost their children — a tragic situation that, in ancient context, meant the end of hope for lineage and inheritance. The word illustrates how central family was to identity and security.
H7908.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 47:8-9, it is used twice in a prophecy against Babylon: God announces to the proud city that she will experience childlessness and widowhood, punishment for her pride. In Psalms 35:12, the psalmist uses the word to express his personal affliction, his solitude in the face of threatening enemies. In all cases, the term evokes a tragic loss and a state of great distress.
H7908.portee: This word helps the believer understand the depth of grief that the Bible recognizes in the face of the loss of children — one of the greatest human sufferings. It also reminds us that God sees the distress of the abandoned and judges those who cause the affliction of others. For the modern reader, it is a call to compassion towards those who have lost loved ones and to trust that God does not leave the afflicted without help.

sens: Who has lost their children, their descendants
Who is barren, without children
Who is empty, devoid
H7909.detail:
1. The word first describes a mother or father who has lost their children — either through death or misfortune. It is the pain of one who had children and no longer has them. In 2 Samuel 17:8, a bear from whom her cubs have been taken is compared to a furious and dangerous animal: she has known motherhood, then mourning.
2. The word can also refer to one who has never had children, one who remains barren. Isaiah 49:21 puts in the mouth of a woman who calls herself "without children" and "barren" — she has suffered from the lack.
3. Broadly, the word can mean "empty, devoid of something." In Song of Solomon 4:2, all the teeth bear twins, none is "barren" — the word plays on the idea of absence, of a lack of fullness.
H7909.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of being "taken away, torn away, deprived." It describes the state of one from whom something — here the child — has been removed. The family of this word includes other terms expressing loss or absence. The concept is very concrete: it starts from the image of the mother dispossessed of her little one.
H7909.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, always to speak of the deprivation of children. It is used for an animal (the bear in 2 Samuel 17:8, in Proverbs 17:12), for a woman (Isaiah 49:21, Jeremiah 18:21), and in a poetic comparison (Song of Solomon 4:2 and 6:6). The context is often one of suffering — a woman in exile who has lost her children, a mother from whom her offspring is taken as punishment. The word always carries an emotional weight: it does not merely describe a state, but a pain.
H7909.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the loss of children — or the absence of children — is a major trial in the Bible. It helps to understand the depth of suffering of biblical characters and the importance that the Bible attaches to descendants. It is a word that invites compassion for those who suffer from mourning or barrenness, as the Bible itself invites.

sens: Who has consumed alcohol and feels its effects
Who stumbles, sways, or loses balance like someone who is emotional or dizzy
Who acts without judgment or discernment
Figuratively: troubled, shaken, unstable in moral or spiritual state
H7910.detail:
1. The primary meaning refers to someone who has consumed alcohol and suffers its effects: the person loses their balance, discernment, and control. In 1 Kings 16:9, King Elah was drinking in the house of an officer, which shows the state of someone who has drunk too much and has lost their faculties.
2. The word extends to someone who stumbles or sways for any other physical cause. In Isaiah 24:20, the earth sways "like a drunk man": the image describes an unstable movement and a loss of balance, even without alcohol being the cause.
3. Sometimes the word evokes someone who lacks judgment or intelligence, because drunkenness clouds the mind. A fool speaking, according to Proverbs 26:9, is "like a thorn in the hand of a drunk man," meaning absurd and hurtful.
4. Figuratively, the word describes emotional or spiritual turmoil: being shaken, losing one's bearings. In Jeremiah 23:9, the prophet is like a drunk man because of the divine word, as it has shaken and troubled him.
H7910.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be intoxicated" or "to be bewildered." The family also includes the noun "wine" and verbs related to drunkenness. The basic image is of someone who has lost their balance and judgment due to a substance. It is a vivid and concrete word, very common in the daily life of ancient Israel where wine played an important role in meals and celebrations.
H7910.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the wisdom and prophetic books. In 1 Samuel 1:13, Eli thinks Hannah is "drunk" while she prays silently, showing how drunkenness makes actions seem strange. The prophets regularly use it to describe divine judgment: in Isaiah 28:3, the drunkards of Ephraim will be brought low; in Isaiah 19:14, the Lord disturbs Egypt as someone would intoxicate them. The word also applies to the entire people: in Joel 1:5, the drunkards lament. Rarely is drunkenness mentioned without a hint of reproach or judgment.
H7910.portee: Drunkenness in the Bible is never presented as a good thing. It symbolizes loss of control, lack of wisdom, and often divine judgment that disturbs and leads astray. The Christian sees it as a call to self-control, to remain clear-headed and vigilant against the traps of the world. It is also a powerful image of the turmoil that the love of God or His justice can create: one is like "shaken," disoriented, transformed.

sens: Lose the memory of something or someone
Cease to think about, no longer care about
Neglect, abandon
Leave aside out of carelessness or indifference
Be forgotten, disappear from memory
H7911.detail:
1. To forget is to lose the memory of an event, a person, or a promise: a person forgets naturally over time (Genesis 40:23, where the cupbearer forgets Joseph in prison) or instantly under the effect of emotion (Psalms 102:5: "I forget even to eat my bread").
2. To cease to care about something means to push it out of one's mind not through passive forgetfulness, but through negligence or inattention: Israel "forgets" God by ceasing to think about His benefits (Deuteronomy 32:18: "You have forgotten the God who gave you birth").
3. To neglect or abandon means to let go of what one should keep or observe: do not forget the teachings received (Proverbs 3:1), do not forget God's covenant (Deuteronomy 4:23).
4. To leave aside out of carelessness: forget the poor (Psalms 10:12), willfully ignore someone as if they did not exist (Genesis 27:45, where Esau forgets Jacob's offense).
5. To be forgotten means to disappear from the memory of others, no longer being mentioned or helped (Psalms 9:13: "Lord, why do you reject my soul? Why do you hide your face?").
H7911.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁכַח comes from a root that primitively means "to let slip away" or "to leave aside." It appears in several forms: simple (to forget), passive (to be forgotten), or causative (to cause to forget). It is a fundamental word in the Old Testament to evoke the rupture of memory or attention, particularly in the context of Israel's unfaithfulness to God.
H7911.emploi: The verb "forget" appears about 95 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the wisdom books (Psalms, Proverbs) and in prophetic calls. In Deuteronomy, it refers to Israel's forgetting of the covenant and divine laws: "Do not forget what your eyes have seen" (Deuteronomy 4:9). In the Psalms, the supplications ask God not to forget the unfortunate: "Do not forget the needy" (Psalms 10:12). In the prophets like Jeremiah, the people's forgetting of God is presented as the source of unfaithfulness: "My people have forgotten me" (Jeremiah 2:32). The word also plays a role in narratives: the cupbearer forgets Joseph (Genesis 40:23), Esau abandons his grudge by forgetting the offense (Genesis 27:45).
H7911.portee: Forgetting God and His commandments is presented in the Bible as a serious unfaithfulness, a source of misfortune and rupture. Conversely, trust in God rests on the certainty that He will never forget His people (Isaiah 49:15: "Can a mother forget her child?"). For the believer, this word calls to remain vigilant not to abandon faith under the pressure of time or circumstances, and to constantly remember God's works and promises.

sens: Discover something or someone while searching or by chance
Locate an object or document after a search
Determine that someone possesses a quality or ability
Accuse someone, reproach them for something
H7912.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to discover, to come upon something that one was searching for: this happens when one searches archives to verify information (Ezra 4:15: "you will find and see in the book of the records").
2. It often refers to locating a material object, such as a written scroll or an official document: "a scroll was found at Achmetha" (Ezra 6:2).
3. The word is also used to recognize or ascertain a quality in someone: "there was found in him light, intelligence, and wisdom" (Daniel 5:11) — meaning that these gifts were discovered in Daniel.
4. In a judicial context, "to find" against someone means to uncover a fault, an accusation (Daniel 6:4: "they sought to find an occasion to accuse Daniel," literally "to find" an occasion against him).
H7912.origine: The Hebrew verb שְׁכַח (shekha'h) in its most active forms means "to find" in the sense of "to discover" or "to come upon." It is a common verb in ancient Hebrew and in post-biblical Aramaic. The biblical uses of this word show the action of searching followed by discovery: one digs, investigates, and arrives at a result.
H7912.emploi: This word appears 15 times in Hebrew and Aramaic in the provided passages, almost all in the book of Daniel and the book of Ezra. The usage is very consistent: it primarily refers to the discovery of official documents (the scroll of the records of Achmetha), or the recognition of qualities in a person (the wisdom and intelligence of Daniel). The context of Daniel 6 shows a judicial nuance: "to find" something against someone means to search for and uncover a fault or accusation. All uses reveal an action of searching followed by discovery.
H7912.portee: For the believing reader, this word reminds us that God sees and discovers everything: nothing remains hidden from Him, neither our actions nor our qualities. In the Old Testament, "to find" is also to be discovered by God. The contrast in Daniel 6:4 is striking: his enemies seek to accuse him but find nothing — because Daniel is blameless. This integrity pleases God and protects him.

sens: Cease to remember something or someone
Willfully neglect, abandon in a culpable manner
H7913.detail:
1. To forget in the primary sense means to lose memory: to let something slip from one's mind, to no longer think of someone. But in the Bible, this forgetfulness is never innocent. In Psalms 9:18, the "nations that forget God" are not simply distracted: they turn their backs on the one who created and sustained them.
2. The second sense goes further: to forget means to deliberately reject, neglect, abandon. In Isaiah 65:11, the Lord rebukes His people for having "forgotten His holy mountain" while they set tables and cups for foreign deities. It is an act of willful rebellion, not a failure of memory.
H7913.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁכֵחַ (shakhéach) comes from a root that evokes the idea of letting fall or setting aside. In biblical Hebrew, it is a simple verb but heavy with meaning: to forget God is to push Him away, to cease to fear Him and obey Him. The word belongs to the family of verbs of abandonment and willful neglect.
H7913.emploi: The verb שָׁכֵחַ appears twice in the provided passages, both in a serious theological context. In Psalms 9:18, it describes the sinful nations that "forget God" and turn to the realm of the dead: it is the sin of indifference toward the Creator. In Isaiah 65:11, the same verb characterizes Israel's unfaithfulness to the Lord, who turns His gaze away from the "holy mountain" to serve other gods. In both cases, forgetting is not an excusable human weakness, but a conscious and culpable act of disobedience.
H7913.portee: The word "forget" reminds the believer that neglecting God is never trivial: it is the sin that the Bible most regularly condemns. Turning away from God is to fall into idolatry and spiritual abandonment. The modern believer may wonder how he "forgets" God in his daily life: through indifference, unfaithfulness to the values of the Kingdom, or the service of new modern gods (wealth, prestige, pleasure). It is a call to vigilance of the heart.

sens: that which pleases the eye, that which is beautiful
that which is pleasant, that which captivates the gaze
H7914.detail: 1. The word designates that which pleases the eye, that which is visually pleasing or beautiful. In Isaiah 2:16, it qualifies "all that pleases the eye" among the riches and ships of Tarshish: the text evokes the splendor of beautiful or precious things that attract the eye and inspire admiration. 2. More broadly, the word refers to that which seduces or fascinates the gaze, to the attractive aspect of something. It is the idea of a visible beauty capable of captivating or charming the viewer.
H7914.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of that which pleases, that which is pleasant to the eyes. Its exact meaning in ancient Hebrew remains uncertain, but the basic image is that of "beautiful to see," that which positively attracts the gaze. The Segond translates it as "pleases" to convey this sense of visual appeal.
H7914.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 2:16. This prophetic passage describes the day of divine judgment when human pride will collapse: the luxurious ships, the beautiful and precious things that pleased the eyes of the rich will be brought down. The context suggests that the word designates objects or things that seduce by their appearance, their brilliance, or their magnificence, and that become symbols of human vanity that God condemns.
H7914.portee: This word reminds us that visible beauty can be a temptation or a trap: that which pleases the eyes and seduces human pride has no lasting value in the eyes of God. The passage invites the believer not to place his trust in the riches or splendors of the world, but to recognize that only the fear of God will endure.

sens: Sharp instrument with a blade and a handle, used for cutting
Figuratively: that which constrains or masters appetite and desires
H7915.detail: 1. The knife is primarily a simple tool: a blade fixed to a handle, used for slicing. In Proverbs 23:2, the expression "put a knife to your throat" literally means to threaten oneself with this instrument, but it rather evokes a symbolic action of extreme self-control. 2. Figuratively, the knife represents the discipline one imposes on oneself to resist temptations — here, the excessive desire to eat in front of a well-stocked table. It is a stark image: one must be as radical and violent toward one's impulses as if one were drawing a knife against oneself.
H7915.origine: The Hebrew word שַׂכִּין (sakkin) simply designates a knife, a common tool in daily life. It is related to Hebrew verbs expressing the action of cutting or slicing. The word belongs to the simple and concrete vocabulary of ancient domestic life.
H7915.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 23:2. It is a saying of wisdom addressed to one who must control himself in the face of an abundant meal. The image of the knife to the throat, extreme and provocative, emphasizes the radical effort that may be necessary to overcome greed. The context is one of self-control and temperance, central values in the book of Proverbs.
H7915.portee: This verse teaches believers that self-discipline, especially in the face of carnal desires, is not an option but a necessity — and that sometimes one must be "violent" toward one's own impulses to remain upright. It is a call to sobriety and caution in daily life.

sens: person hired for a job for pay
animal rented for a service
soldier or worker without personal loyalty, motivated solely by gain
H7916.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a person hired to perform a specific task in exchange for pay. It is a temporary worker, distinct from a slave or a family member. Leviticus 19:13 commands to pay the mercenary's wages without delay, showing that it is an economic arrangement: you owe me payment because I have rented my services.
2. The word also applies to an animal rented for work — a donkey, an ox, or a horse — which produces value from which compensation is calculated, as explained in Exodus 22:15 regarding an animal damaged by the one who borrowed it.
3. Figuratively, the word paints the image of a worker without personal attachment to his master. Job 7:1-2 compares the human condition to that of a mercenary counting the days until the end of his contract: it is someone who acts only for pay, without passion or devotion.
H7916.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "sakhir," related to the idea of renting or temporarily hiring. It never designates the Hebrew slave (eved) or the permanent servant, but the person bound by a limited-time work contract. It is a neutral, factual word: it describes a type of economic relationship very common in ancient Israel, where poor workers rented themselves to the rich to survive.
H7916.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Bible, mostly in the Pentateuch and the Prophets. It is used in the context of labor rights: the Law of Moses protects the mercenary by prohibiting stealing from him (Leviticus 19:13) and guaranteeing him a share during the Sabbath (Leviticus 25:6). Deuteronomy 15:18 establishes a reference value: six years of work from a mercenary represent a standard of compensation. Job uses the word poetically and movingly to express existential anguish: human life resembles that of a soldier or a mercenary, counting the days, without hope beyond the contract.
H7916.portee: This word reminds the reader that biblical law grants dignity and protection even to the most precarious of workers. God cares for the resource-less mercenary, who can only count on his daily wage. It is a call to social justice: do not steal from the poor, pay him what he is due without delay. In Job, the word invites reflection on the mortal condition: are we, before God, merely mercenaries counting our days?

sens: Action of hiring a service or a person for a wage
What is hired, what is made available for payment
Paid service of a worker or a beast of burden
H7917.detail:
1. Hiring is the action of renting something or someone for a specified period in exchange for a wage or payment. It is an agreement between the one who needs a service and the one who provides it for compensation. In Isaiah 7:20, the razor taken on "hire" means a razor that would have been borrowed or brought in from outside, for remuneration.
2. Hiring also refers to the hired person, that is, the worker engaged for a task, or the animal hired for work (a mount, a beast of burden). It is the provision itself of a paid service.
3. By extension, hiring can evoke the temporary and mercenary nature of a relationship: one hires something or someone as long as there is a need and as long as payment is made.
H7917.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root שׂכר (sakhar), which means "to hire," "to engage," or "to pay a wage." The feminine noun שְׂכִירָה (sekirah) literally refers to the action of hiring, paid employment. In the same family, we find the word שׂכִיר (sekir), "hired worker," and שׂכִּיר (sakkir), "mercenary." The basic theme expresses the idea of exchange: one hires a person or an animal in return for payment.
H7917.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 7:20. In this apocalyptic passage where the prophet describes future judgments, the context refers to a razor taken on hire — probably a metaphor to designate the king of Assyria as an instrument of punishment sent by the Lord. The term emphasizes the idea that this judgment comes from the outside, from one whom we must "pay" or with whom we must negotiate. Although rare, this word fits into the economic and social world of the Old Testament where paid work and the engagement of personnel or animals was common.
H7917.portee: This word reminds us that every work or service relationship is based on a fair agreement and compensation. For the believer, it sheds light on the value of work and the importance of treating fairly those who labor for us — a lesson that Jesus will reiterate when speaking of the worker's wage. It also invites reflection on what we offer or accept for remuneration, and on integrity in our commitments.

sens: To calm down, decrease in intensity (referring to a force, agitation)
To cease or reduce (an agitation, an emotion, a threat)
To diminish, become less violent
H7918.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of an agitation or force that calms naturally: the waters of the flood "calmed" (Genesis 8:1), meaning they ceased to rise and swirl, returning to their normal state. The image is that of a storm that stops.
2. The word can also mean to cause something active to cease or diminish: God says He will "cease" the murmurs of the Israelites (Numbers 17:5), putting an end to their complaints. It is to put an end to an agitation.
3. Applied to emotions, particularly anger, the word expresses the calm that returns: "the anger of King Ahasuerus calmed" (Esther 2:1) means that his fury gradually extinguished, that he regained his composure.
H7918.origine: The Hebrew root fundamentally means "to diminish" or "to become tranquil." The word can take the simple form (the subject calms down) or the causative form (someone causes something to calm). The starting image is that of an agitation or turbulence that gradually decreases until it disappears — like water calming after a storm.
H7918.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 8:1, it describes the withdrawal of the floodwaters, a natural calming after God's judgment. In Numbers 17:5, it expresses God's action to end the criticisms against Moses and Aaron. In Esther 2:1 and 7:10, it speaks of royal anger calming — it is an emotional calming. Finally, in Jeremiah 5:26, a rare occurrence uses a derivative of the word to refer to traps; the meaning has specialized, and the link with "trap" remains debated among scholars.
H7918.portee: This word reminds us that destructive forces — God's judgment, anger, conflicts — are not eternal. The calming of the floodwaters signifies that even after punishment, God restores order and life. For the believer, it is an assurance that divine anger has an end and that mercy can follow judgment.

sens: To have discernment, to understand wisely
To succeed, to prosper, to have success
To act with caution, to conduct oneself wisely
To teach, to give understanding to someone
To give importance to, to consider with attention
H7919A.detail:
1. To have discernment and understand wisely: it is to grasp the deep meaning of things, to see beyond appearances. In Genesis 3:6, the serpent promises the woman that the fruit of the tree will open her "understanding" — a comprehension that seemed forbidden. This is also what the psalmist seeks: a heart sufficiently "understanding" to perceive God where others see nothing (Psalms 14:2).
2. To succeed, to prosper, to have success in one's endeavors: this is the concrete fruit of prudence. When one "succeeds" in all that one does, as Joshua must do by keeping the Law (Joshua 1:8), one sees what one has undertaken come to fruition. David "succeeds" in all his military campaigns (1 Samuel 18:14-15) and the gifts themselves "succeed" (Proverbs 17:8).
3. To act with caution and wisdom: it is to conduct oneself with prudence and attention, to weigh one's actions. The wise "prospers" because he carefully observes the Law (1 Kings 2:3), while the foolish shepherds "have not prospered" for failing to seek God with discernment (Jeremiah 10:21).
4. To teach and give understanding to someone: this is the role of one who can say, like the psalmist: "I am more learned than all my teachers" (Psalms 119:99). The prophets with this ability "will give understanding to the people" (Daniel 12:3).
5. To give importance to, to consider thoughtfully: it is to pay attention to something in a reflective manner. The psalmist wants to "consider" his ways (Psalms 101:2), as one looks attentively at what truly matters.
H7919A.origine: The verb comes from a Semitic root that expresses the idea of grasping, understanding, seeing with acuity. It is related to the notion of success and prosperity that results from wise and thoughtful conduct. The parallel Aramaic (שְׂכַל, se.khal) reinforces this sense of contemplation and understanding. The family of this verb includes the noun "wisdom" and the adjective "wise," all connected around this practical intelligence that leads to success.
H7919A.emploi: This verb appears 61 times in the Old Testament, very concentrated in the poetic and wisdom books (Psalms, Proverbs, Job), but also present in historical narratives and the prophets. In Proverbs, it regularly describes the success of the wise contrasted with the failure of the fool: the "intelligent" servant prospers while the "foolish" fails. Among the prophets, particularly Daniel, it designates prophetic understanding, the gift of grasping divine will — a gift that God "gives" to His servant. The verb thus encompasses both an attitude (prudence, discernment) and a result (success, prosperity), showing that, in the biblical view, wisdom is never in vain: it bears fruit.
H7919A.portee: This word reminds the reader that biblical wisdom is not a mere accumulation of knowledge, but a practical understanding that changes life and brings success. It invites cultivating discernment by scrutinizing the Word of God — not passively, but by "meditating" on it like the psalmist — in order to truly prosper. It is a promise: whoever understands God's way and keeps it succeeds, not by chance, but by the divine grace that blesses wisdom.

sens: Examiner attentivement, porter son regard et son attention sur quelque chose
Réfléchir à ce qu'on observe, en comprendre le sens
H7920.detail:
1. To consider is first to fix one's gaze on something to examine it in detail. Daniel "considers" the horns of the beast: he scrutinizes them, he carefully observes their characteristics, he sees this new little horn appear among them (Daniel 7:8). It is an act of concentrated observation.
2. But to consider also implies reflection: it is not just a passing glance. It is weighing what one sees, understanding it, drawing meaning from it. Daniel does not merely look at the horns; he analyzes them to discern what they signify in this prophetic vision.
H7920.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root כול (shakhal), which means "to be prudent" or "to have understanding." In Daniel, it is in Aramaic (the language God chooses to speak to pagan empires). This root evokes the idea of vigilant and thoughtful attention, that of someone who observes with intelligence, who weighs things rather than ignoring them.
H7920.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:8 in its Aramaic form. Daniel pronounces it while describing his vision of the four beasts coming out of the sea: he looks at the horns, observes the details, and suddenly sees a fifth horn arise that overturns three of the first ones. It is in this context of prophetic vision that the verb takes on its full force: Daniel must look, discern, to understand what God is showing him.
H7920.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that to consider is not passive: it is to engage one's intelligence to understand what one sees. When reading Daniel's visions, we are invited to do as he does—to observe, to reflect, to seek the hidden meaning of the signs. It is an invitation to spiritual vigilance and wisdom.

sens: Être privé d'enfants, perdre ses enfants
Rendre stérile, empêcher d'avoir des enfants
Causer une fausse couche, un avortement
Dépeupler un territoire en tuant ses habitants
H7921A.detail:
1. To suffer the loss of one's children or to be in mourning for having lost them: this is the experience of Rachel who complains of being "deprived" of her two sons, or of Jacob who believes he has lost Joseph and Benjamin (Genesis 42:36; 43:14). The word evokes the deep pain of a parent who no longer has descendants.
2. To be rendered sterile or incapable of bearing children: this is the idea of a blessing refused or a curse that strikes. God promises that no woman in His people will be "deprived of children" if the people obey Him (Exodus 23:26).
3. To cause a miscarriage or render a pregnant woman unable to carry her child: a punishment or a violent act against a mother. This is one of the plagues that God can send to correct His rebellious people (Leviticus 26:22; Jeremiah 15:7).
4. To depopulate a land by killing its inhabitants until extinction: the image of a territory emptied of its inhabitants, rendered desolate, as if fierce beasts or the sword deprived it of its living population (Ezekiel 14:15; Deuteronomy 32:25).
H7921A.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁכל (shakhal) fundamentally expresses the idea of deprivation and loss, particularly in the realm of family and descendants. The root evokes the emptiness caused by absence: a parent deprived of children, a sterile woman, a land emptied of its inhabitants. In biblical Hebrew, this word is used to describe the most painful consequences of God's curse or judgment: the broken family, the interrupted lineage, the destroyed future.
H7921A.emploi: This verb appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mostly in contexts of punishment or calamity. Genesis (loss of children), Exodus and Leviticus (sterility as punishment), and then widely in Jeremiah and Ezekiel where it describes the consequences of divine judgment on a rebellious people: deprivation of children, forced abortions, depopulation (Jeremiah 15:7; Ezekiel 36:14). In 1 Samuel 15:33, it echoes the principle of retribution: "You have deprived your mother of children, your mother will be deprived of children." The word is also used simply to express the absence of offspring (Job 21:10). Its intensity shows that the interruption of lineage is perceived as the gravest loss.
H7921A.portee: For an Israelite, having children was a fundamental blessing, promised by God's covenant. This word reminds us that the deprivation of descendants was a feared curse, a sign of divine rejection. For the Christian reader, it helps to understand the stakes of God's judgment in the Old Testament: it is not an abstract punishment, but the destruction of a person's or a people's future. It is also an image of spiritual barrenness when a man or a people turns away from God.

sens: Inability of land to produce crops or fruit
Absence of life or fertility in a place
H7921C.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the infertility of land, its inability to nourish what inhabits it. When the inhabitants of Jericho complain to Elisha that "the land is sterile" (2 Kings 2:19), they refer to a region where the waters are corrupted and prevent any plant and animal life from developing. This is a calamity for an agricultural society, as a sterile land cannot sustain its inhabitants.
2. By extension, the word expresses the overall absence of fertility or prosperous life in a place. In 2 Kings 2:21, the Lord promises "that there will no longer be death or sterility," meaning that the healed waters will bring life instead of causing destruction. The word thus embodies the threatening emptiness, the impossibility for a place to support life.
H7921C.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of drying up or impoverishment. It is formed as a feminine noun and literally translates the image of dry, sterile land. The concept appears in the Old Testament as a radical contrast to divine blessing, which is always linked to fertility and multiplication.
H7921C.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the account of 2 Kings 2:19-21. It describes the catastrophic situation of Jericho after its conquest: the spring waters are "bad" and the territory is struck by sterility. Elisha, sent by God, performs a miracle that transforms the waters and cleanses the place, thus eliminating death and sterility. The word illustrates a concrete human problem and its miraculous resolution by the power of God.
H7921C.portee: This story reveals that the sterility of a region is not a fatality, but a situation that God can transform. It invited the Israelites to recognize that their prosperity depended on divine blessing, not on uncontrollable natural forces. For us, it emphasizes how God intervenes to heal what is dead or broken, bringing life where destruction reigned.

sens: Ability of the mind to understand, judge, and reason soundly
Practical good judgment, wisdom that guides actions
Correct understanding of a situation or a word
Skill, cunning, sometimes in a negative sense (malicious calculation)
H7922.detail:
1. Intelligence is primarily the ability to understand and reason: it is grasping the meaning of something, as when the Levites give the "sense" of the law to make clear what is read (Nehemiah 8:8). It is having enlightenment in the mind.
2. It also denotes practical good judgment, the wisdom that governs actions — what is called "common sense." Abigail is praised for her "good sense" and uprightness (1 Samuel 25:3). A man is esteemed for his intelligence in everyday life (Proverbs 12:8).
3. Intelligence also produces understanding of divine and moral realities: he who fears the Lord and keeps His commandments possesses a "sound" and true "reason" (Psalms 111:10). It is born from the fear of God.
4. The word can finally denote cunning skill, an understanding of the means to achieve a goal — sometimes a malicious cunning, as in one who acts with "intelligence" by deceiving (Daniel 8:25).
H7922.origine: The Hebrew word שֵׂכֶל comes from a root that means "to have sense," "to be prudent." It is related to verbs expressing reflection and judgment. The term denotes the action of the mind that "sees" things clearly, that discerns and evaluates. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates φρόνησις (phronèsis), the practical wisdom that differentiates good from evil and true from false.
H7922.emploi: This word appears sixteen times in the Old Testament, especially in the Wisdom Books (Proverbs), the Chronicles, and historical texts. It characterizes wise individuals: Abigail with good sense, Zechariah as a wise counselor, Hezekiah seeking intelligent men (1 Chronicles 22:12). Proverbs often place it in the moral and spiritual domain: intelligence is a precious good that preserves the one who possesses it (Proverbs 16:22), it produces prudence and grace (Proverbs 3:4). Intelligence is also one of the virtues expected in the service of God (2 Chronicles 30:22). Finally, it can describe a bad cunning: the power of deception of one who acts against the truth (Daniel 8:25).
H7922.portee: Intelligence is not a neutral quality: it takes its true value when it is linked to the fear of God and respect for His law. It helps us discern good from evil, understand God's will, and act wisely. It should keep us from malicious cunning and lead us toward righteousness and truth.

sens: State of a person or a region without children
Grief caused by the death of children
Desolation and figurative sterility
H7923.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the absence or loss of children — a condition feared in ancient Israel, where children ensured the future and inheritance. In Isaiah 49:20, desolate Jerusalem exclaims: "The children of my sterility say to me: The place is too narrow for me." The image is that of a city emptied of its children, reduced to desolation.
2. Beyond mere physical absence, the word carries an emotional weight: it is the grief, the pain of one who has lost their children. This refers to the worst misfortune one can imagine in the Bible.
3. Used figuratively for a community or place, it evokes spiritual sterility and curse — the absence of posterity and hope for a glorious future.
H7923.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be deprived of" or "to be stripped of." It belongs to the semantic field of loss and mourning. The absence of children was considered a form of curse or judgment in biblical thought, hence the strong connotation of this term that unites concrete absence and moral suffering.
H7923.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 49:20. It is placed in the mouth of Jerusalem in exile, which suddenly sees itself filled with a multitude of children — a miraculous reversal of its condition of desolation. The context is that of the restoration of Israel after exile: from sterile and abandoned, the city becomes fertile and populated. This unique occurrence underscores the dramatic intensity of the term and its eschatological use, directed toward future redemption.
H7923.portee: This word reminds Christians that God transforms desolation into fullness, death into new life. For Israel in exile, it embodied the hope that even the worst ruin — the silence of children, the silence of the future — could be restored by divine power. It is a word of comfort for all those going through times of sterility or abandonment.

sens: Capacity of the mind to understand, discern, and interpret
Practical wisdom and discernment in accomplishing a task
Divine gift of insight and understanding of mysteries
H7924.detail:
1. It is the mental faculty to grasp the meaning of something, to discern what is true or false, to understand things deeply. It is an active intelligence, capable of solving riddles and difficult questions, like the one Daniel possesses to explain the king's dreams (Daniel 5:12).

2. This word also denotes practical wisdom — the ability to apply one's understanding to successfully accomplish a task, or to correctly interpret what is hidden or mysterious. Nebuchadnezzar sees in Daniel an exceptional intelligence, capable of deciphering what no one else can understand.

3. In the context of the book of Daniel, this intelligence is presented as a gift from God — it comes from the divine Spirit that dwells in the one who possesses it ("the spirit of the holy gods" in Daniel 5:11). Therefore, it is not merely a natural skill, but a spiritual insight.
H7924.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew sekhel (שׂכל), which literally means "to have discernment" or "to be prudent." The Hebrew root first evokes the idea of looking attentively, scrutinizing, from which the idea of understanding deeply arises. It is a word from the family of the verb "to prosper" or "to succeed" — for one who has intelligence succeeds in their endeavors.
H7924.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only three times in the Bible, all in chapter 5 of the book of Daniel, at the time when King Nebuchadnezzar questions the wise men of Babylon about the interpretation of the mysterious writing on the palace wall. Daniel's intelligence is associated with complementary gifts — light (clarity), wisdom, and the ability to interpret dreams and solve riddles. It is an intelligence recognized even by pagans as extraordinary and superhuman.
H7924.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage shows that true intelligence — the kind that matters — comes from God and is manifested in the ability to discern divine will and interpret His signs. Daniel receives this gift only because he walks in faithfulness to God. It is a reminder that our spiritual understanding is always a gift, and it should serve to glorify God rather than exalt ourselves.

sens: To rise early from bed, at dawn
To start an action at the break of day, to undertake something without delay
To act with eagerness and zeal
To get moving, to depart quickly
H7925.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to get out of bed early, before the sun rises. It is the physical action of leaving one's bed at the moment when day is just beginning (Exodus 24:4: "he rose early; he built an altar").

2. The word also denotes the act of starting an action at the first hour of the day, with promptness. This is why it is said "to rise early" to undertake a task without delay: Abraham rises early to offer his son (Genesis 22:3), Moses at dawn to write and build.

3. This early rising often expresses eagerness, diligence, sometimes zealous obedience. Soldiers rise early to enter into battle (Joshua 6:12-15), the townspeople to witness the miracle accomplished during the night (Judges 6:28).

4. Figuratively, the word can evoke readiness and vigilance: to rise means to be active, alert, ready to act. It is the image of a person who does not sleep, who is on alert.
H7925.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁכַם (shakam) comes from a root that evokes the idea of rising or standing up. The word is formed to express the action of getting up early, particularly in the morning (שָׁכָר, shakar, denoting morning or dawn). In Hebrew, this morning action was associated with diligence and obedience, valued qualities. The verb is used in the Hiphil (causative or intensive form), emphasizing the action of rising voluntarily, deliberately.
H7925.emploi: The verb appears 64 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and among the prophets (Jeremiah, Isaiah, Hosea). It describes concrete actions: Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Joshua rise early to accomplish important tasks — to offer a sacrifice, flee, build an altar, lead the people. In Jeremiah, the word takes on a theological dimension: God says "I spoke to you early" to express His incessant call to repentance (Jeremiah 7:13, 25:3). The expression "to rise early" becomes a figure of eager obedience and spiritual vigilance.
H7925.portee: For the Christian, this verb reminds us of the value of diligence and prompt obedience to God. The patriarchs and servants of God rise early to fulfill His will, without delay or hesitation. It is also an invitation to spiritual vigilance: to be "standing" morally and religiously, ready to respond to God's call. Jeremiah's words show that God Himself acts consistently "early in the morning," an image of His patient love and renewed call to His people.

sens: Part of the human body between the neck and the arm
Part of the back or the entire back
What one carries on their shoulders (responsibility, burden, object)
H7926.detail:
1. The shoulder is the part of the body located between the neck and the arm. It is a very common and concrete word: Rebecca carries a jug on her shoulder (Genesis 24:45), Shem and Japheth put a cloak on their shoulders to cover their father (Genesis 9:23).
2. The word also denotes the back in general, or the dorsal region: "As soon as Saul turned his back to separate from Samuel" (1 Samuel 10:9) uses this term in the sense of the back of the body.
3. By extension, the shoulder represents what one carries, hence the idea of charge or burden. God "removes the shoulder" of the people from their burden (Psalms 81:7), and Isaiah announces that the yoke will be removed from the shoulder (Isaiah 10:27). It is a vivid image: to carry something on one's shoulders means to bear its weight.
H7926.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁכֶם (shékem) comes from a root that evokes the idea of carrying or lifting. It appears in several forms: a feminine variant (שִׁכְמָה, shikhmah) also exists. In Aramaic and later Hebrew, the same root has retained this physical sense of the shoulder. The underlying image is that of support: the shoulder is what carries, what supports a load.
H7926.emploi: The word appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in historical narratives and among the prophets. In ancient times, men carried objects on their shoulders (Exodus 12:34, where the Israelites carry their kneading troughs). The meaning is often very physical and concrete. But, gradually, the image becomes metaphorical: God removes the burdens from the shoulders of His people (Psalms 81:7), or the future king will bear the insignia of power on his shoulder (Isaiah 9:5). Likewise, the false gods that weigh heavily on the shoulders of the idolatrous people (Isaiah 10:27) symbolize moral and religious oppression.
H7926.portee: The shoulder in the Bible is a symbol of support and burden. When God promises to remove the burden from the shoulder, it is the assurance that He removes the weight of guilt and oppression. When the Messiah bears "the insignia of power" on His shoulder, it is the image of a just authority that rests entirely upon Him. This word reminds us that we carry burdens — sin, pain, responsibility — and that only God can remove them.

sens: city located in the mountain of Ephraim, in the valley between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim
political and religious center of Northern Israel
place of gathering and collective decisions for Israel
H7927G.detail:
1. Sichem is an important city in Canaan, established in a strategic valley of the mountain of Ephraim, about 54 km north of Jerusalem. It is a major urban center where civil and religious affairs of Israel took place (Joshua 24:1, where Joshua convenes all the people to renew the covenant with God).

2. Sichem is a hub of political power, particularly for the Northern Kingdom of Israel after the division: Jeroboam made it his first royal residence and built fortifications there (1 Kings 12:25).

3. The city is the scene of internal struggles and family dramas: it is here that Abimelech commits the massacre of his seventy brothers, inciting the inhabitants against their own interest (Judges 9:2-24), which shows how Sichem was a center of power and political influence capable of mobilizing the crowds.
H7927G.origine: The Hebrew name שְׁכֶם (shékhem) literally means "shoulder" or "back," an image likely evoking the geography of the city, nestled between two mountains like on shoulders. It is a geographically distinctive place: its position in a valley between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim makes it a natural passage and a strategic center in ancient Palestine.
H7927G.emploi: Sichem appears 43 times in the Hebrew Bible, first as a holy place where Abraham built an altar when he arrived in Canaan (Genesis 12:6). It becomes a center of covenant: it is here that Jacob buries foreign idols (Genesis 35:4) and where Joshua convenes Israel to renew its pact with God (Joshua 24:1-25). After the division of the monarchy, Sichem takes on major political importance for the Northern Kingdom, serving as the capital for Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:25). It also appears as a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7) and as a hub of rivalries: the account of Abimelech (Judges 9) makes it a place of conspiracies and political instability.
H7927G.portee: Sichem is more than just a geography: it symbolizes the key places where God establishes His covenants with His people. The gathering at Sichem under Joshua reminds Christians of the importance of collectively renewing their faith in God. At the same time, the dramas that unfold there (the massacre of Abimelech, political rivalries) teach that holy places do not guarantee obedience of the heart: a city can be at the center of God's promises and become the theater of human injustice.

sens: Son of Hamor, Hivite prince at the time of Jacob
H7927H.detail: Sichem is a character from the time of the Patriarchs, the son of the Hivite chief Hamor. He lives in the city that bears his name, in Canaan. His story, reported in Genesis 34, first shows him guilty of abducting and dishonoring Dinah, the daughter of Jacob (Genesis 34:2), then seeking to make amends by asking to marry her (Genesis 34:4). He addresses Dinah's father and brothers, imploring their grace and committing to pay the bride price (Genesis 34:11-12). Despite his attempts at reconciliation, he becomes a victim of the vengeance of Jacob's sons, who kill him along with his father Hamor and the men of their city.
H7927H.origine: The Hebrew name שְׁכֶם means literally "back" or "shoulder." This same word also designates the city of Sichem, reputed to be located in a valley between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. The name of the character and that of the city share the same etymology, suggesting an ancient link between the Hivite chief and the place where he lived.
H7927H.emploi: Sichem appears eleven times in the Bible, exclusively in the account of Genesis 33-34. He is first mentioned in Genesis 33:19, where Jacob buys a field from the sons of Hamor, the father of Sichem. The heart of the narrative (Genesis 34) recounts the abduction of Dinah by Sichem and the ensuing negotiations: Sichem asks his father to intervene (Genesis 34:8), then he directly addresses Dinah's brothers (Genesis 34:11-12), offering considerable gifts. Throughout these passages, Sichem appears not only as a powerful prince but also as a man torn between his desire and his guilt, seeking to correct his act through a peace initiative that fails in the face of Jacob's sons' anger.
H7927H.portee: The story of Sichem illustrates the consequences of sexual sin and the violation of honor. It also shows how cunning and deceit can serve vengeance: Jacob's sons accept a marriage in appearance, but do so only to massacre all the men of the city. This account invites the reader to reflect on the gravity of the wrong committed, the cost of failed restoration, and the spirals of violence that sin triggers.

sens: son of Gilead and grandson of Manasseh
ancestor of a family in the tribe of Manasseh
H7928G.detail: Sichem is a man from the tribe of Manasseh mentioned at the time of the census of the people of Israel after the exodus from Egypt. He is the son of Gilead and the grandson of Manasseh (Numbers 26:31). Through his descendants, the family of the Sichamites, he becomes an eponymous ancestor whose name is borne by a branch of the tribe of Manasseh, alongside the families of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Hepher, and Shemida (Joshua 17:2).
H7928G.origine: The name Sichem literally means "back" or "shoulder" in Hebrew. This sense of strength or bearing may reflect the importance of this ancestor in the constitution of the tribe. The word is related to the Hebrew root evoking the dorsal structure of the body.
H7928G.emploi: Sichem appears twice in the Bible, in the genealogical lists of the tribe of Manasseh. In Numbers 26:31, he is listed among the sons of Gilead during the census of the Israelites after the wilderness. In Joshua 17:2, during the allocation of territory to the tribes, his descendants—the family of the Sichamites—receive a portion of land in Canaan, alongside the other families of Manasseh. His name remains an identity marker for his lineage through the generations.

sens: son of Shemida, of the tribe of Manasseh
H7928H.detail: Sichem is a man from the tribe of Manasseh, mentioned only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 7:19. He is the son of Shemida and the brother of Achjan, Likchi, and Aniam. His name appears in the genealogy of Manasseh, one of the sons of Joseph, which places him in the time of Egypt and the wilderness.
H7928H.origine: The name Sichem literally means "back" or "shoulder." It is an ancient Hebrew name borne by several people in the Old Testament, the most famous being the city of Sichem in Canaan. This name evokes the idea of strength and solidity, qualities symbolized by shoulders.
H7928H.emploi: Sichem appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:19, where he is cited in the genealogical list of the descendants of Manasseh. This mention is part of an enumeration of the sons of Shemida, with no further detail about his life or deeds. He simply represents a link in the genealogical chain that connects the patriarchs to the later generations of Israel.

sens: the joint of the arm to the body, between the neck and the elbow
the part of the back that rises to this joint
the back, the upper body in general
the ability to bear a weight, to support a load
H7929.detail:
1. The shoulder is the joint where the arm attaches to the body — it is the joint of the shouldering. Job 31:22 asks that his shoulder "be torn from its socket," meaning dislocated: it is a curse where Job invokes a physical curse upon himself if he has committed the injustice he denies.
2. The shoulder also refers to the entire area of the back that bears this joint, along with the musculature and the shoulder girdle — this robust zone of the body.
3. By extension, the shoulder can refer to the back and the upper body in general, the part that bears the burden when something is loaded onto oneself.
4. Finally, the shoulder symbolizes strength and the ability to endure: "to place a burden on someone's shoulders" means to entrust a responsibility, which is why the gift of responsibilities is expressed by this gesture of weight placed on the shoulders.
H7929.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁכְמָה (shikhemah) is related to verbs that mean "to hold, to lift." The root expresses the idea of strength capable of carrying, of supporting a weight — the shoulder is literally "that which bears." In the Greek Old Testament, this word is generally translated by the Greek word ὦμος, which has exactly the same meaning.
