H7929.emploi: This word appears once in the Hebrew Bible in the provided contexts, in Job's speech where he defends himself against any injustice. Job 31:22 uses the image of the shoulder being torn off as an extreme curse: if I am guilty of oppression against the weak, may my body be dislocated, may my shoulder be torn off. It is a solemn oath that shows how much the shoulder symbolizes physical strength — to lose it is to lose the ability to act and to stand. The verb used expresses a violent separation, a tearing away.
H7929.portee: For the Christian, the shoulder evokes strength and responsibility. Jesus states: "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest." He himself takes upon his shoulders the burden of our sins. Understanding that the shoulder is the place of responsibility helps the reader grasp the biblical image of bearing burdens and the strength that corresponds to it.

sens: descendants of Shechem, son of Gilead
H7930.detail: 1. The Shechemites are the descendants of Shechem, a man from the tribe of Manasseh living during the time of Egypt and the wilderness. The name designates the family clan descended from this ancestor, following the biblical practice that links each clan to its founder. In Numbers 26:31, during the census of the Israelites before entering Canaan, Shechem is listed among the sons of Gilead with his brothers Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Chemidah, and Hepher — a group of six brothers who founded as many families in the tribe of Manasseh.
H7930.origine: The word comes from the proper name Shechem (שֶׁכֶם), which means "shoulder" in Hebrew. Shechem was the son of Gilead, himself the son of Machir and grandson of Manasseh. The suffix -i marks belonging to a group: the Shechemites are those who descend from Shechem. The name evokes an image of strength and a burden carried, recalling the stable foundations of an established family.
H7930.emploi: The Shechemites are mentioned only once in the Bible: in Numbers 26:31, during the great census of the Israelites in Moab after the forty years in the wilderness. They are listed among the families of Manasseh, alongside the Asrielites, Helekites, Abiezerites, Chemidahites, and Hepherites — six fraternal clans born from the six sons of Gilead. This census context shows that Shechem and his descendants formed an established and recognized household within the chosen people.

sens: To establish one's home in a place, to live there stably
To reside in a location, especially as a people or community
To remain, to stay in a state or condition
To find rest, to rest in a place
To occupy a space, to be present and established somewhere
To stay durably, to fix one's residence
H7931.detail:
1. To establish one's home in a place, to live there stably: this means to take possession of a territory and settle there durably. When God tells Jacob "stay in this land," he asks him to fix his dwelling there and live with his family. It is the idea of an anchored presence, not of passing through (Genesis 26:2).

2. To reside in a location, especially as a people or community: this meaning concerns mainly peoples and nations. Balaam sees Israel and says, "it is a people that dwells apart" — he recognizes that Israel has established itself as a distinct and formed group (Numbers 23:9).

3. To remain, to stay in a state or condition: the word also expresses persistence in a situation. The feet of the wayward woman in Proverbs "did not stay in her house" — she did not faithfully remain in her place (Proverbs 7:11).

4. To find rest, to rest in a place: to dwell also means to enjoy the calm and stability that a home brings. The psalmist wishes, "if only I had the wings of a dove, I would fly away and find rest" (Psalms 55:7).

5. To occupy a space, to be present and established somewhere: this is a broader usage, which includes the very presence of the divine. When God "will dwell" in Jerusalem or when His glory "rests" on the Tabernacle, it means that God establishes Himself and makes His dwelling (1 Chronicles 23:25, Exodus 24:16).
H7931.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "camping" or "settling down." It is related to words meaning "neighbor" and "peace," which shows the positive and secure image associated with stable dwelling. It is the same verb found in expressions like "the Shekinah" (the divine Glory that dwells), although this noun is derived. Aramaic retains the same root, attesting to the antiquity of the word in both Semitic languages.
H7931.emploi: The verb to dwell is extremely frequent in biblical Hebrew (over 124 occurrences) and appears in all literary genres. It first appears in the account of origins: man dwells in the garden, the patriarchs dwell in the promised land. It becomes crucial in the Torah to speak of Israel's settlement in Canaan after the Exodus. A prominent theological usage concerns the divine presence: God "dwells" in the Temple, His glory "rests" on the Tabernacle (Exodus 29:45, Exodus 40:35, 1 Kings 6:13). In the Psalms and Proverbs, the word is also used to denote personal rest or faithfulness to one's place. Among the prophets, to dwell refers either to the dwelling of nations or the hope that God will restore rest to Israel in its land.
H7931.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God seeks a dwelling among His people — this is the heart of the biblical story. From the Exodus to the Temple, through the Tent of Meeting, God wants to "dwell" in the midst of His people. This invites each believer to recognize their own life as the place where God desires to establish His presence. It is also a promise of stability and peace: whoever "dwells" with God finds rest and security.

sens: To establish someone in a place, to give them a place to live
To fix, install in a stable and lasting manner
To provide with a dwelling, a residence
H7932.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to establish or place someone somewhere so that they may dwell there. In Ezra 6:12, King Darius speaks of the God who "makes His name dwell" in this place — that is, who establishes His presence, His glory, in the temple of Jerusalem. The image is one of a stable installation: God's name does not pass away; it remains there.

2. Figuratively, the word denotes the action of giving asylum or refuge. In Daniel 4:21, the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky "made their dwelling" among the branches of the wonderful tree: the tree welcomes them, shelters them durably. The verb emphasizes not a fleeting passage, but an establishment, an installation.
H7932.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root expressing the idea of residing, settling. In biblical Aramaic (the language of Ezra and Daniel), this verb connects with ancient Hebrew through its family of words. The basic meaning is physical — to find a dwelling, to stay there — but it also applies to the divine: it is God who "makes His presence dwell," His glory, in a given place.
H7932.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Aramaic New Testament. In Ezra 6:12, it describes how God establishes His name in the rebuilt temple of Jerusalem: it is a solemn act of consecration, of divine presence. In Daniel 4:21, it characterizes the refuge that the royal tree offers to the creatures that shelter there. In both cases, the verb emphasizes a stable and voluntary installation, not a passing one.
H7932.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's presence is not fleeting or abstract. When God "makes His name dwell" somewhere, He chooses to establish Himself there, to manifest Himself durably. It is an act of love and commitment to His people. For the believer, this invites recognition of the places where God has chosen to dwell and to seek His face there with respect.

sens: One who lives near someone, in the same place or nearby
One who shares the same house or home
The inhabitant of a region or territory
One with whom one has regular relations or close connections
Figuratively: one who is close, in a moral or social sense
H7934.detail:
1. A neighbor is primarily one who lives near you, in the same village or city. Exodus 3:22 shows Egyptian women asking their neighbors for silver and gold vessels: these are women from the same neighborhood or household that they regularly interact with.
2. Sometimes the word refers to one who shares the house, who dwells under the same roof: "she who dwells in her house" (Exodus 3:22) specifies this notion of very close proximity.
3. An inhabitant is a neighbor in a broader sense — someone who lives in the same place. Isaiah 33:24 speaks of the inhabitants of Jerusalem who receive forgiveness: these are all those who dwell in the city.
4. The neighbor can also refer to neighboring peoples or nearby powers: Jeremiah 49:10 lists the neighbors of Edom who will perish with him, meaning the nations surrounding him.
5. In a figurative sense, the neighbor becomes one whom we associate with socially or morally: Proverbs 27:10 urges not to forsake your friend nor the neighbor of your father, meaning those who are close to you through daily life or family tradition.
H7934.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁכֵן (sha-khen) comes from the root שׁכן (sha-kan), which means "to dwell" or "to reside." A neighbor is literally "one who dwells nearby." This root evokes the idea of taking residence somewhere, of establishing oneself in a place. Words from the same family designate the tabernacle (the place where God dwells) or the Shekinah (the divine presence that dwells among His people).
H7934.emploi: This word appears about 20 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, the Wisdom Books, and the Prophets. It primarily designates neighbors in a concrete sense: the close women who name the newborn of Elimelech (Ruth 4:17), or those of Esau who will disappear (Jeremiah 49:10). It also applies to the neighboring nations of Israel, often in a context of conflict or judgment (Psalms 44:14, 80:7: the neighbors mock Israel). Finally, it can simply designate the inhabitants of a region (Isaiah 33:24) or regular life companions (Proverbs 27:10). The word often carries a tone of distance or separation — the neighbor is not an intimate friend, but someone external with whom one coexists.
H7934.portee: This word teaches us that those around us — our neighbors in the broadest sense — deserve attention and respect. The Law of Israel emphasizes care for the neighbor (Exodus 3:22 even shows Egyptians borrowing goods from one another). But the Psalms also show that neighbors can be critical or mocking (Psalms 44:14), reminding us that living in community requires discernment. Finally, this word invites the reader to see that one never exists alone: one is always a neighbor to someone else, which holds us accountable to others.

sens: Descendant of Zerubbabel whose descendants returned from exile with Ezra
Son of Schemaiah who repaired part of the wall of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah
H7935G.detail:
1. Shecaniah is a man's name from the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He is a descendant of Zerubbabel (the leader of the return from exile under the Persians). In 1 Chronicles 3:21, Shecaniah appears as one of the sons of Hananiah, himself a son of Zerubbabel, and he is the father of Schemaiah.

2. Through his descendants, Shecaniah is linked to the history of the return from exile and the reconstruction of Jerusalem. His son Schemaiah was a man of value who participated in the restoration of the city wall during the time of Nehemiah, as indicated by the genealogies detailed in 1 Chronicles 3:22.
H7935G.origine: The name Shecaniah means "he who dwells with Yahweh" (from the Hebrew "skn," to dwell, and "Yah," divine name). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God within it, expressing the idea that the bearer of the name dwells in the presence of God or enjoys His favor. This type of name was common among the Hebrews and always reminded them of the relationship of the people with their God.
H7935G.emploi: Shecaniah designates several characters of the same name in the genealogy of Judah and in the history of the return from exile. The two occurrences in the Segond 1910 (1 Chronicles 3:21-22) place him in the direct lineage of Zerubbabel, showing that his family played an important role among those returning from Babylonian captivity. His appearance in the genealogies emphasizes that, despite the exile, the continuity of the royal lineage of Judah was preserved. The Bible mentions several men bearing this name at different periods (in the time of Ezra, Nehemiah, and King Hezekiah), all figures of the post-exilic period linked to the restoration of Jerusalem.

sens: Priest who served during the time of King David
H7935H.detail: 1. Shecaniah is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, in the enumeration of the divisions of the priestly service established by David. He is designated as the head of the tenth division of priests (1 Chronicles 24:11), which means he led a group of priests who served in turn at the temple.
H7935H.origine: The name Shecaniah means "he who dwells with Jehovah" or "dwelling near the Eternal." It is composed of Hebrew roots evoking dwelling and the divine name. This name was borne by several characters at different times in Israel's history, particularly after the Babylonian exile, but this one was a priest during the time of David, long before.
H7935H.emploi: Shecaniah appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 24:11, in the list of the twenty-four priestly divisions that David and the priest Zadok organized. Each division served in turn at the temple. Shecaniah led the tenth of these divisions. This mention shows the importance of the priestly rotation system in Israel's worship and testifies to the place of this family among the temple servants.

sens: man of the people of Judah during the divided monarchy
H7935I.detail: Schecania is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 31:15. He lived during the time of the divided kingdom of Judah and Israel. According to this passage, he was a man placed under the direction of King Hezekiah in the priestly cities, responsible for faithfully distributing provisions to his brothers, whether they were great or small, according to their respective divisions.
H7935I.origine: The name Schecania means "he who dwells with the Lord" or "inhabitant with God." It is composed of two Hebrew roots: the word "dwell, inhabit" and the name of God (Yah). This type of theophoric name, which contains the divine name, was common in ancient Israel to express a blessing or belonging to God.
H7935I.emploi: Schecania appears only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Chronicles 31:15. He was a royal servant during the time of King Hezekiah of Judah, responsible for administering the distribution of provisions in the cities where the priests of the Lord resided. His role reflects the organizational system established to support the worship and servants of God in the temple.

sens: Homme de la famille de Zerubbabel qui revint d'exil avec Esdras
H7935K.detail: 1. Schecania is a character from the Exile and return period, mentioned only in Ezra 8:5. He is a descendant of Zerubbabel whose descendants returned from captivity in Babylon with the scribe Ezra to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. His name indicates that he was a man devoted to the Lord, as it literally means "he who dwells with God."
H7935K.origine: The name Schecania is composed of the Hebrew "shkn" (to dwell, to inhabit) and "Yah" (abbreviated name of God, Yahweh). It thus means "he who dwells with Jehovah" or "the Lord dwells there." This composition reveals the faith hope of Jewish families of that time: even in exile, God remained with His people.
H7935K.emploi: Schecania appears in the account of the return from exile under the leadership of Ezra. In Ezra 8:5, he is presented as a family leader whose descendants—three hundred men—return with Ezra from Babylon to Jerusalem to participate in the restoration of God's people. This return marks a decisive moment in Israel's history: the end of captivity and the renewal of the covenant with the Lord.
H7935K.portee: The return of Schecania and his family with Ezra symbolizes for every believer the possible restoration after trial and discipline. It is a reminder that even when God's people are far from Him, they can always return and be restored. The very name of Schecania—"he who dwells with the Lord"—encourages the reader to seek this intimacy with God despite difficult circumstances.

sens: Jewish figure from the time of exile and return
Father-in-law of Tobiah, the adversary of Nehemiah
H7935M.detail: 1. Schecania is a Jewish man who lived during the time of exile and the return to Jerusalem (around the 5th century BC). His name means "he who dwells with the Lord." He appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 6:18, where he is presented as the father of Arah and the father-in-law of Tobiah. 2. Schecania is primarily known as the father-in-law of Tobiah, this formidable adversary of Nehemiah who opposed the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem. In Nehemiah 6:18, we learn that several Jewish nobles were bound by oath to Tobiah because of this family alliance with Schecania, which demonstrated the political influence that Tobiah wielded in Jerusalem.
H7935M.origine: The Hebrew name Schecania (שְׁכַנְיָהוּ) literally means "he who dwells with Yah" or "dwelling with the Lord." It is composed of two elements: "shakan" which means "to dwell" or "to reside," and "Yah," the abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh. It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, expressing a relationship of closeness with God.
H7935M.emploi: Schecania appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 6:18, during the account of the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem. He is mentioned as the father of Arah and the father-in-law of Tobiah. This Arah is an influential figure in Jerusalem, and his marriage alliance with Tobiah gave him political weight. Thus, Schecania represents a man of the Jewish elite of his time, involved in the power networks of Jerusalem at the time of the return from exile.

sens: Priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
Descendant of Zerubbabel whose descendants returned from captivity with Ezra
Son of Jehiel, among the sons of Elam, who took a foreign wife during Ezra's time
Father of Shemaya who repaired a part of the wall of Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time
Son of Arah, father-in-law of Tobiah who opposed Nehemiah
Priest during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah
H7935O.detail: The name Schecania refers to several figures from the time of the Exile and the Return. In the biblical usage retained (Nehemiah 12:3), it refers to a priest who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel and whose name appears in the list of the heads of priests. The same name or a very similar one (Shebania) is borne by other figures from this period: a son of Jehiel among the sons of Elam who, during Ezra's time, had contracted a mixed marriage; a father of Shemaya involved in the reconstruction of the wall under Nehemiah; a father-in-law of Tobiah, the adversary of Nehemiah; and a priest who served under King Hezekiah. All these men played a role in the major events of the return from exile and the restoration of Jerusalem.
H7935O.origine: The name Schecania (in Hebrew Shekhanyahu) means "he who dwells with the Lord" or "dwelling with God," composed of two roots: one that evokes dwelling (shakan) and the divine name (Yah). It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, where the name expresses the relationship of the bearer to God. Several people bore this name during the return from exile, which shows its commonality among the faithful of that period.
H7935O.emploi: Schecania primarily appears in the records of the return from exile and the restoration of Jerusalem, mainly in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. The specific occurrence in Nehemiah 12:3 mentions him as a priest among those who returned with Zerubbabel. The same name or a variant (Shebania) also designates other important figures during this period: some were involved in religious reforms (notably the issue of mixed marriages during Ezra's time), others participated in the reconstruction of the wall or maintained ties with civil authorities. These various figures reflect the involvement of priests and leaders in the religious and civil life of restored Judah.

sens: To hire someone for a wage
To pay to obtain a service or work
H7936A.detail: 1. To hire means to engage someone to do a job in exchange for money. This is the most direct use of the word: one pays a person to work. In Ezra 4:5, the adversaries hire (engage) counselors for money to fight against the project of rebuilding the temple — they pay these men to act against the Jews.
H7936A.origine: The Hebrew root literally means "to close" or "to seal" (the agreement between two parties). It evokes the idea of concluding a fixed arrangement, a contract where each party fulfills their role: one "seals" the commitment in exchange for compensation. This link between the act of closing and that of concluding a deal reflects a common image: one "closes" a matter by paying money.
H7936A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 4:5. It describes the action of the enemies of the Jewish people who pay counselors to sabotage the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem. It is an act of corruption: they hire the influence and advice of men in positions of authority to thwart a project. The context shows that hiring someone means buying their compliance or assistance against a cause.
H7936A.portee: This passage reminds us that money can be used to divert people from justice and truth. Those who resort to corruption "hire" hearts and voices to hinder the work of God. For the believer, this serves as a warning: neither money nor influence can stop God's plan, even if men are willing to sell themselves.

sens: to hire someone for a wage
to pay to obtain someone's services
to acquire by money
to receive a salary or wages
H7936B.detail:
1. To hire someone means to engage them for work by paying an agreed salary. This is what David does when he hires Syrian mercenaries (2 Samuel 10:6). The master pays, the worker works.
2. More broadly, it means to pay to obtain someone's services: one hires a mercenary, one hires a priest, one hires a carpenter (2 Chronicles 24:12). Money creates the obligation to serve.
3. The word can also mean "to buy" in the sense of acquiring rights over someone: Leah says to Jacob, "I have bought you" in exchange for mandrakes (Genesis 30:16) — she has redeemed her right to the marital night.
4. In passive or reflexive form, it means "to hire oneself," "to earn one's salary": to accept a wage, to receive pay for one's work.
H7936B.origine: The Hebrew verb חִשְׂכַר comes from a root that evokes the idea of exchange: giving money to receive a service. The noun סָכַר (sakhar) denotes salary, wages, and derives from the same verb. It is a fundamentally economic concept: money changing hands creates an obligation of work or service.
H7936B.emploi: This verb appears seventeen times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical and legislative narratives. It is encountered in three main contexts: the hiring of mercenaries (2 Samuel 10:6, 1 Chronicles 19:6), the wages of labor or craftsmanship (2 Chronicles 24:12), and the more general notion of compensation or price (Genesis 30:16, where Leah "hires" Jacob with mandrakes). The word also appears in the context of privileges denied to the Ammonites and Moabites (Deuteronomy 23:4, Nehemiah 13:2), where being unable to hire a prophet becomes a curse. Isaiah uses it metaphorically: giving one's money to a worker who is not worth it (Isaiah 46:6).
H7936B.portee: This word reminds us that work has value and that those who work deserve their wages. It also shows how money structures social relationships and obligations: one cannot obtain the services of others without paying them justly. For the believer, this invites honoring the worker deserving of their wages, not scheming to avoid compensating work, and viewing wages as a right, not charity.

sens: To be under the influence of alcohol, to lose clarity of mind by drinking wine
To give alcohol to someone to make them drunk
To fill the soul or spirit with an intense emotion that overwhelms
To saturate, to completely soak as one intoxicates someone
H7937.detail:
1. To be under the influence of alcohol means to lose clarity due to wine. This is what happens to Noah in Genesis 9:21: "He drank of the wine, became drunk, and uncovered himself in the midst of his tent" — he drank so much that he lost awareness of his actions and found himself in a shameful position.
2. To give alcohol to someone to make them drunk is the deliberate action of someone pouring wine. David "intoxicated" Uriah with wine (2 Samuel 11:13) to befuddle him and execute his wicked plan.
3. To fill the soul or spirit with such a strong emotion that it overwhelms: "Eat, friends, drink, be intoxicated with love!" (Song of Solomon 5:1) — love acts like wine, it transports the heart and delights the mind.
4. To soak, to completely saturate, as when something is dipped in a liquid: God says, "I will intoxicate my arrows with blood" (Deuteronomy 32:42) — the arrows will be soaked, saturated with blood until completely filled.
H7937.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁכַר comes from a root that evokes drunkenness and loss of clarity. It belongs to the family of words related to intoxication and mental disturbance. The literal meaning of "to drink wine until intoxicated" quickly expands to the figurative: one can "intoxicate" someone with blood, anger, or love — that is, fill them, saturate them with a substance or emotion that transports them as wine would.
H7937.emploi: The verb appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mostly among the prophets. In the literal sense, it means to become drunk on wine (Noah in Genesis 9:21) or to make someone drink to intoxicate them (David with Uriah). In the figurative sense, God "intoxicates" the nations with His judgment: He fills them with fear and confusion (Jeremiah 51:7: "The nations have drunk of the wine" of Babylon and "have been like madmen"). Love also "intoxicates" those who experience it (Song of Solomon 5:1). The word plays on the image of loss of clarity and total filling: whether one is soaked with wine, blood, anger, or love, one is overwhelmed and beside oneself.
H7937.portee: This word reminds us that drunkenness — whether spiritual or carnal — removes self-control from a person and makes them vulnerable to judgment or seduction. For the believer, it invites vigilance and clarity, urging one to guard their heart rather than surrender it to passions that intoxicate. But it also shows that certain states — like love for God or divine judgment — can "intoxicate" the soul in a way that surpasses human reason.

sens: Agreed price for work, a service rendered
Compensation for a soldier or hired worker
Reward or result of an action, conduct
H7938.detail:
1. The wage is the price received in exchange for work: it is the pay an employer gives to someone who has served them. In Isaiah 19:10, the "hired workers" (literally "those who receive wages") are workers hired to work in the fields and textiles; their souls are saddened because Egypt is collapsing and they can no longer be paid.
2. The wage extends beyond mere money: it is the fruit of what one has sown, the consequence of one's conduct. Proverbs 11:18 contrasts the "deceptive gain" of the wicked with the "true wage" of the one who sows righteousness — the righteous receive a lasting, true reward, while the unjust only gather goods that evaporate like the wind.
H7938.origine: The Hebrew word sèkher comes from a root that means "to employ, to hire." It primarily denotes the price paid for work done, and then by extension the result or reward of an action. It is a concrete word, rooted in economic life: every worker knows what it is to receive their wage.
H7938.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 19:10, it refers to the hired workers in Egypt, those men who live from daily labor. In Proverbs 11:18, it takes on a broader and moral sense: the wage becomes the reward that naturally follows each conduct, whether just or unjust. The context of wisdom shows that the Bible does not see the wage as a mere commercial transaction, but as the expression of divine justice that rewards each according to their works.
H7938.portee: This word reminds the believer that every work deserves its just reward, and that God does not overlook the toil of those who work with integrity. More deeply, it invites reflection on true wealth: a wage earned through righteousness has lasting value, while goods obtained through deception melt away like snow. It is a word of hope for the honest worker.

sens: What one receives in exchange for work or service
Compensation, reward that God gives for works
Price paid for the use of something or transport
H7939.detail:
1. The wage is primarily the payment received for having worked: the Levites receive in share the tithes as "wages for the service" they render at the tabernacle (Numbers 18:31), and Jacob asks for a wage from Laban for his years of work (Genesis 30:28). It is the regular remuneration of one who rents out their labor or time.
2. God also promises a wage that is not money: Abram receives from Him a "great reward" (Genesis 15:1), and God says that works will have a wage (2 Chronicles 15:7). This is the notion of divine, moral retribution: the one who does good will receive their share, and the one who serves God will not labor in vain. Isaiah sees the Lord coming "and the wage is with Him" (Isaiah 40:10).
3. The wage can also refer to the price paid for a service rendered, such as the price of transport or the use of something — it is a broader material compensation than just daily work.
H7939.origine: The Hebrew word שָׂכָר comes from a root that means "to hire, to arrange an agreement." The word thus evokes the price set by agreement between the one who works and the one who pays. It belongs to the family of words that speak of exchange and contract: the wage is the fruit of a mutually agreed relationship between two parties.
H7939.emploi: This word appears 25 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the books of the Law and the prophets. It primarily denotes earthly wages: Jacob negotiates his wage with Laban (Genesis 30:28-33), the Law protects the wage of the worker (Deuteronomy 24:15), and even rented animals require a price (Exodus 22:15). But it quickly takes on a spiritual sense: God's promise to Abram (Genesis 15:1) transforms the wage into a metaphor for eternal reward. The Psalmist sees children as a wage from the Lord (Psalms 127:3). Among the prophets, the word emphasizes that God rewards each according to their deeds, a promise of hope or punishment (Isaiah 40:10, Malachi 3:5).
H7939.portee: This word teaches that work has dignity and that those who do it deserve their pay — a principle of justice that the Law firmly defends. But it also opens our eyes to a higher truth: God sees our works and rewards them. The Christian who serves never works in vain, even if the promised reward is not gold or silver, but the presence and favor of God.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi during the time of the united monarchy
Fourth son of Obed-Edom
Levitical gatekeeper in the service of the temple
H7940G.detail: Sacar is a man of the tribe of Levi mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:4. He is the fourth son of Obed-Edom, who was a gatekeeper of the temple during the reign of King David. Like his brothers Schemaiah, Jozabad, Joach, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar, and Peullethai, Sacar is part of the Levitical family responsible for guarding the gates of the sanctuary. His name means "wage" or "payment" in Hebrew, a common meaning in the Bible to denote rewards and compensations.
H7940G.origine: The name Sacar comes from the Hebrew root meaning "wage" or "payment" — the payment received for work. It is the same word found in 1 Samuel 4:4 and Genesis 30:18, where it refers to rewards or compensations. This theophoric or simply descriptive name was common among Levitical families during the time of David.
H7940G.emploi: Sacar appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 26:4, where he is named in the list of the sons of Obed-Edom. The latter was a Levite blessed with many sons by the Lord, all destined for service in the temple. The mention of Sacar among his brothers indicates that he shared with them the responsibilities of a gatekeeper, an important function in the organization of worship at the temple in Jerusalem during David's reign.

sens: Father of Ahiam, one of David's mighty men
Another name for Sharar
H7940H.detail:
1. Sacar is the father of Ahiam, a warrior of David. Ahiam is listed among the "mighty men" of the king (1 Chronicles 11:35), meaning the elite military leaders who formed David's inner circle and led his armies.
2. Sacar is another name given to the same person also called Sharar. This dual naming was common in ancient Israel: the same character could bear multiple names depending on the context or the tradition from which the account originated.
H7940H.origine: The name Sacar literally means "wage" or "payment" in Hebrew. It derives from the root that denotes the idea of a payment or reward for work. This name may evoke a child received as a reward or blessing. The existence of another name, Sharar, shows that this character is known under two variants in biblical traditions.
H7940H.emploi: Sacar appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:35, where he is identified as the father of Ahiam. This mention is part of the list of "mighty men of David," renowned warriors who served the king in the early years of his reign, particularly during the capture of Jerusalem and his campaigns to consolidate the kingdom. His son Ahiam is mentioned alongside other famous warriors, indicating that he had a respectable warrior stature.

sens: any fermented or distilled beverage that contains alcohol and intoxicates
alcoholic drink consumed during feasts and meals
drink that makes one drunk, that disturbs the senses
beverage forbidden to priests on duty and to Nazarites
strong liquor offered to the dying or the unfortunate
object of debauchery and moral disorder
H7941.detail:
1. Intoxicating drink is any alcoholic beverage capable of disturbing the senses and causing one to lose reason when consumed. It includes fermented wine, but also other stronger alcohols (Isaiah 24:9 speaks of bitter strong liquors for the drinker).
2. During festive meals and celebrations, it is consumed freely: in Deuteronomy 14:26, it is among the goods that can be purchased to rejoice before the Lord.
3. It is forbidden to priests when they enter the sanctuary, as it alters the judgment necessary for divine service (Leviticus 10:9).
4. It is forbidden to Nazarites, who dedicate themselves to God by a special vow (Judges 13:7: a woman pregnant with a Nazarite must abstain from it).
5. It can be given as medicine to those who suffer or to those who are dying, to relieve their pain (Proverbs 31:6: give strong liquors to him who is perishing).
6. It is often criticized as a source of drunkenness, debauchery, and distancing from God: the prophets denounce those who abandon themselves to it (Isaiah 5:11; 28:7).
H7941.origine: The Hebrew word shekar comes from a root that means "to be strong" or "to be powerful": the intoxicating drink is called so because it has a strength that acts on the body and mind. It is an ancient word that originally designated any alcoholic beverage other than ordinary wine, but in the biblical text, it often opposes or accompanies wine (yayin) to denote the entire range of fermented drinks that cause intoxication. The Greek word methē and the word methuon ("wine") translate this term in the Septuagint.
H7941.emploi: The word shekar appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Law (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in the prophets (Isaiah). It is often associated with wine in contexts of feasting and celebration, but also in prohibitions and warnings. It appears in three major contexts: (1) the ritual prohibition for priests on duty (Leviticus 10:9) and Nazarites (Numbers 6:3; Judges 13:4, 13:7); (2) lawful consumption during feasts and meals (Deuteronomy 14:26; Numbers 28:7, where it is included in libations); (3) the prophetic condemnation of drunkenness and debauchery (Isaiah 5:11; 28:7; Isaiah 29:9). Wisdom also warns against it: Proverbs 20:1 and 31:4 caution against the dangers of alcoholic drink for those who wish to remain self-controlled.
H7941.portee: This word teaches Christians that the Bible does not absolutely condemn alcoholic drink — it is blessed during the feasts of the Lord — but it warns seriously against drunkenness and loss of self-control. Priests and Nazarites, dedicated to God, must abstain from it: this is a sign that the service of God requires clarity of mind. For today's believer, it serves as a reminder that legitimate pleasures (eating, drinking, celebrating) must remain under the control of the Spirit, never under that of alcohol.

sens: Location on the northwestern border of Judah
H7942.detail: Shicron is a city or landmark located on the northern border of the territory of Judah. It was situated between Ekron (a city of the Philistines) and Jabneel, in a mountainous region. This is where the western border line of the tribal territory of Judah passed, as seen in Joshua 15:11.
H7942.origine: The name Shicron may derive from a Hebrew root evoking drunkenness or intoxication, but the exact etymology remains uncertain. It is a typical toponym (place name) found on maps of the borders of the ancient Near East, serving to precisely define territorial limits.
H7942.emploi: Shicron appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:11. It is included in the systematic description of the border of the territory of Judah, one of the passages where the text enumerates the cities and landmarks that marked the boundaries of the lands allocated to each tribe of Israel. This type of geographical list was essential for the distribution of the land after the conquest.

sens: The state of a person intoxicated by alcohol
Dizziness and loss of reason caused by an intoxicating drink
Figuratively, a form of judgment or divine punishment that disturbs understanding
H7943.detail:
1. Intoxication refers to the state of a person who has consumed too much alcohol: their senses are dulled, their judgment is obscured, and they lose control of their actions. In Ezekiel 39:19, the word evokes the physical intoxication of a feast of victims where blood will flow abundantly.

2. Among the prophets, intoxication becomes the image of divine judgment: God fills with confusion and disorientation those whom He strikes. In Jeremiah 13:13, God announces that He will fill the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the kings, and the priests with intoxication — not of alcohol, but of a spiritual intoxication that signifies their wandering and ruin. The people will understand nothing, blinded by punishment.

3. In Ezekiel 23:33, intoxication accompanies desolation: it is the bitter cup of judgment, which confuses and destroys the one who drinks it. The word paints a picture of total confusion, as if God removes all clarity from His people to leave them to their ruin.
H7943.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root שכר (šakar), which means "to be drunk." This root evokes the immediate effect of alcohol on the body and mind: stupor, loss of consciousness. The family of this word also includes the noun שכר (šekar), "intoxicating drink," and the adjective שכור (šakour), "drunk." The basic image is that of disturbance of the senses.
H7943.emploi: The word שִׁכָּרוֹן appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the prophets (Jeremiah and Ezekiel). In all cases, it carries a figurative meaning: God inflicts intoxication as punishment, to mislead the people and leave them defenseless. In Jeremiah 13:13, it is the judgment on Jerusalem and its leaders. In Ezekiel 23:33 and 39:19, intoxication is associated with destruction, desolation, and also with the feast of victims where blood becomes the drink of judgment. The word never simply refers to a drinking spree: it always speaks of confusion or wandering inflicted by God.
H7943.portee: The spiritual intoxication that God inflicts reminds the believer of a serious truth: divine judgment deprives man of his clarity and ability to act. It invites one not to mock God's punishment, nor to believe that one can escape His will while remaining in control. It also shows that intoxication — both that of alcohol and that of sin — distances one from God and prepares for ruin.

sens: Failure to adhere to what is right or proper
Act or omission contrary to the will of God
H7944.detail: 1. The word denotes a fault, a failure — something one should not do or something one should have done. In 2 Samuel 6:7, Uzzah touches the ark of the covenant without permission: this is a violation of the respect due to the holiness of God, an act that transgresses established boundaries. 2. This failure is not a mere innocent mistake, but a fault in the eyes of God — an action that offends His holiness and provokes His judgment. The death of Uzzah shows how serious this fault is in His eyes.
H7944.origine: The Hebrew word shal expresses the idea of a deviation from the desired order. Its exact meaning remains debated among scholars, but it clearly denotes an act that should not be committed — a fault or failure. In the Old Testament, faults against God are always serious: they disturb the holy relationship that should bind Him to His people.
H7944.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 6:7. It qualifies the act of Uzzah, who reached out to steady the ark of the covenant as it slipped from the cart. Although the gesture seems natural and protective, it crosses a forbidden boundary: only the Levitical priests had the right to touch the ark. This fault immediately provokes the anger of the Lord and the death of Uzzah.
H7944.portee: This account teaches the believer the seriousness of God's holiness and the importance of obeying His commandments, even when one believes they are doing the right thing. There is no room for improvisation or personal initiative in worship and relationship with God: the boundary exists for our good and to honor His majesty. The fear of the Lord begins with respect for His commands.

sens: State of material comfort and security
Peace of mind and absence of worry
Prosperous and happy life
H7946.detail:
1. Well-being primarily refers to a physical state of comfort and material security. It is living without lack, enjoying abundance. In Job 21:23, the man he speaks of "dies in the midst of well-being, peace, and happiness": he has everything he needs for his body and daily life.
2. It is also the inner state of tranquility and absence of worry, the feeling of having nothing to fear. One who enjoys well-being sleeps without fear, lives without anxiety.
3. By extension, it is a wholly prosperous and happy life, where everything goes according to the desires of the one who enjoys it — what Job describes as the experience of the wicked who prosper despite their impiety.
H7946.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means to be at peace, to be comfortable, without agitation. It evokes the image of a person who can rest, who does not have to strain to survive. It is the opposite of anxiety and servitude. In Greek, this word is rendered by a term meaning "safe tranquility."
H7946.emploi: This word appears only once in biblical Hebrew, in Job 21:23. It is a rare term used to describe the envied fate of the prosperous wicked. Job uses it to paint the existence of one who, in his eyes, has no reason to believe in God and yet enjoys a life filled with ease and happiness. It is an image that raises the great question that Job poses: why does the wicked prosper? Well-being is thus presented here as a false security or deceptive prosperity.
H7946.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on true Christian security. Material well-being and tranquility of circumstances can be deceptive: the man who has everything believes he has all he needs and closes his heart to God. The Christian is called to seek a deeper peace, based not on external abundance but on trust in God and the awareness of his salvation.

sens: Joined, attached to one another
United in a stable and functional manner
H7947.detail:
1. The word describes two tenons (the protrusions of a board) that are attached together, forming a single solid piece. It is the concrete image of a joint, an assembly: in Exodus 26:17, the two tenons of each board of the tabernacle are "joined" together, ensuring the coherence of the structure.
2. More broadly, "joint" expresses the idea of a stable and functional union: the elements are not merely brought close together, but linked in such a way as to form a coherent and solid whole, capable of fulfilling its function (here, supporting the tabernacle).
H7947.origine: The Hebrew root literally means "to assemble" or "to join together." It expresses the action of bringing things closer by attaching them, as one joins construction elements so that they hold together. The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of woodworking and carpentry.
H7947.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Exodus (26:17 and 36:22), and always in the passive voice ("to be joined"). Both passages identically describe the boards of the tabernacle: each has two tenons that are "joined" together. It is the same event reported twice (the first time Moses receives the command, the second time he executes it). The word is entirely technical and architectural: it denotes the result of precise assembly work.
H7947.portee: For the believer, this architectural detail reveals the order and rigor that God demands in the construction of the tabernacle. The precise joining of the tenons symbolizes the importance of unity and spiritual solidity: just as the boards of the tabernacle are firmly joined so that the structure stands, believers are called to unity in faith.

sens: Vertical piece that connects or frames other elements
Structural bar of a piece of furniture or construction
H7948.detail:
1. A montant is a piece of wood (or metal) placed vertically to join and support other elements. In the bases of the Temple that Solomon built, the montants connected the panels to each other at the corners, thus forming a solid structure (1 Kings 7:28).
2. These montants also served as a frame or border on which ornaments could be placed. On the panels between the montants appeared lions, oxen, and cherubim, while the montants themselves bore festooned ornaments (1 Kings 7:29).
H7948.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "side" or "to join." It literally designates what binds together, what connects the parts of a structure. It is a technical term in the vocabulary of construction and furniture in the Old Testament.
H7948.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the context of the detailed description of the bronze bases that Solomon had made for the Temple. These bases were refined works of cabinetry and foundry, intended to support the purification basins. The two uses (1 Kings 7:28 and 7:29) precisely describe how the montants structured these bases and served as support for the decorations.
H7948.portee: This word reminds us that in the construction of the Temple, God required care, precision, and beauty even in the humblest details. Every element — even a simple montant — contributed to the harmony and solidity of the whole, reflecting the order that God brings to all creation.

sens: To fall as snow, to snow
H7949.detail: 1. The verb means that snow falls, or that an area is covered with snow. The image is that of white rain descending from the sky and covering the earth. In Psalms 68:15, the psalmist says that the earth "became white like the snow of Tsalmon," expressing a spectacular transformation of the landscape: an entire mountain becomes so white with snow that it shines like a spotless mantle.
H7949.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁלג (shalag) comes from a root that designates snow itself (שׁלג, shalèg). It is a concrete word of nature: it paints the image of a white and silent fall that transforms the visible world. Snow, in the Old Testament, often symbolizes purity (see the contrast between the red of sin and the whiteness like snow in Isaiah 1:18).
H7949.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 68:15, in a poetic context where the psalmist celebrates the divine power that scattered kings. He uses the image of snow to express the dazzling whiteness of the mountain of Tsalmon, a mountain famous for its snows. It is a hapax (unique word), which testifies to the rare and solemn character of this verb in biblical language.
H7949.portee: This word reminds us that snow, although ordinary in nature, was remarkable enough in the Holy Land to inspire the poets of Scripture. It becomes an image of purity and beauty: it symbolizes the transformation that God works in repentant hearts, made white by His grace.

sens: White crystalline precipitation that falls from the sky when it is cold
Dazzling whiteness, visible purity
Cold, frost, harshness of the climate
H7950.detail:
1. Snow is frozen rain that falls in white flakes; the Bible mentions it mainly in the mountains (Jeremiah 18:14) or in harsh winter (Proverbs 31:21). It is a rare phenomenon in Palestine, hence its use to describe something remarkable.

2. The whiteness of snow becomes the image of total purity: it is seen in leprosy, which whitens the skin "like snow" (Exodus 4:6), or more magnificently when God promises to make sins "white as snow" (Isaiah 1:18), a symbol of complete forgiveness.

3. Snow also represents biting cold, the winter trial: a wise woman does not fear snow for her house because she has well protected it (Proverbs 31:21), an image of preparation and vigilance in the face of difficulties.
H7950.origine: The Hebrew word שלג (shéleg) comes from a root that designates what is white and cold. A very similar Aramaic form תלג (telag) shows the antiquity of the word in Semitic languages. The image of whiteness dominates: snow is "what is white par excellence."
H7950.emploi: The word appears 20 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in wisdom poetry (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and in the prophets. Job mentions it as a natural phenomenon that one observes (Job 37:6, Job 38:22); the Psalms integrate it into God's governance over creation (Psalms 147:16, Psalms 148:8). But its richest use is metaphorical: the whiteness of snow serves to describe both disease (leprosy) and God's divine purification of sin (Isaiah 1:18, Psalms 51:9), creating a striking contrast between visible evil and invisible forgiveness.
H7950.portee: Snow teaches two things to the believer. First, it shows the sovereignty and majesty of God over creation, who sends His chastisements and blessings according to His orders (Psalms 148:8). Secondly, its radical whiteness offers the sinner the most powerful image of forgiveness: no matter how black your guilt may be, God can make it white as snow (Isaiah 1:18), a promise of total and visible restoration.

sens: State of calm and absence of trouble
Tranquility and security of the heart
Prosperity and material well-being
State of rest and quietness
H7951.detail:
1. The state of calm and absence of trouble: it is primarily the rest of body and mind, when nothing disturbs (Job 3:26: "I have no tranquility, no peace, no rest").
2. Tranquility and security of the heart: it is enjoying an inner serenity, feeling that one has nothing to fear (Psalms 122:6: "May those who love you enjoy rest").
3. Prosperity and material well-being: when everything is going well, when one lives in safety without lack or threat (Job 12:6: "There is peace under the tent of the plunderers").
4. The absence of conflict or judgment: it is also living without being troubled, at peace with one's situation (Jeremiah 12:1: "Why do all the treacherous live in peace?").
H7951.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁלָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of rest and stability. The cognate Aramaic form שְׁלֵה means "to be safe." The word belongs to the same semantic family as שָׁלוֹם (shalom, "peace"), although it designates more the state of one who enjoys peace rather than peace itself. It is a verb that describes a condition rather than an action.
H7951.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of wisdom and lamentations. Job uses it to express his agitation and absence of inner peace (Job 3:26), and also to describe the apparent rest of the wicked despite their impiety (Job 12:6). In Psalm 122, it is a wish for rest and prosperity for Jerusalem. Jeremiah uses it in the sense of the unjust prosperity of the wicked who live without apparent punishment. In Lamentations, it refers to the false security of enemies at the time of divine judgment. The word oscillates between a positive reality (true rest) and a deceptive reality (false security of the wicked).
H7951.portee: This word teaches that true peace is not primarily the absence of external troubles, but a state of the heart. For the believer, it is a call to seek peace in God rather than to marvel at the false security of the wicked. It reminds us that only God can give lasting peace, and that prospering far from Him is an illusion.

sens: Lead astray, give false hope
Be negligent, inattentive to one's duties
H7952.detail:
1. To deceive someone is to deliberately lead them to believe something that is not true or to hope for something that cannot be fulfilled. In 2 Kings 4:28, the woman says to the prophet Elisha: "Did I not say: Do not deceive me?" — she implores him not to make her believe in a son if it is not true, for a deceived hope would be more painful than the absence of hope.
2. To be negligent is to relax one's attention or effort towards what one should do: neglecting one's work, responsibilities. In 2 Chronicles 29:11, King Hezekiah reproaches the Levites for being "negligent" in the service of the temple; he calls them to cease this inattentiveness and to fully dedicate themselves to their function.
H7952.origine: This Hebrew root expresses the idea of error or deviation from the truth. It is related to the notion of straying from what is right or reliable. The Aramaic שְׁלָה (shela) means "error," which confirms the fundamental meaning: deception or negligence is a form of deviation, a way of straying from the right path. The verb can take two forms — passive ("to be deceived") or causative ("to deceive others") — depending on the context.
H7952.emploi: This Hebrew verb appears only twice in the Old Testament, in these two usages of the Segond. In 2 Kings 4:28, it carries the active meaning of "to deceive" (to give false hope); in 2 Chronicles 29:11, it takes the meaning of "to be negligent" (weakness in action). These two meanings are actually close: deception is a form of betrayal of trust, and negligence is a way of abandoning one's duty — in both cases, one drops or misleads.
H7952.portee: This word reminds us that faithfulness and honesty are essential values at the heart of the relationship with God and with others. Being negligent in God's service is, in a way, to deceive Him, as it denies Him the attention He deserves. It prompts us to examine our sincerity and commitment to what we promise.

sens: Slice, abruptly interrupt
Tear away, forcibly remove
Deny, deprive someone of something
H7953.detail:
1. The verb שָׁלָה describes the action of cutting or slicing, like cutting a thread or a rope. In Job 27:8, it refers to cutting the thread of life — a striking image to say that God abruptly ends existence.
2. The word evokes the idea of tearing away or extracting, removing something or someone from their situation. It is to forcibly take away, to remove without care.
3. In the biblical context, to cut means to deprive someone of what sustains them: to deprive of life, protection, hope. God "cuts" the soul of the one who refuses to listen to Him, meaning He takes it away from them.
H7953.origine: The verb שָׁלָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of extracting, pulling towards oneself, or separating. The basic image is that of a thread being cut: one divides, interrupts, or removes. It is a rare word in Hebrew, belonging to the family of action and separation verbs.
H7953.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 27:8, in a context of divine judgment. Job describes the wicked confronted with the question: "What hope remains?" When God cuts the thread of his life and takes away his soul, all hope disappears. The usage emphasizes the irreversibility of judgment and the absolute sovereignty of God over life. The context of Job, a meditation on suffering and divine justice, gives the word its significance: to cut is to bring a definitive end.
H7953.portee: This word reminds us that human life is fragile, fragile like a thread. It remains entirely in the hands of God, who disposes of it according to His justice. This should inspire the believer with a respectful fear and a trusting dependence on the Creator, rather than a hope based on the rejection of God.

sens: Be in a state of rest, without agitation
Enjoy a peace of mind, free from worries
Live in safety, without fear of danger
H7954.detail:
1. The word describes a physical rest, a state of relaxation away from all agitation. It is the situation of Nebuchadnezzar in his palace: he is not in motion, not in action, but established in a place where he rests (Daniel 4:4).
2. Beyond physical rest, the word evokes tranquility of mind, the absence of concern or anxiety. When one is quiet, one is not troubled by worries or threats.
3. To be quiet also means to live in safety, protected from danger and instability. One can rely on it, one can count on a stable future.
H7954.origine: The Aramaic word שְׁלֵה comes from the root שׁלה (shalah), which means "to prosper" or "to extend in peace." The Hebrew carries the same meaning: it is a verb that denotes the state of one who enjoys prosperity and security. The family of words revolves around the idea of letting go, releasing tension, hence this feeling of ease and rest.
H7954.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Aramaic in the book of Daniel. Daniel 4:4 puts it on the lips of King Nebuchadnezzar who describes his own happiness: he lived quietly in his house, happy in his palace. It is the state of one who possesses power, wealth, and the absence of threat — a false security that precisely precedes the humiliation that God will send him. This moment of tranquility is the calm before the storm.
H7954.portee: This unique occurrence of "quiet" in Aramaic reminds us that true peace does not rest on material goods, power, or the temporary absence of problems. Nebuchadnezzar believes he is secure while God is about to overthrow him. This invites us to seek peace not in circumstances, but in a right relationship with God.

sens: Son of Judah and Bathshua, the youngest of Judah's three living sons
Eponymous ancestor of the Shelanite clan in the tribe of Judah
H7956.detail:
1. Shelah is the third son of Judah and Bathshua, born at Chezib (Genesis 38:5). He is the youngest of Judah's three living sons, as his two older brothers, Er and Onan, died in the land of Canaan (Genesis 46:12). Judah promises Tamar, widow of Er, to give her to him in marriage when Shelah is grown, but this promise is never fulfilled (Genesis 38:11, 14, 26).
2. Shelah is also the head of the family from which the Shelanite clan descends, one of the clans of the tribe of Judah (Numbers 26:20). His name appears in the genealogies of the tribe as the founder of a distinct lineage, alongside that of Perez and Zerah.
H7956.origine: The Hebrew name Shelah (שֵׁלָה) literally means "a petition" or "a request." It evokes the idea of supplication or request. Shelah is the youngest son of Judah, and his story is set in the context of the genealogies of the patriarch Judah, from whom the kingship of Israel will descend.
H7956.emploi: Shelah is mentioned eight times in the Bible, primarily in the account of Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38). He first appears at his birth (Genesis 38:5), then in the marriage promise made to Tamar (Genesis 38:11, 14, 26), where Judah ultimately refuses to give him to her. He is then found in the genealogical lists (Genesis 46:12 and Numbers 26:20), where he is named among the sons of Judah and where it is noted that his descendants form the Shelanite clan. A final mention in 1 Chronicles 4:21 confirms his place in the genealogy of Judah.

sens: Jet of fire that rises from a hearth
Intense light and heat that consumes
Passionate or divine fervor
H7957.detail:
1. A flame is the visible fire that rises and burns: it is the image of fire in action, both destructive and illuminating. In Ezekiel 21:3, God announces a fire that devours trees, and His burning flame that will not be extinguished — the word here denotes fire in its most visible and terrifying manifestation.
2. By extension, the flame represents a force that consumes and destroys: it embodies the idea of inevitable destruction. In Job 15:30, the unfortunate cannot escape the darkness, and the flame will consume his offspring — it embodies divine judgment that annihilates.
3. The flame also becomes the image of fervor, intense passion, whether celestial or earthly. In Song of Solomon 8:6, love is compared to the ardors of fire, to a flame of the Lord — the word then reveals a passion that burns, unquenchable, divine.
H7957.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁלְהֶבֶת (shalevet) comes from a root that evokes fire that rises and spreads. It belongs to the family of Hebrew terms designating fire in its most visible forms: the flame is fire in its momentum, where it consumes and illuminates. The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to emphasize the devastating or passionate aspect of fire.
H7957.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 15:30, it describes the fire of divine judgment that consumes the children of the wicked. In Ezekiel 21:3, it designates the burning flame of the prophetic fire that God will ignite, a fire that devours everything and will not be extinguished. In Song of Solomon 8:6, the context changes radically: the flame becomes the poetic image of passionate love, an ardor of the Lord that burns like fire. The word always retains its sense of intense and irresistible force, but shifts from judgment to love depending on the context.
H7957.portee: The word flame reminds us of the terrifying power of divine judgment, which does not tolerate sin: it is an image that invites us to take seriously the holiness of God. But it also speaks to us of divine love as a burning passion that consumes, unquenchable — a love that seizes and transforms us. Between threat and comfort, this word confronts us with the irresistible force of God, whether it be righteous anger or tender fervor.

sens: Small migratory bird with speckled plumage
Miraculous food sent by God to the people of Israel in the desert
H7958.detail:
1. The quail is a small bird that travels in large flocks during its migrations. In the Sinai desert, it moves close to the ground and can be easily captured. During the exodus from Egypt, the Lord sent myriads of them that covered the camp: "there were about two cubits above the surface of the earth" (Numbers 11:31). The Israelites gathered large quantities and spread them out to dry around the camp (Numbers 11:32).
2. In the history of the desert, the quail is an act of divine compassion. When the people complained about lacking meat, the Lord sent these birds as a direct response to their requests: "At their request, He brought quails" (Psalms 105:40). It symbolizes God's providence in nourishing His people, alongside the heavenly manna.
H7958.origine: The Hebrew word שְׂלָו specifically designates this migratory bird. The quail is a biblical symbol of divine protection and God's response to the needs of His people. It is a real animal, known since antiquity, that the Egyptians and the peoples of the Levant were familiar with and consumed.
H7958.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in connection with the events of the desert. Exodus 16:13 recounts the first miraculous arrival of the quails, which covered the camp. Numbers 11:31-32 describes a second spectacular intervention: the Lord causes a wind to blow from the sea that brings quails in such great numbers that they accumulate to two cubits high. The people gather so much that the minimum collected is ten homers (a huge measure). Psalms 105:40 recalls this event as proof of God's care for His people. All these uses are related to God's faithfulness to Israel.
H7958.portee: The quail teaches that God responds to the needs of His people with generosity, even in the most arid circumstances. It reminds us that faith can rely on divine protection and provision, not just once, but repeatedly. It is a reason for thanksgiving and trust in the One who nourishes and sustains.

sens: State of one who feels safe, without danger or fear
Well-being and peace of mind, confidence in one's stability
False assurance, carelessness in the face of real risks
H7959.detail:
1. Security describes the state of one who feels protected and safe from danger, who has nothing to fear. The psalmist uses it to express his absolute confidence: "I said in my security: I shall never be moved!" (Psalms 30:7), showing how he believed himself to be unshakeable and tranquil.
2. More broadly, the word denotes the well-being and tranquility that accompany this confidence: an inner peace, a feeling of having set aside all worry. It is the ease of one who can live without anxiety.
3. Security can also be dangerous when it becomes blind carelessness, a naive trust that ignores real threats. The context of Psalm 30 bears witness to this: the psalmist firmly believed in his stability, but the Lord humbled him, revealing that his security was fragile and deceptive.
H7959.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁלוּ (shalu) etymologically designates the state of one who is "at rest," whose root evokes the idea of sitting or dwelling in peace. It belongs to a family of words expressing calm and the absence of trouble. In biblical Hebrew, this notion of carnal security often contrasts with true trust in God, as it relies on circumstances rather than faith.
H7959.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Psalms 30:7). It is used to express the deceptive confidence of the psalmist before his fall: convinced of his invulnerability and lasting prosperity, he does not realize that his security is illusory and dependent on divine favor. The context reveals that this false assurance always precedes a spiritual crisis or correction from the Lord.
H7959.portee: This word teaches believers the dangers of self-reliance and temporal well-being detached from God. The psalmist shows us that the security we find in our circumstances, our wealth, or our apparent stability can suddenly collapse. It is a call to place our trust in God rather than in the fragile things of this world.

sens: Failure to fulfill a duty, fault due to inattention or neglect
Deficiency, absence of what should be present
Reprehensible or blameworthy word or act
H7960.detail: 1. Negligence is primarily the forgetting of duty, the lack of attention to what one should do. In Ezra 4:22, the king orders that one should "take care not to be negligent in this matter": it concerns not allowing the temple work to stop, not relaxing the effort. It is also the absence or lack: in Ezra 6:9, the priests will receive the necessary things "without lacking", meaning that there should be no deficiency. 2. The word sometimes takes on the meaning of what is defective, blameworthy: in Daniel 3:29, speaking "ill" of the God of the three young men is to utter a blasphemy worthy of punishment. 3. By extension, it is a fault or defect in a person: in Daniel 6:4, Daniel's enemies seek an "occasion", a "thing to accuse him of", but they do not find it because he is faithful and "no fault or anything bad is found in him."
H7960.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁלוּ comes from a root that expresses the idea of slipping, deviating, missing the goal. It belongs to the family of Hebrew words denoting absence, forgetfulness, or breach of duty. The fundamental meaning is that of a failure: to leave something aside, not to accomplish what is expected.
H7960.emploi: This word appears four times in the Old Testament, only in the Aramaic texts (Ezra and Daniel), which reflects the language spoken during the time of exile and return. In Ezra 4:22, it refers to administrative negligence that would interrupt the temple work. In Ezra 6:9, it signifies the absence or lack of necessary resources for sacrifices. In Daniel 3:29 and 6:4, it takes on the meanings of reproach, blame, or moral defect. The legal and political context (accusations, royal orders) gives the word a serious tone: it is a serious failure in the eyes of the law.
H7960.portee: This word reminds believers of the importance of faithfulness and attention in fulfilling God's will. Like Daniel, who offered no ground for accusations, the Christian is called to be vigilant and not to relax in service: a watchful heart prevents sin. It is also an exhortation to constancy: the temple sacrifices should not "lack" resources, just as the prayer and obedience of the believer should not "lack."

sens: State of one who lives without agitation, in rest and peace
Feeling of well-being, prosperity, and contentment
Character of a place or a people that is safe, without fear of enemies
Lack of vigilance, carelessness that can become dangerous
H7961.detail:
1. Peaceful primarily describes one who lives without agitation or trouble: a person at rest, without immediate worry. Job was peaceful when God suddenly seized him by the neck (Job 16:12), showing that he was at peace before the shock.

2. The word also means happiness and well-being, a happy prosperity: one who lives in well-being, who accumulates wealth and joys (Job 21:23; Psalms 73:12). It is the state of one whom everything seems to favor.

3. Peaceful applies to a country or a people living in safety, without enemies at the gates: the land of Jeremiah 49:31 is peaceful, without defenses, inhabited alone. This is also the case for the fertile pastures of 1 Chronicles 4:40, which offer peace.

4. The word can point to a dangerous carelessness: one who lives peacefully may be vulnerable, like this nation that naively trusts in its security (Jeremiah 49:31). The greed of the wicked (Job 20:20) shows that tranquility can mask limitless covetousness.
H7961.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁלֵו (shâlêv) comes from a root expressing the idea of rest, calm, and absence of fear. It is related to the notion of solidity and stability: one who is peaceful remains in place, without being agitated. Its basic image is that of a person or land that can finally breathe, free from turmoil.
H7961.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Poetic and Prophetic books. It describes very different states: the peace of a fertile region (1 Chronicles 4:40), the temporary rest before suffering (Job 16:12), the well-being of the prosperous (Psalms 73:12; Job 21:23), or the camouflaged insecurity of a nation (Jeremiah 49:31). Job uses the word to contrast lost tranquility with sudden rupture; the Psalms and the Prophets use it to question whether earthly tranquility is truly secure. The context shows that human tranquility is fragile and can mask either a blessing or a dangerous illusion.
H7961.portee: This word invites the reader to a joyful vigilance: peaceful tranquility is a gift from God, but it should not create an illusion of definitive security or spiritual carelessness. It reminds us that our true rest does not reside in the absence of earthly troubles, but in trust in God. To be peaceful in faith is to accept the trials He allows, knowing that they do not destroy the true well-being of the heart.

sens: State of calm, absence of trouble
Safety, situation without danger
Inner peace, rest of the soul
Material prosperity and well-being
Carelessness, lack of vigilance
H7962.detail:
1. Tranquility is primarily a state of calm: the absence of noise, conflict, or disturbance. This is what the psalmist wishes for within the walls of Jerusalem (Psalms 122:7), as if the physical peace of the places brings serenity.

2. It also denotes safety, the feeling of being protected from danger: among the foolish who refuse warning, this false security leads them to ruin (Proverbs 1:32), for they believe themselves safe while danger threatens them.

3. It is also an inner peace, a tranquility of the soul: better is a little with peace than much with strife (Proverbs 17:1), for what matters is the quietness of the heart.

4. Tranquility accompanies prosperity: God spoke to Israel in times of abundance (Jeremiah 22:21), when the people enjoyed wealth and well-being.

5. It can also be a dangerous carelessness: Sodom lived in abundance and careless security (Ezekiel 16:49), ignoring the impending disaster and closing their eyes to injustice.
H7962.origine: The Hebrew word shalvah comes from a root that means "to be tranquil" or "to be at ease." It is linked to the image of rest, the absence of agitated movement. The Aramaic has a very similar word (shelevah), showing that this concept is ancient in both Semitic languages. The root also expresses the idea of a movement that calms down, like waters that settle.
H7962.emploi: This word appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the wisdom books (Proverbs) and the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel). In Proverbs, it qualifies a state that must be sought or that one can lose. Among the prophets, especially in Ezekiel and Daniel, tranquility becomes a dangerous carelessness: it is the state of one who does not see divine judgment approaching. Daniel 8:25 shows a leader who destroys "those who lived peacefully," revealing that this tranquility can be illusory. The meaning thus oscillates between a good to cultivate and a trap to avoid.
H7962.portee: For the believer, this word invites discernment between two types of tranquility: that which God gives, based on trust and justice, and that which the world offers, which can mask sin and indifference to God. It is a call to seek true peace, rooted in obedience to God, rather than to be lulled by a false security that ignores divine judgment.

sens: State of calm and well-being, free from worry or trouble
Material prosperity and stability of life
Tranquility of one who enjoys peace and abundance
H7963.detail:
1. Happiness here refers to a state of inner serenity, the absence of torment or anxiety. It is the peace of one who knows no agitation or disorder in their life. In Daniel 4:27, the prophet promises the king that his happiness "may be prolonged" if he abandons his sins and practices righteousness.
2. This happiness also has a dimension of concrete prosperity: material abundance, stability of power and fortune. It is the well-being of the powerful who reigns without trouble and whose affairs prosper.
3. The central idea is that of maintained or lost tranquility: one possesses happiness only as long as they do not undergo trial, deprivation, or interruption of their prosperity. That is why it is necessary to "practice righteousness" to "prolong" it — it is a fragile condition, subject to the will of God.
H7963.origine: The word is Aramaic *shelvah*, borrowed or parallel to the Hebrew *shalvah* (H7962), which comes from a root expressing the idea of being stretched out or extended without constraint, thus resting quietly. The Hebrew family also includes *shalev* ("in peace"), which reinforces this image of relaxation and absence of disturbance. It is a very rare word in the Bible.
H7963.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:27, in Daniel's speech to King Nebuchadnezzar. It is a conditional promise: if the king practices justice and mercy, his happiness "may be prolonged." The context is that of divine warnings addressed to a powerful but proud monarch, who risks losing his well-being and power. The word emphasizes that the king's prosperity is not guaranteed forever, but depends on his obedience to God's justice.
H7963.portee: This verse teaches the believer a fundamental truth: happiness and stability of life do not depend solely on wealth or power, but on justice and compassion. True happiness is fragile and conditional — one must "prolong" good by walking in righteousness. For the Christian, it is a call to seek first the kingdom and the righteousness of God, rather than prosperity for its own sake.

sens: the act of sending someone away, of dismissing them
the gift given to someone upon parting
the abandonment, the renunciation of something
H7964.detail: 1. Dismissal is primarily the act of sending someone away: one dismisses them or frees them from their presence. Zipporah, Moses' wife, was sent back to her father Jethro (Exodus 18:2), which means she left Moses, probably temporarily, returning to her family. 2. This dismissal is often accompanied by a gift, a present offered to the one being dismissed to honor the separation or facilitate their journey. Pharaoh gave Gezer as a dowry — as a parting gift — to his daughter when marrying her to Solomon (1 Kings 9:16), which solidified their alliance through this generous exchange. 3. In a broader sense, the word can also mean abandonment or renunciation of something: Micah 1:14 announces that the city of Moresheth-Gath will be abandoned, lost — one will have to renounce it — as the threat approaches.
H7964.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root שׁלח (shalach), which means "to send, to launch, to release." It has a strong connection with the idea of ending a relationship or attachment. The forms of the word often express the action of breaking a bond or separating: a divorce, a dismissal, a discharge. The concept of "farewell gift" or "parting present" is characteristic of ancient Near Eastern customs, where significant separations (alliances, marriages, departures) were marked by material exchanges.
H7964.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 18:2, it describes Zipporah's return to her father. In 1 Kings 9:16, it takes on the technical meaning of "dowry" or "marriage gift," marking the honor given to a royal woman. In Micah 1:14, the prophet uses it to express the loss and abandonment of a city in the face of divine judgment. The word plays on the image of "dismissal" — physical separation accompanied by a symbolic or material act — and adapts to each context: familial, diplomatic, or prophetic.
H7964.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, significant separations are never taken lightly. They are marked by acts that respect the honor and dignity of the one being left. For the believer, this suggests that even in difficult breakups or renunciations, there is room for generosity and honor. It is also a reminder that God may ask us to abandon certain things — as Micah announces — to purify us or fulfill His purposes.

sens: Absence of conflict, war, hostility between people or nations
State of security, safety of body and life
