Well-being, prosperity, health in daily life
Inner tranquility, rest of the soul, contentment
Harmony and friendship in human relationships
Harmony with God, particularly through the covenant
H7965G.detail:
1. Peace primarily denotes the absence of war and conflict: when two peoples or two persons are at peace, they do not fight and can live together without fear. In Judges 19:20, the old man welcomes the stranger by saying, "Peace be with you," meaning he will do him no harm and that he is welcome.
2. It then signifies the security of the body and person: to be at peace is to be protected from danger and injury. In Leviticus 26:6, God promises "a deep peace" that drives away the fear of wild beasts.
3. Peace also includes prosperity and material well-being: a life without misery, with health and abundance. In Genesis 41:16, Joseph fears nothing for his possessions before Pharaoh, for all is well with him.
4. It is also the inner state of calm and contentment of one who rests in God without worry. In Isaiah 26:3, the one who trusts in God receives "peace, peace."
5. Peace among humans is sincere friendship and brotherhood: in 1 Samuel 20:42, Jonathan and David part "in peace," bound by a deep love.
6. Peace with God is the harmony of the covenant: when man lives in accordance with God and His commandments, he enjoys His favor. In Numbers 25:12, God grants "the covenant of peace" to the one who has shown zeal for His cause.
H7965G.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) comes from an ancient root that evokes the idea of completeness and wholeness: something that is "complete" is in good condition, whole, without rupture. This root also produces words that mean "to make complete," "to pay in full," "to reimburse." The basic image is that of a restored totality: when nothing is lacking and everything is in harmony, one has peace. That is why the word encompasses both the absence of conflict, physical integrity, and general well-being.
H7965G.emploi: The word appears about 148 times in the Old Testament, particularly in the historical books, the psalms, and the prophets. It is used very concretely: peace between two kings or two peoples who make a covenant (Joshua 9:15), the peace that God grants to the victor (Judges 6:23), the peace of Solomon's reign without wars (1 Kings 4:24). But it also enriches in meaning: peace is the prosperity of the land (1 Kings 4:24), the health of the one who is healed (2 Kings 5:19), the calm of the righteous (Psalms 37:37). Gradually, especially among the prophets and in the psalms, peace becomes the supreme gift of God to the faithful believer: it is no longer just the absence of war, but total harmony of the soul with its creator.
H7965G.portee: For the Christian, shalom reveals that true peace is not primarily the absence of external problems, but a wholeness, a completeness restored when one is in harmony with God. It is a total peace: it touches the body, the soul, relationships, and the spirit. It calls us to seek first peace with God through trust, and then to live it out in relationships with others.

sens: God who gives completeness and harmony
God who establishes peace between Himself and His people
God present in rest and security
H7965H.detail:
1. This divine name expresses that God is the source of fullness and harmony. The word "peace" (shalom in Hebrew) refers not only to the absence of conflict but to completeness, integrity, wholeness — the state where nothing is lacking and everything is in its rightful place.
2. This title reveals that God Himself is the one who restores peace between Himself and sinful humanity, and who offers deep reconciliation. When Gideon builds an altar to "The Lord, our Peace" (Judges 6:24), he acknowledges that God has calmed his anxiety and restored an intact relationship with him.
3. This name also emphasizes that God dwells in absolute and unshakeable peace, and that He can bestow this gift upon those who believe in Him — not as mere tranquility, but as total well-being that flows from His divine presence.
H7965H.origine: The name "Shalom" (peace) comes from a Hebrew root that denotes the state of completeness and integrity. In the Old Testament, this term encompasses much more than "peace" in the modern sense: it describes a state of wholeness, of nothing lacking, of inner and outer completeness. Used as a divine name, it proclaims that God is the source of this state of fullness and that His very nature is absolute peace and eternal stability.
H7965H.emploi: This particular name of the Lord appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 6:24, when Gideon builds an altar after encountering the angel of the Lord and receiving assurance of His protection against the Midianites. In this moment of fear and divine revelation, Gideon names the altar "The Lord, our Peace" to commemorate the calm and certainty that God has just given him. This context shows that the name affirms God's ability to transform fear into trust and to offer unshakeable assurance.
H7965H.portee: This name invites the believer to recognize that true peace comes neither from circumstances nor from our efforts, but from God alone. For those going through fear or doubt, this title reminds that the Lord does not promise the absence of difficulties, but His presence and goodwill — an inner peace that remains even in the midst of trial. It is a timeless word of encouragement for anyone seeking stability and harmony in God.

sens: The absence of conflict, trouble, or danger in a region or between people
The state of calm, serenity, and physical or moral well-being
The health and prosperity of a person or people
Integrity, completeness, and soundness, without lack or flaw
The harmony of a person with God, particularly in the covenant
The state of personal tranquility, contentment, and absence of fear
H7965I.detail:
1. It is the absence of war, violence, or threat: the opposite of armed conflict. Jeremiah asks God why He announced peace to the people when the sword threatens (Jeremiah 4:10).
2. It is also the inner calm, the serenity of a person or community that does not live in fear. Job speaks of those who live without trouble, in "peace" (Job 21:9).
3. Often the word denotes good health and well-being: when someone asks, "How is your brother?", they are asking if he is in good "health" (Genesis 29:6, 1 Samuel 17:18).
4. It is also completeness, integrity: nothing is lacking, everything is whole and robust. Psalms 72:3 speaks of the mountains bringing peace to the people.
5. Finally, it is peace with God, the harmony of the heart that knows it is reconciled with Him. Jeremiah 29:11 promises Israel peace and a kind thought from God.
6. From a personal perspective, it is the feeling of security and contentment that comes when one knows there is nothing to fear (2 Samuel 18:32 contrasts Absalom's peace with those who wish harm to the king).
H7965I.origine: The Hebrew word shalom comes from a root that means "to be whole, to be complete." It is related to words that express totality and integrity. The basic image is that of something complete, without rupture: a whole body is healthy, a relationship without rupture is harmonious, a country without invasion is at peace. This is why the word naturally extends from external peace (absence of war) to internal peace (calm of the heart) and overall well-being.
H7965I.emploi: The word shalom appears 46 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives, the Psalms, and the prophets. It is first used in greetings: "How are you?" (literally "Shalom?"). It is then found to describe the state of someone (their health) or a community (its well-being, its prosperity). The prophets, particularly Jeremiah, use it to evoke the peace promised by God or, conversely, denounced as false when enemies threaten: Jeremiah 4:10 speaks of a deceptive "peace," while Jeremiah 29:11 promises the exiled Israel true peace coming from God. The word also applies to situations: a victory that leaves in peace (Joshua 10:21), a house where tranquility reigns (Job 21:9). Gradually, peace becomes associated with the covenant with God and the salvation He brings.
H7965I.portee: This word invites the Christian to seek not only the absence of external conflict but especially inner harmony and reconciliation with God. Biblical "peace" is not merely the absence of problems, but an integrity, a totality of well-being that comes from God. Jeremiah 29:11 promises that God thinks of us for our good and gives us this peace: it is the fruit of trust in God's goodness and obedience to His covenant.

sens: State of absence of conflict or war
Agreement, friendly understanding between people
Tranquility, security, physical and moral well-being
State of integrity and completeness
Spiritual well-being, especially in relation to God
H7965J.detail: 1. Peace primarily refers to the absence of conflict or war between people or nations — it is the situation where one is not afraid, where tranquility reigns. 2. It is also the agreement or trust shared with someone: being "at peace" with someone means having made an agreement, a covenant, trusting them (Psalms 41:10: "the one with whom I was at peace" speaks of a broken friendship). 3. The word encompasses everything that contributes to well-being: health of the body, prosperity, security, rest — everything that makes life complete and tranquil. 4. It also signifies integrity and wholeness: nothing is lacking, nothing is broken, everything is whole and complete. 5. In relation to God, peace is the spiritual well-being that arises from a respected covenant and a fearless trust in the Lord.
H7965J.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) comes from a root that means "to be whole, complete, intact." The basic idea is that of something that is not destroyed, that functions well, that is healthy — hence the sense of general well-being. It is a rich word that has generated many derivatives in Hebrew and has become embedded in Jewish greetings: saying "shalom" to someone is wishing them to be whole and flourishing. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), this word is rendered by "eirene" (εἰρήνη), which has given its meaning to the Greek of the New Testament.
H7965J.emploi: Shalom appears five times in these usages in the Hebrew Bible. It first describes a broken relationship of trust or friendship: in Psalms 41:10 and 55:21, treacherous enemies abandon or betray the one with whom they were "at peace." In Jeremiah 20:10 and 38:22, false prophets promise "peace" (security, deliverance) to deceive the people; it is a false peace, an empty promise. These usages show that biblical peace is not simply the absence of noise, but a relationship of mutual trust, true security based on loyalty and covenant — and that it can be betrayed or counterfeited.
H7965J.portee: For the Christian, this word is fundamental: the Bible speaks of the peace that God gives through the covenant, particularly in Jesus Christ. Understanding that biblical peace is primarily a matter of true relationship and trust (and not merely the absence of problems) helps to grasp why the Bible calls us to seek peace with God and with others — which requires honesty, loyalty, and forgiveness. It is also a call to discern true peace from false peace, that which the promises of the world offer without solid foundation.

sens: Completeness, wholeness of a thing or person
State of health, physical or moral well-being
Prosperity, wealth, peaceful possession
Absence of conflict, war, tranquility
Harmony in human relationships, friendship
Greeting, expression of goodwill
H7965K.detail:
1. Peace in its primary sense means totality, the absence of rupture: a thing complete, whole, without lack or damage. This is why one can ask someone, "How are you?" — literally, "What is your state of integrity?" (1 Samuel 10:4).
2. The physical well-being of a person: their health, strength, bodily condition. David asks his brothers, "How are you?" — he inquires about their health and vigor (1 Samuel 17:22).
3. What accompanies a good existence: material prosperity, the possession of goods. Nabal is wished peace, meaning that his house and all he possesses remain stable and flourishing (1 Samuel 25:6).
4. The absence of trouble, danger, hostility. It is peace opposed to war, calm after turmoil, guaranteed security.
5. Harmony between people, sincere friendship, agreement of wills. Nabal is greeted "in peace," meaning that the messenger brings him a peaceful and friendly intention (1 Samuel 25:5).
6. A formula of benevolent greeting: a welcoming word that expresses the wish that all is well with the person being addressed.
H7965K.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) comes from a root meaning to accomplish, to fill, to make whole. This is why it first evokes the idea of completeness: nothing is lacking, nothing is broken. Throughout the Bible, peace never refers only to the absence of war, but to a positive state of wholeness, well-being, and prosperity. The word is central to Hebrew thought: it is the normal and desired state of creation, opposed to chaos and disorder.
H7965K.emploi: The word shalom appears 8 times in these passages, showing its remarkable scope. It can refer to the physical state of a person — how they are, their health (1 Samuel 10:4, 17:22, 30:21); the state of affairs — the condition of war or troops (2 Samuel 11:7); friendly relations — greeting someone in peace means bringing them a good intention (1 Samuel 25:5, 25:6). It functions as a courteous polite formula: it is a wish for well-being addressed to someone important. Biblical peace thus encompasses personal well-being, stability in affairs, social harmony, and, in broader biblical theology, reconciliation with God.
H7965K.portee: Understanding that biblical peace is not a fleeting feeling, but a state of integrity and completeness, helps the Christian grasp what is meant when one wishes "the peace of Christ." It is a wish for total restoration — body, heart, affairs, relationships — as God offers through Christ. Peace is never a passive luxury, but the fruit of a life ordered according to God's will.

sens: Absence of war or conflict
State of tranquility and rest
Physical well-being and prosperity
Harmony and friendship between people
Completeness and integrity
Right relationship with God through the covenant
H7965L.detail: 1. The absence of war or conflict between peoples or nations: it is the opposite of violence and combat, the calm after troubles. 2. The state of inner tranquility and rest, the serenity of the heart: one who enjoys peace is not agitated by any fear. 3. Physical well-being, health, and material prosperity of a person or people: when all is well, when nothing is lacking. 4. Friendship, harmony, and good understanding between two people or two communities: living together without disagreement or hostility. 5. Integrity, totality, fulfillment: the Hebrew word suggests a certain fullness, as if nothing is lacking. 6. The right and harmonious relationship between man and God within the framework of the covenant: a peace that comes from reconciliation and trust in Him.
H7965L.origine: The Hebrew word שׁלוֹם (shalom) likely comes from a root that evokes the idea of completeness and wholeness. It is related to verbs meaning "to fill" or "to finish." Shalom fundamentally denotes the state of one who lacks nothing, who is whole and in their place. The Greek word eirènè in the New Testament regularly translates this Hebrew term and carries over its nuances: the absence of conflict, but also inner well-being and relationship with God.
H7965L.emploi: Shalom is one of the major terms of the Hebrew Bible, used more than 200 times. It appears in greetings ("Peace be with you"), in messianic promises (the Messiah is called "Prince of Peace"), and in descriptions of the rest and prosperity brought by God's reign. The word varies according to contexts: it can refer to political peace between kingdoms, the well-being of a person, the absence of inner conflict, or harmonious relationship with God. In passages concerning the covenant, shalom takes on a profound spiritual significance: it is the benefit that God grants to His faithful people. The context of Jeremiah 13:19 shows a people devoid of peace, taken into captivity: peace is lacking there because harmony with God has been broken.
H7965L.portee: For the Christian, the word peace summarizes much of what Christ brings: reconciliation with God (Romans 5:1), cessation of the inner struggle against guilt, and hope for a restored world. Jesus says to His disciples: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give you" (John 14:27). This peace is not the absence of difficulties, but a deep tranquility, a restored integrity, and the certainty that our relationship with God is restored. It invites the believer to seek peace with their brothers and to become a peacemaker.

sens: Action of returning evil for evil, seeking revenge
Divine retribution, punishment that God inflicts for sin
Wage or remuneration, especially that which is unjustly demanded
H7966.detail:
1. Retribution is the act of returning blow for blow, seeking revenge against one who has wronged you. It is retaliation, vengeance. In Isaiah 34:8, the Lord announces "a day of vengeance" and "a year of retribution for the cause of Zion": God will punish the enemies who have harmed His people.
2. Retribution is the punishment, the just consequence of the evil committed. Hosea 9:7 speaks of the "days of retribution" coming for Israel because of its sins: the people will discover that their iniquities merit judgment.
3. A wage is a remuneration, a price: it can be justly claimed for one's work, or unjustly demanded. In Micah 7:3, the judge "demands a wage," meaning he allows himself to be corrupted and asks for money to render his judgments — a serious injustice.
H7966.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to pay," "to reimburse," or "to complete." The initial image is that of returning what is due, of "making change" for a debt or an offense. Retribution or recompense is thus the fulfillment of what must happen in exchange for an act: the return of the same measure.
H7966.emploi: This word appears three times in the prophets (Isaiah, Hosea, Micah). It almost always designates the punishment or divine vengeance that responds to the sin of the people or the injustice of oppressors. In Isaiah 34:8, it is God who takes vengeance. In Hosea 9:7, it is the terrible consequences of sin. In Micah 7:3, the word pivots: it speaks of a corrupt remuneration, a wage demanded by corrupt judges. Biblical usage reveals that God settles accounts with justice, while humans allow themselves to be corrupted.
H7966.portee: This word reminds us that nothing escapes God: every act, every injustice, every sin has a consequence. Divine retribution is not blind vengeance, but restoration of justice. For the Christian, it invites trust — God protects His own — and humility before the judgment that weighs on unpardoned sin.

sens: king of northern Israel for one month
son of Jabesh who assassinated king Zechariah
conspirator overthrown and killed by Menahem
H7967G.detail: Shallum is a king of the northern kingdom of Israel, mentioned only in the second book of Kings. He appears as the son of Jabesh who conspired against king Zechariah, struck him down before the people, and killed him to take his place (2 Kings 15:10). Shallum reigned in Samaria for only one month, making him one of the most ephemeral kings of Israel. His reign ended quickly: Menahem, son of Gadi, came up from Tirzah, struck him down in Samaria, and killed him, then reigned in his place (2 Kings 15:14). The brevity of his power and the violence of his rise and fall illustrate the political instability of the northern kingdom at that time.
H7967G.origine: The name Shallum means "retribution" or "vengeance" in Hebrew, which is particularly fitting given that this king ascended to the throne through violence and met a violent end himself. The name reflects divine justice at work in the history of Israel.
H7967G.emploi: Shallum is mentioned only four times in the Bible, all references found in 2 Kings 15:10-15. These verses briefly recount how he conspired against Zechariah, killed him, and became king, then how he reigned for a month before being assassinated in turn by Menahem. His reign marks a moment of great political turmoil in the northern kingdom, during the time of the division of the monarchy of Israel and Judah.
H7967G.portee: The brief and violent story of Shallum reminds readers that power gained through violence does not last and invites retribution in return. It also illustrates how God allows political disorder to affect a people that turns away from Him.

sens: Husband of the prophetess Huldah during the reign of king Josiah of Judah
Keeper of the king's garments
H7967H.detail:
1. Shallum is a man from Jerusalem who lived during the reign of king Josiah (seventh century BC). He is known as the husband of Huldah, a respected prophetess whom the king and his officials consult to know the word of God. It is through this connection with a female prophet that Shallum appears in biblical accounts.

2. Shallum holds an official position at the royal court: he is the keeper of the king's garments, a role that requires trust and responsibility. This seemingly humble position places him close to the central power of the kingdom and explains how his household could receive official delegations coming to consult the prophetess.
H7967H.origine: The name Shallum means "retribution" or "compensation" in Hebrew, derived from a root that evokes the idea of paying or reimbursing. Although the meaning of the name carries a religious connotation, Shallum himself in the Bible is presented simply as a servant of the king, with no apparent link between his name and his role.
H7967H.emploi: Shallum appears only twice in the canonical Bible, in the two parallel passages of 2 Kings 22:14 and 2 Chronicles 34:22. In both cases, he is mentioned only as the husband of the prophetess Huldah, with no additional details about his life or deeds. The Bible also designates him as "keeper of the garments," a function in the royal household. The text does not report any events directly concerning him, but his indirect presence illustrates how the families of royal servants could participate in significant moments of the kingdom's history.
H7967H.portee: Shallum reminds us that in the history of salvation, secondary characters and modest roles are not without importance. His discreet mention alongside a prophetess shows that God can honor humble households and that faithfulness in ordinary tasks can place a family at the heart of decisive events for God's people.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
Son of Shimeah and father of Jekamiah
Genealogical figure of the clan of Jerahmeel
H7967I.detail: Shallum is a man's name from the tribe of Judah mentioned in the royal and family genealogies of the Old Testament. He appears in the genealogical line of Jerahmeel, where he is presented as the son of Shimeah and the father of Jekamiah (1 Chronicles 2:40-41). This Shallum is known only through these two genealogical verses that establish his place in the family succession of God's people.
H7967I.origine: The name Shallum (שַׁלּוּם in Hebrew) means "retribution" or "compensation," derived from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of giving back, reimbursing, or compensating. This name reflects a biblical vision where God settles accounts and restores balance. It was a name borne by several men in Israel at different times, including kings and important temple figures.
H7967I.emploi: Shallum appears twice in the Bible, exclusively in 1 Chronicles 2:40-41, in the genealogy of the clan of Jerahmeel belonging to the tribe of Judah. It is a simple father-son succession in a genealogical list: Shimeah fathered Shallum, and Shallum fathered Jekamiah. These genealogies served to establish family rights and heritage within God's people, particularly important after the Babylonian exile.

sens: Son of Josiah, king of Judah
Also called Jehoahaz
H7967J.detail: 1. Shallum is a prince of Judah, son of king Josiah. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:15 as the fourth son of Josiah, listed after Johanan, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. 2. This same character is also referred to by the name Jehoahaz in other biblical passages: he became king of Judah after the death of his father Josiah, but reigned only three months before being captured and taken to Egypt, where he was put in chains and ended his days.
H7967J.origine: The name Shallum means "retribution" or "reward" in Hebrew. It was a name borne by several men in the history of Israel and Judah: some were kings (like this Shallum of Judah), others were priests, Levites, or military leaders. The name reflects common biblical values related to justice and divine retribution.
H7967J.emploi: Shallum appears only once in the Bible as such: in 1 Chronicles 3:15, where he is listed among the sons of Josiah. However, this character is well known in the history of Judah under his other name, Jehoahaz. After the death of king Josiah at the battle of Megiddo, Shallum/Jehoahaz was proclaimed king by the people, but Egypt defeated this designation. Pharaoh Necho took him away, deported him to Egypt after only three months of reign, threw him in prison, and he died there as a captive.
H7967J.portee: This character illustrates the fragility of royal power when it does not rely on the will of God. Despite his status as a prince and the initial choice of the people, Shallum could not withstand foreign powers and met a tragic end. His story reminds readers that even kings are subject to divine providence and the consequences of turning away from the Lord.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon
Son of Saul
H7967K.detail:
1. Shallum is a man belonging to the tribe of Simeon, mentioned in the genealogies of Israel. He appears in the list of descendants of Simeon during the time of Egypt and the wilderness (1 Chronicles 4:25).
2. He is specifically identified as the son of Saul and the father of Mibsam, which places him in a precise genealogical lineage within the tribe of Simeon.
H7967K.origine: The name Shallum means "retribution" or "compensation" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of repair or balance. It comes from a Hebrew root related to the action of giving back or restoring. The name is borne by several characters in the Bible, but this one is specifically a descendant of Simeon.
H7967K.emploi: Shallum is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of the sons of Simeon in 1 Chronicles 4:25. It is a simple genealogical entry, with no particular narrative concerning his deeds or life. This type of genealogical mention served to preserve the memory of the families of Israel and to establish the lines of descent within the tribes.

sens: Priest of the lineage of Zadok, father of Hilkiah, mentioned in the genealogy of the high priests
One who exercises retribution or judgment (meaning of the name)
H7967L.detail: 1. Schallum is a priest who belongs to the family of Zadok, himself a famous priest of Israel. He is the father of Hilkiah, who will also become an important high priest. He is found in the genealogical list of priests who served in the temple, passing on their priestly duties from generation to generation (1 Chronicles 6:12-13). He is a link in this unbroken chain of servants of the Lord who ensured the correct worship in the temple.
H7967L.origine: The name Schallum means "retribution" or "one who recompenses," coming from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of rendering justice or giving according to what is due. It is a name that reflects the character of one who exercises religious authority: he must give to each according to his conduct. The name appears in several forms in ancient Hebrew (Schallum, Meshullam), but always denotes an action of retribution or judgment.
H7967L.emploi: Schallum is mentioned exclusively in the priestly genealogies of the first Book of Chronicles and in the Book of Ezra. These three occurrences invariably place him in the genealogical line of the high priests: son of Zadok and father of Hilkiah (1 Chronicles 6:12-13), and also listed in the genealogy of Ezra the priest (Ezra 7:2). No particular narrative concerns him, but his presence in these records underscores the importance of the continuity of the priesthood in temple worship.
H7967L.portee: This priest reminds the reader that the service of God passes through a faithful and regular transmission, from father to son, from generation to generation. Schallum embodies this unbroken chain of those who have maintained pure and official worship, even if his name alone has reached us, without spectacular details. It is an invitation to value daily and humble faithfulness in service, far from the spectacular.

sens: Levite gatekeeper of the temple at the time of the return from exile
Chief of a family of Korahite porters
Father of Matthithia
H7967M.detail:
1. Schallum is a Levite from the family of Korah who lived during the time of the exile and the return to Jerusalem. He served as a gatekeeper of the temple, an important responsibility in Israelite worship. In 1 Chronicles 9:17, he is presented as the chief of the porters: "Schallum was the chief."
2. He belonged to the family of the Korahites, a lineage of Levites specialized in guarding the sacred thresholds. His ancestors had guarded the entrance of the Lord's camp in the desert (1 Chronicles 9:19). This responsibility had been passed down from generation to generation.
3. Schallum was the father of Matthithia, who in turn became an important Levite, taking care of the cakes prepared for worship (1 Chronicles 9:31). His descendants continued to serve in the temple after the return from exile, as shown in the lists of Ezra and Nehemiah.
H7967M.origine: The name Schallum means "retribution" or "compensation" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of giving, rewarding, or restoring balance. This name was borne by several people in the history of Israel, but this one is specifically identified as a Levite from the period of the return from exile.
H7967M.emploi: Schallum appears in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles 9 as the chief of an important family of Korahite porters at the return from the Babylonian exile. He is also mentioned in the lists of Ezra 2:42 and Nehemiah 7:45, which count the sons of Schallum among the porters who returned from captivity: one hundred thirty-nine according to Ezra, one hundred thirty-eight according to Nehemiah. These numbers likely reflect slightly different administrative lists. His lineage has continued in the service of the temple, as evidenced by his son Matthithia.

sens: Man living during the divided monarchy, mentioned in 2 Chronicles 28:12
Father of Jehizkiah
H7967N.detail: Schallum is a character from the Old Testament living during the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible in 2 Chronicles 28:12, where he is identified as the father of Jehizkiah, one of the leaders of the sons of Ephraim who rose against those returning from the army. His name means "retribution" in Hebrew, reflecting God's justice. Although few details are given about his life and exact role, his appearance alongside other Ephraim leaders suggests that he played a role of responsibility and influence in the northern kingdom.
H7967N.origine: The name Schallum comes from the Hebrew שַׁלּוּם and means "retribution" or "reward," derived from a root expressing the idea of payment or compensation. This theophoric name reflects the biblical conviction that God rewards the actions of men, either in blessing or in judgment. Several characters bore this name in the history of Israel, showing its popularity among Hebrew families.
H7967N.emploi: Schallum appears only once in the provided biblical usages, in 2 Chronicles 28:12. There he is presented as the father of Jehizkiah, a leader of Ephraim who, along with his colleagues Azariah and Berechiah, opposed those returning from the army. This contextual mention suggests that he was a man from the tribe of Ephraim whose son played a political and military role at the time of the division of the kingdom. His unique appearance in the Bible makes it difficult to analyze his character or historical significance more deeply.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi, gatekeeper of the temple at the time of Ezra
H7967O.detail: 1. Schallum is a Levite gatekeeper, meaning he guards access to the temple. His name appears in the list of Levites who had married foreign women and had to repudiate their wives at the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:24). He represents those members of God's people who had strayed from the Law during the exile and who, upon returning to Jerusalem, repent and return to the established order.
H7967O.origine: The name Schallum means "retribution" or "restoration" in Hebrew. It comes from a root evoking the idea of paying, rewarding, or giving back. This name carries a nuance of divine justice: the one who bears it is marked by the expectation of a just divine action. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, including kings of Judah and Israel, but this one is a humble servant of the temple.
H7967O.emploi: Schallum appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Ezra at chapter 10, verse 24. He is mentioned among the temple gatekeepers who had taken foreign wives during the Babylonian exile. This list marks a pivotal moment: the return of the people to the Holy Land and their separation from pagan influences. Schallum symbolizes the act of repentance of the returning people: accepting to correct themselves to honor the covenant with God.
H7967O.portee: For the Christian reader, Schallum reminds us that repentance is a concrete act, often difficult and costly. The fact that a temple gatekeeper, a man in the service of God, fell into this trap shows that no one is immune to compromise. His name, however, gives a note of hope: God's retribution is not always judgment; it can also be restoration and a new chance for those who sincerely repent.

sens: Name of about fourteen men in the Bible, including a king of Israel and a king of Judah
H7967P.detail: Shallum is a name borne by several biblical characters at different times. The most notable is Shallum son of Jabesh, who conspired against King Zechariah of the Northern Kingdom, killed him, and took the throne; he reigned only one month before being assassinated by Menahem. Another Shallum was the third son of King Josiah of Judah; he became king but reigned only three months before being taken captive to Egypt, where he died in chains. Other bearers of the name include the husband of the prophetess Huldah, the uncle of the prophet Jeremiah, various Levitical figures (temple porters, notably at the eastern gate), and men who had foreign wives at the time of Ezra, such as the one mentioned in Ezra 10:42.
H7967P.origine: The name Shallum literally means "retribution" or "compensation," derived from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of payment or restoration. This meaning reflects biblical themes of judgment and restoration. The name appears throughout all periods of biblical history, from the Northern Kingdom to the time of the Exile and return.
H7967P.emploi: Shallum is the name of multiple biblical personalities, particularly during the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, and especially during the time of the Exile and return. In Ezra 10:42, he is listed among the men who had taken foreign wives and were called to repudiate these unions. The two major royal figures bearing this name — the conspirator who reigned one month in the North and the son of Josiah in the South — mark the political crises of each kingdom. Several Shallum also held priestly or Levitical roles, notably as temple gatekeepers.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah living in the time of Nehemiah
Leader of half of the district of Jerusalem
Rebuilder of the wall of Jerusalem
H7967Q.detail:
1. Shallum is a proper name designating a man from the time of Nehemiah, mentioned only once in Scripture. He is a secondary character but plays an important role in the reconstruction of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:12).
2. He is presented as the chief responsible for half of an administrative division of Jerusalem. His title indicates that he held civil and administrative authority in the city.
3. During the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, Shallum actively participated in this great collective work, even working alongside his own daughters, highlighting the personal and family involvement in this task.
H7967Q.origine: The name Shallum (שַׁלּוּם in Hebrew) means "retribution" or "reward." It is borne by several different characters in the Old Testament, including the son of Hallohesh mentioned here. The Greek form of the name appears in some traditions.
H7967Q.emploi: Shallum appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:12. He is introduced as the son of Hallohesh and leader of half of the district of Jerusalem. The mention of his daughters working alongside him emphasizes that the reconstruction of the wall was an effort involving entire families. His administrative role shows that local civil authorities of Jerusalem actively participated in this major restoration project of the city after the exile.

sens: Uncle of the prophet Jeremiah
Man of the tribe of Judah living in the time of the prophet Jeremiah
H7967R.detail:
1. Shallum is the paternal uncle of the prophet Jeremiah, mentioned only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 32:7, where his son Hanamel comes to propose to Jeremiah to buy a field at Anathoth.
2. He lived during the time of Jeremiah, that is, in the seventh century B.C., in the kingdom of Judah. His existence is known to us only through this passage where his son appeals to Jeremiah's right of redemption over the family field.
H7967R.origine: The name Shallum (in Hebrew Shallum) means "retribution" or "compensation." It comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of payment or replacement. It is a relatively common name in the Old Testament, borne by several different characters, including kings of Israel and Judah and Levites. This one is distinguished by his familial relationship with the great prophet Jeremiah.
H7967R.emploi: Shallum appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 32:7. He is the father of Hanamel and the uncle of Jeremiah. The context of this mention is crucial: during the siege of Jerusalem by the Babylonians, while the situation seems desperate, God commands Jeremiah to buy the field from his cousin Hanamel. This family transaction carries prophetic significance: it symbolizes hope for the future restoration of the people of Judah after the exile, despite the walls collapsing around Jeremiah.
H7967R.portee: The mention of Shallum invites the reader to reflect on the value of family ties even in the gravest crises. The mere fact that Jeremiah had a right of redemption over his uncle's field shows the importance of family structures in the life of ancient Israel. More deeply, this family of the prophet—his uncle, his cousin—figures in a passage where God reassures about future restoration, suggesting that family order and trust in God will survive judgment.

sens: Character from the time of the divided monarchy, father of Maaseiah
H7967S.detail: 1. Shallum is a man living at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 35:4, where he is presented as the father of Maaseiah and as the gatekeeper of the temple of Jerusalem. His role was to monitor access to the temple, an important function in the worship of the Lord.
H7967S.origine: The name Shallum means "retribution" or "reward" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of compensation or payment. This name was quite common in Israel and Judah, borne by many important figures: kings, priests, Levites, and officials. The Shallum mentioned here in Jeremiah 35:4 is distinct from all these other bearers of the same name.
H7967S.emploi: Shallum appears only once in the French translations of the Bible, in Jeremiah 35:4. In this passage, he is identified as the gatekeeper of the temple, a position of responsibility that required a certain level of trust. His son Maaseiah is associated with a chamber of the temple, suggesting that the family was linked to the sacred service of the sanctuary. The context of this passage concerns the family of the Rechabites and their practices of fidelity, but Shallum appears simply as a genealogical marker and an officer of the temple.

sens: Son of Naphtali, of the tribe of Israel
H7967T.detail: Shallum is a name borne by several men in biblical history. In the usage provided in 1 Chronicles 7:13, it designates a son of Naphtali and Bilhah, one of the twelve sons of Jacob from whom the tribes of Israel descended. The name means "retribution" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of a reward or divine recompense.
H7967T.origine: The name Shallum (in Hebrew שַׁלּוּם) literally means "retribution" or "reward." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of giving back, rewarding, or making payment. This name has been borne by several important people in the history of Israel, including kings and temple servants, all marked by destinies linked to this notion of judgment or divine consequences.
H7967T.emploi: Shallum is a name borne by at least fourteen different men in the Old Testament. The usage provided shows him first as the son of Naphtali, listed among the descendants of Jacob. But the name also designates a king of Israel who reigned for one month, sons of King Josiah of Judah, Levitical temple guardians, and other figures from post-exilic history. Each of these Shallum occupies a place in the biblical narrative, marking how this name has been passed down through the generations of Israel.

sens: son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned for three months before being taken captive to Egypt
another name for King Jehoiachin (also called Coniah or Jeconiah)
a conspirator who killed King Zechariah and reigned for one month over the Northern Kingdom
husband of Huldah the prophetess
uncle of the prophet Jeremiah
various men of Israel in biblical times
H7967U.detail:
1. Shallum is the name of the third son of King Josiah of Judah, who became king after his father. He reigned only three months before being captured and taken to Egypt, where he was imprisoned and died in captivity (Jeremiah 22:11). He is an example of the weak and idolatrous kings at the end of the kingdom of Judah before its fall.

2. This same name (Shallum) also refers to Jehoiachin, king of Judah, known also by the names Coniah or Jeconiah in other biblical passages. These different names refer to the same person.

3. A Shallum appears as a conspirator who killed King Zechariah of the Northern Kingdom (Israel) and became the 15th king of Israel, but reigned only one month before being killed by Menahem.

4. Shallum is also the name of the husband of Huldah, the prophetess who intervened during the time of King Josiah.

5. A Shallum was the uncle of the prophet Jeremiah.

6. Several other men bore this name: a Simeonite, Judeans, an Ephraimite, a son of Naphtali, Levites gatekeepers of the temple, and other figures from the times of Nehemiah and Ezra.
H7967U.origine: The name Shallum means "retribution" or "compensation" in Hebrew. It is a proper name borne by many individuals in the history of Israel, primarily during the late monarchy and after the exile. The Hebrew root evokes the idea of a reward or a judgment that returns to someone.
H7967U.emploi: Shallum appears as the name of several important or secondary characters in biblical history. The most well-known is the son of Josiah who became king of Judah and reigned very briefly: the Bible mentions him notably in Jeremiah 22:11, where God declares through the prophet that he will never return to Jerusalem. Another Shallum, a conspirator of the Northern Kingdom, reigns for one month over Israel before his death. Other Shallums are attested during the times of Nehemiah and Ezra, notably among the Levites and temple gatekeepers. The name was quite common among leaders and men of rank in ancient Israel.
H7967U.portee: King Shallum (son of Josiah) illustrates the fragility of human power in the face of God's judgment: in only three months of reign, he is captured and exiled, symbolizing the inevitable decline of the kingdom of Judah. His story reminds us that God's promises are fulfilled, and that even a king does not escape the consequences of his actions and unfaithfulness.

sens: Jewish figure living during the exile and return
Son of Col-Hozeh
Leader of the district of Mizpah
H7968.detail: 1. Shallum is a Jewish man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile to Babylon. He lived at a time when the Jewish people were regaining their freedom and rebuilding their capital. 2. He was the son of Col-Hozeh, indicating his origin and place in the genealogy of the returning community. 3. Shallum was the chief (or governor) of the district of Mizpah, an important region of Judah, which shows that he held a position of responsibility in the local administration of the reconstituted province.
H7968.origine: The name Shallum means in Hebrew "retribution" or "reward." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of payment or reward. This type of theophoric name was common among the Jews, often reflecting a hope or religious conviction of the parents.
H7968.emploi: Shallum appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:15. He is presented as one of the main officials in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile. His role is detailed: he repaired the Fountain Gate and built the wall of the Pool of Siloam to the steps that descend from the City of David. This mention shows that he was a prominent figure in the restoration project of the capital.

sens: The whole number that comes after two and before four
A quantity, duration, or distance expressed by this number
A rank or position: the third in a series
A number of hundreds, thousands (in ancient texts)
H7969.detail:
1. The word simply designates the number 3: it is the digit used for counting or enumerating. Enoch "walked with God three hundred years" (Genesis 5:22): here we count the time that has passed.
2. In a context of measurement or counting, "three" expresses a concrete quantity. The army of Israel "consisted of fifty-three thousand four hundred men" (Numbers 2:30): the number specifies how many warriors there were.
3. Applied to a rank or succession, "three" or "third" marks the position in an order. The three branches of the golden lampstand (Exodus 25:32): the number indicates how the branches are distributed.
4. "Three hundred" or "thirteen" combine with other numbers to express magnitudes. The seven hundred women and three hundred concubines of Solomon (1 Kings 11:3): the repetition of "three" in these large numbers emphasizes abundance.
H7969.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁלֹשׁ comes from a very ancient root common to Semitic languages. In Aramaic (the language spoken by the neighboring Arameans of Israel), the equivalent word is תְּלָת (telat). The number three was probably linked, in ancient cultures, to the idea of a totality or completeness: after one, two, three, a group was formed. The word has retained this simple and direct meaning throughout all biblical texts.
H7969.emploi: The word "three" appears 382 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, and in genealogical lists. It is used to count people (three sons of Noah in Genesis 9:19, three hundred years in Genesis 5:22), days and durations ("three days" in Exodus 5:3 or 19:15), the dimensions of objects in the Tabernacle (the three branches of the lampstand in Exodus 25:32), and ranks (the "third" day of creation). Sometimes it enters into a composite number: "thirteen" (three + ten), "thirty," "three hundred," "three thousand." The meaning remains always numerical and concrete, never metaphorical.
H7969.portee: For the reader, "three" in the Bible can carry a symbolic weight: for example, rejection or trial lasting three days or three years often prepares for restoration, and the number three recurs in decisive moments of salvation history. But the word itself does not add hidden meaning; it is the context that can imbue this number with spiritual significance. Knowing the usage of the number three helps to notice patterns in biblical narration.

sens: the number 30
age or duration of 30 years or 30 days
quantity, weight, or measure equal to 30 units
H7970.detail:
1. The number thirty simply designates the numerical quantity 30, like any other number used for counting or enumerating (Numbers 7:85: "each silver platter weighed one hundred thirty shekels").
2. Thirty also marks a duration or age, expressed in years or days. Adam was one hundred thirty years old when he fathered Seth (Genesis 5:3), and a woman is unclean for thirty-three days after childbirth (Leviticus 12:4). The number often appears to date the age of an ancestor or the duration of a reign.
3. Thirty can qualify a measure of weight, length, or capacity: the silver utensils of the Tabernacle weighed one hundred thirty shekels (Numbers 7:85), or Noah's ark was thirty cubits high (Genesis 6:15).
H7970.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root שלש (shaloosh), which means "three." Thirty is thus literally "three times ten," like all multiples of ten: forty (four times ten), fifty (five times ten), etc. It is a simple and practical number for counting and enumerating in the daily and administrative life of ancient Israel.
H7970.emploi: The word thirty appears 170 times in the Segond, mainly in Genesis, Exodus, and Numbers, where it serves to enumerate the ages of the patriarchs, the durations of legal periods, the quantities offered at the Tabernacle, or the numbers of the tribes. It is also used in historical books to date reigns or military events (for example, Judges 20:39: about thirty men killed). Its usage is neutral and purely numerical: it has no particular theological significance, but it remains an important number in the narrative and legal structure of the biblical text.

sens: To send someone or something to a recipient or direction
To let go, release, give permission
To extend, stretch, direct (an arm, a ray)
To send back, dismiss, remove
To entrust a mission, delegate
To set in motion, propel
H7971G.detail:
1. The primary meaning: to send someone or something away to go elsewhere. Moses says, "The Lord sends me to Bethel" (2 Kings 2:2): God commands him to go there. Abraham sends a servant to find a wife for Isaac (Genesis 24:7): he dispatches him on a distant mission.
2. To let go, give permission to leave. Noah releases the raven from the ark (Genesis 8:7): he frees it to fly away. In 1 Samuel 20:22, David tells the young man, "The Lord sends you away": go, you are free to leave.
3. To extend or direct something forward: to stretch out an arm, shoot an arrow, make branches grow. It is the image of movement that stretches out.
4. To send someone away, dismiss them, remove them. Genesis 3:23: the Lord drives Adam out of the Garden of Eden. It is a forced sending, a dismissal.
5. To give someone a mission, a charge. God says in 2 Chronicles 36:15 that He gave His messengers the mission to warn Israel. The messenger becomes a bearer of the authority of the one who sends him.
6. To set something in motion: plagues that strike Egypt are "sent" by God (Exodus 9:14). It is to bring forth, to advance a force.
H7971G.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of releasing, freeing, setting in motion. The word belongs to a large family: the noun "שָׁלוּחַ" (sent one, messenger) directly derives from it, meaning one who is sent. Fundamentally, to send is to remove something or someone from one's presence so that it may fulfill a function elsewhere. It is an act of will, often of authority.
H7971G.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, with 630 occurrences. It appears in all historical and prophetic books. God sends His servants (prophets, angels, messengers) to communicate, warn, or fulfill His will (Jeremiah 23:32: "I did not send them"). Men send messengers (Numbers 22:5: Balak sends for Balaam), dismiss their wives, free their servants. The meaning varies slightly depending on the context: to send can be an order (a mission), a permission (to leave), a punishment (to be sent away), or a natural act (to release an animal). But the core remains the same: to make something depart from its place.
H7971G.portee: This word touches the heart of the relationship between God and His creatures. For God to send you is to be called, bearing a divine mission. To be sent away is to face judgment or trial. In reading the Bible, we discover that sending is never trivial: it is God who sends His prophets, His angels, ultimately His own Son. Understanding this verb is to grasp how God acts in history and how He entrusts us with responsibilities.

sens: To send someone or something to a place or person
To let go, release, grant freedom
To dismiss, send away, discharge
To extend, project forward
To deliver, abandon to a state or authority
H7971H.detail:
1. The most common meaning: to send someone or something in a direction or to a destination. Pharaoh refuses to send the people of Israel: "If you do not let my people go" (Exodus 8:17). Moses asks Pharaoh to let him go to offer a sacrifice: "Permit me to go quickly see my brothers" (1 Samuel 20:29). It is the action of dispatching someone or something, often in an authoritative manner.
2. To grant freedom, release, not hold back. Jacob refused to let the mysterious visitor go: "I will not let you go unless you bless me" (Genesis 32:26). It is the idea of opening the hand and saying, "you are free."
3. To send someone away, dismiss them, or divorce. In Exodus and Deuteronomy, it refers to letting go of a servant or slave, granting them their freedom (Deuteronomy 15:12-13). It is to end a relationship by granting freedom to the other.
4. To extend, project something forward, like an arrow or a branch that grows. The image is one of movement that leaps, unfolds outward.
5. To entrust someone to a power or destiny, to abandon them to a loss of control. God has "delivered them to the desires of their hearts" those who refused to listen to Him (Psalms 81:13). It is to let go by entrusting to another will or authority.
H7971H.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁלַח (shalach) comes from a root that evokes the image of stretching, throwing, projecting forward. The word is very ancient and very common in biblical Hebrew. It is related to other verbs of sending and movement. The root fundamentally expresses the idea of releasing something from one's hand or initial position, letting it go or projecting it toward a goal.
H7971H.emploi: This verb is among the most frequent in the Old Testament (86 occurrences) and appears in all types of texts. Its use varies according to the context: in the story of the Exodus, it describes the repeated order that Pharaoh refuses to follow: "let my people go." In the laws of Deuteronomy, it concerns the manumission (release) of Hebrew slaves after six years of service. In narratives, it means sending someone on a mission or letting them go (Jacob asks the visitor to let him go, Genesis 32:26). In the Psalms and Jeremiah, it takes on a theological dimension: God "sends" plagues or "delivers" His people to the consequences of their unfaithfulness (Psalms 78:49; Psalms 81:13). In Jeremiah 34, the verb applies to the release of Hebrew slaves as an act of justice. The scope is both concrete (sending someone on an errand) and profound (the freedom granted by grace).
H7971H.portee: This word reveals the biblical tension between authority and freedom. To send someone is to acknowledge that they can exist on their own, outside of my presence. In Pharaoh's case, the refusal to send the people expresses slavery and the refusal to liberate. In God's case, "to send" often expresses love (He sends His prophets, His messengers), but also judgment when He "delivers" someone to their own choices. For the Christian reader, this verb invites reflection on true freedom: the freedom that God grants to those He loves, and the call to liberate those who are under our responsibility.

sens: Send someone away, make them leave
Drive or expel someone from a place
Let go, release
Repudiate a wife, send her away from her home
Allow to fly away or escape
H7971I.detail:
1. Send someone away, make them leave: this is the action of sending someone or something to a distant place. Abraham sends Hagar, his servant: he sends her into the desert (Genesis 21:14), where she must go alone.
2. Drive or expel someone from a place: to send away also means to put someone outside, depriving them of their place. In marriage law, a man cannot send away his wife if he himself has dishonored her (Deuteronomy 22:29) — it is a definitive and unilateral act.
3. Let go, release: this means to give freedom, to allow departure. The word can also evoke letting go or releasing something.
4. Repudiate a wife, send her away from her home: this is the most serious marital meaning. The Law allows divorce by repudiation: if a man discovers "something shameful" in his wife, he writes a divorce letter and sends her away from his house (Deuteronomy 24:1). This sending away is irrevocable: once repudiated and remarried, the woman cannot return to her first husband (Deuteronomy 24:4).
5. Allow to fly away or escape: the word can also refer to letting go of branches or arrows — the underlying idea of propulsion or sending outward.
H7971I.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁלַח (shalach) comes from a very ancient root that evokes the idea of sending, putting into motion towards the outside or towards someone else. The root carries within it the image of departure or propagation. It appears in several grammatical forms: the simple form (Qal) for "send" or "send away", the passive form (Niphal) for "be sent", and causative or intensive forms (Piel, Hiphil) to amplify or detail the action. It is a very frequent word in the Hebrew Bible.
H7971I.emploi: The verb shalach appears about ten times in the provided usages, mainly in Deuteronomy and the prophets. Its primary meaning is "send away" in the sense of distancing or expelling. In the marital context of Deuteronomy (chapters 22 and 24), it specifically denotes the act of repudiation: the husband sends away his wife by giving her a divorce letter and putting her outside. The Law strictly regulates this right: a husband cannot send away his wife if he has himself dishonored her, except to compensate her (Deuteronomy 22:19, 22:29). Once sent away, she acquires a new status that prevents a return to the first husband (Deuteronomy 24:4). The prophets use this same language to describe the breaking of the Covenant: God says to Israel, "I have sent you away" (Jeremiah 3:8, Isaiah 50:1), using the image of divorce to express rejection or abandonment.
H7971I.portee: This word reminds the reader that marriage is a serious covenant, protected by the Law. Repudiation is never trivial: it breaks a relationship before God and affects the woman's life. By transposing this image to the rejection of Israel, the prophets show that infidelity to the Covenant leads to serious consequences. For the Christian, this word sheds light on the gravity of divorce in Scripture and the ethical stakes of marriage as a sacred commitment.

sens: Unite a woman to a man through marriage
Give a woman in marriage, establish a marital union
H7971J.detail:
1. Unite a woman to a man through marriage: this is the action of establishing a marital bond between two people. The verb evokes the idea of "sending" or "entrusting" the woman to her husband's household. In Judges 12:9, Jephthah "married thirty daughters outside," meaning he gave them in marriage to men from other families or cities, while he welcomed women for his sons.
2. Give a woman in marriage, establish a marital union: more broadly, the verb denotes the act of entrusting a young woman to a husband, either as a father or guardian who "sends" her to her spouse, or as a social process that "binds" two people together. This action creates a new family and a new alliance between two lineages.
H7971J.origine: The verb שׁלַח (shala'h) primarily means "send" or "let go." Its basic image is that of letting something or someone go, of "extending" or "projecting" towards a goal. It is a very common verb in Hebrew with many nuances: sending a messenger, letting go of a slave, driving away, directing, extending hands. In the context of marriage, it retains this idea of "sending": one "sends" the woman to her husband's household, one "entrusts" her to him. The root also appears in contexts like "send away," "repudiate," or "dismiss."
H7971J.emploi: This verb is used here in the specific sense of marriage, although its primary usage in biblical Hebrew is "send." In Judges 12:9, it describes the act of marrying: Jephthah "married" (literally "sent") thirty of his daughters to men, while taking thirty other young women in marriage for his sons. It is a normal and expected social act of a father or clan leader: establishing marital alliances for the next generation. The text shows that this practice involved both directions: giving and receiving wives. Although this is the only usage in the precise sense of "marry" in the Segond translation, the verb שׁלַח is extremely frequent in the Bible with the meaning of "send" or "let go."
H7971J.portee: This verse reminds of the importance of marriage in ancient Israel as a fundamental structure of society and alliances between families. For the Christian reader, it invites consideration of marriage not as a purely personal matter, but as a social bond that engages families and creates mutual responsibilities. This aligns with the New Testament teaching on marriage as a serious commitment and covenant before God.

sens: To lengthen, deploy (one's hand, arm, a branch)
To direct towards, point in a direction
To act upon, intervene with (in the sense of extending one's power, authority)
To send, dispatch (someone or something)
To let go, release, abandon
To ward off, remove a danger or threat
H7971K.detail:
1. To lengthen and deploy one's hand or arm towards something or someone: the primary image of the verb is physical and concrete. Jeroboam "extended" his hand against the man of God, who was struck with dryness (1 Kings 13:4). A gesture of extension of the whole body is also found: Gideon "extended" the staff he held in his hand (Judges 6:21).
2. To direct or point one's hand or weapon towards a target, with the intention to strike or seize. To advance the hand "against" someone means to threaten or mistreat them: the king's servants refused to "advance" their hand to strike the priests of the Lord (1 Samuel 22:17).
3. To exercise one's authority or power over someone: God "extends" His hand to save, strike, or protect. The Psalmist says: "You extend your hand against the anger of my enemies" (Psalms 138:7) — God masters the threats that weigh upon the one who prays.
4. To send someone on a mission or dispatch something: less frequent, but the verb can denote the action of "bringing" a word or message. Jeremiah receives God's command: "Extend your hand and take this scroll" (Jeremiah 1:9) — to extend also means to gather, to pick up.
5. To let go or release: Job says, "If I stretch out my hand" (Job 30:24), the one who bends can release. The idea of abandonment or letting go is added.
6. To ward off a danger, to remove a threat by exercising protective force, a divine intervention that diverts evil. It is the extension of protective authority in the face of enemies.
H7971K.origine: The verb שׁלח (sha.lach) comes from a root that evokes the gesture of lengthening, projecting, letting something move away. The original image is very corporeal: extending the arm or hand. It has been enriched with figurative meanings: to send someone is to "extend" them far from oneself; to let go is to release this extension. The word has a strong presence in biblical and rabbinic Hebrew, with variations of aspect (simple Qal, passive Niphal, intensive Piel, intensive passive Pual, causative Hiphil) that nuance the action.
H7971K.emploi: This verb appears about 61 times in the Old Testament, notably in the accounts of Genesis and Exodus, the historical books, and the Psalms. It primarily describes concrete gestures: extending the hand to seize, strike, or bless (Genesis 22:10, where Abraham extends his hand to sacrifice Isaac). Then it takes on meaning in power relations: refusing to extend the hand means refusing to act, to commit an act (1 Samuel 22:17). In contexts of relationship with God, extending the hand becomes the image of divine intervention: God extends His hand to save (Exodus 3:20), and His arm's stretching symbolizes deliverance. The verb is also used for warlike or destructive actions (Joel 3:13: putting the hand to the harvest = reaping the harvest of judgment).
H7971K.portee: This verb reminds the believer that our hands, our gestures, and our intentions are visible to God. Refusing to extend the hand towards evil means standing in righteousness (1 Samuel 22:17). Conversely, the image of God "extending His hand" reassures: it means that God acts, intervenes, protects, and delivers His people. It is a powerful biblical image of providence and salvation.

sens: To ignite, to cause something to burn by setting it on fire
To destroy by fire
To subject to total destruction
H7971L.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: to cause an object or building to start burning. When the Israelites attack Jerusalem, they "set fire to the city" (Judges 1:8), meaning they create destructive flames there.
2. More broadly, it means to destroy by fire. In Judges 20:48, it is not just one or two houses: they "set fire to all the cities," which completely annihilates these places. The act is not isolated but global.
3. Finally, the verb evokes total catastrophe, annihilation. When Elisha prophesies that Hazael "will set fire to their fortified cities" (2 Kings 8:12), he describes a systematic ravaging of the entire country. And when one "sets fire to the sanctuary" (Psalms 74:7), they desecrate the most sacred place.
H7971L.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁלַח (shala'h) primarily means "to send" or "to launch" — the idea of projecting something towards a goal. Here, it denotes the action of projecting or releasing fire onto something. The root evokes a gesture of propulsion: one "sends" the flames, "launches" the fire, "releases" it to do its destructive work. This meaning is closely related to the idea of projecting or directing something forcefully.
H7971L.emploi: The verb appears four times in the provided passages, always to describe an act of destruction by fire in a war context. In Judges 1:8 and 20:48, it is an act of war: the Israelites burn the conquered cities. In 2 Kings 8:12, it is a prophecy of doom: the Syrian king Hazael will destroy Israel by fire. In Psalms 74:7, it is the desecration of the temple during an invasion. In all cases, the action is irreversible, total, and marks a destruction of urban or religious fabric. The term refers to ancient warfare, where burning cities was a classic act of conquest and domination.
H7971L.portee: Understanding this word helps grasp the gravity of God's judgments on idolatry and rebellion in the Old Testament. The fire is not a detail: it is the very image of complete destruction, of annihilation that a faithless people confronts. For the Christian reader, it serves as a reminder that divine judgment is real and reaches its targets mercilessly — but also that God always warns before acting, as Elisha prophesies before the catastrophe.

sens: To address someone or something to a place or destination
To let go, dismiss, send away
To extend, deploy (a branch, a hand)
To release, let go
To expel, banish, reject
To direct, orient (an action, a word)
H7971M.detail:
1. To send means to make someone or something go to a place: one entrusts a message to a messenger, sends a child on an errand, sends servants ahead.
2. To let go or dismiss someone: one sends away a servant, sends someone from their presence, frees them from their obligations.
3. To extend or project something: a branch that extends, a hand that is reached out, a weapon that is thrown toward its target.
4. To release or abandon: to loosen one's grip, to let go of what one was holding, to end the restraint.
5. To expel or exile: to drive someone from their territory or home, to banish them, to forcibly remove them, as in Isaiah 27:8 where God "punishes" Israel by scattering them with the desert wind.
6. To direct or orient an action toward someone: to send a blessing, to send a judgment, to bring something upon someone.
H7971M.origine: The verb שׁלח comes from a root that expresses the fundamental idea of "letting go" or "putting into motion." The initial image is that of a hand extending, reaching toward a target, or letting go. The word appears in many forms (simple, passive, intensive, causative) to mean "send," "send back," "drive out," "extend," each nuance adding to the central idea of "putting in direction." It is one of the most common verbs in biblical Hebrew.
H7971M.emploi: The verb שׁלח is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible. It is used to send a messenger, a servant, or an ambassador to someone; to send away a wife (divorce), a servant, or a supporter; to extend a hand or a weapon; to release animals or troops; to scatter or banish a people. In Isaiah 27:8, it takes on the meaning of "punish" or "discipline" through exile: God has driven Israel far from Him as the wind carries away leaves. The meaning varies according to context and object: sending a prophet means charging them with a mission; sending someone far means distancing them; sending judgment or plague means being the source of it.
H7971M.portee: This verb shows us that God sends: He sends His prophets to warn His people, He sends His judgments to correct them, He also sends help and blessing. For the Christian, it reminds us that every true sending comes from God — which is why prophets and apostles emphasize their divine sending. Understanding the verb שׁלח helps to see how the Bible speaks of divine action: God does not abandon His people, He sends them, He drives them out to bring them back, He acts through word and sending.

sens: to make someone or something go to a place or person
to transmit a message or written order
to give an order, summon
to be sent, to be put in motion
H7972.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to make someone or something go: a letter is sent to the king (Ezra 4:11), an order is transmitted from one authority to another. It is the physical movement of something from the one who sends to its recipient.

2. The word is regularly used for the transmission of written messages or official orders: in Ezra 6:13, King Darius sends an order to the governors. It is less about the action of sending off than the act of addressing something to someone with intention.

3. In a context of summoning or commanding, to send means to give an order that sets something in motion: in Daniel 3:2, the king summons the satraps by sending for them. The sending becomes an act of authority.

4. The passive form "to be sent" appears when what is mentioned undergoes the action: a letter is sent by someone else, an order reaches us because it has been sent.
H7972.origine: The Hebrew root שׁלח (sh.l.ch) fundamentally expresses the idea of putting in motion, letting go, or dispatching. It is a very common verb in biblical Hebrew, used both to send a person and a message, a weapon, or even a divine judgment. The word always implies a separation: one sends what moves away from oneself.
H7972.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the provided Aramaic texts (books of Ezra and Daniel), mainly in an administrative and official context. Persian governors and kings send letters, orders, and decrees. It is the technical vocabulary of political and religious correspondence of that time. The word retains a very concrete meaning: it is always about delivering something to someone, never just a simple intention. The references show that in the exilic empires, to send is to exercise authority from a distance through written communication.
H7972.portee: For the believer reading these exile accounts, seeing this verb reminds us that even under foreign domination, God maintains an order in which orders are transmitted and things are accomplished. The letters sent by the adversaries of God's people and the decrees of kings are ordinary human acts, but they fit into a story that God governs. The word invites us to recognize that everything that moves toward us — opposition or help — comes within the framework of divine providence.

sens: Combat weapon, instrument of war
Projectile thrown or shot
Blow dealt by a weapon
Young shoot of a plant
H7973.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a combat weapon, the instrument carried by a warrior. In Nehemiah, the builders of the wall held "a weapon in the other" hand while working (Nehemiah 4:17), and each kept their weapons close even at night (Nehemiah 4:23). It is a general term for military equipment: sword, spear, or other combat gear.
2. The word can also refer to the blow struck by a weapon, or the weapon itself as it inflicts harm — which translations render as "sword" or "sword blow." In Job, it speaks of the soul "guaranteed from the pit" by the blows of the sword (Job 33:18), where the word evokes the deadly instrument.
3. A young shoot, a bud of a plant (this meaning appears in the references but more discreetly). It is the image of a young branch springing from the trunk or root, like a weapon that emerges.
4. Finally, the word can designate a shot or projectile launched with force — the image of the projectile flying toward its target.
H7973.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of throwing, projecting, or making spring forth. The word can be linked to the quick and precise action of a weapon that departs or a young shoot that springs up. It is a noun that describes the object by what it does: it is "thrown" or "springs forth." This image of springing relates the two main meanings: a weapon that rushes toward its target, a shoot that springs from the earth.
H7973.emploi: The word appears about 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in historical and poetic books. It is particularly frequent in contexts of war and fortification: Hezekiah prepares a quantity of "weapons" when he fears an invasion (2 Chronicles 32:5), and the Judeans who rebuild the wall remain armed (Nehemiah 4). In Job, the word returns with the nuance of the deadly blow: death strikes "by the sword" (Job 36:12). The meaning of plant shoot, also attested (Joel 2:8, Song of Solomon 4:13), remains less frequent. The word thus primarily denotes a weapon in a concrete and military sense.
H7973.portee: The word reminds the Christian reader that the lives of believers are not exempt from conflicts and threats. But it is also the image of vigilance: Nehemiah and his people never let their guard down, they work with weapons in hand. For the believer, it is a call to remain vigilant against evil, spiritually armed. And the meaning of "shoot" invites us to see how life springs forth and renews itself, even in a difficult context.

sens: Antediluvian patriarch, son of Arphaxad and father of Eber
H7974.detail: Shelach is one of the patriarchs in the genealogy tracing back to Noah. He is the son of Arphaxad and the father of Eber, appearing in the genealogical line of the ancestors of Abraham and the people of Israel. According to the account in Genesis, he lived a long life: he fathered Eber at thirty years old (Genesis 11:14), and then lived four hundred three years after this birth before he died (Genesis 11:15). His name means "shoot" or "sprout," evoking the image of a young plant, which aligns with his role in the chain of transmission of life and divine promise through the generations.
H7974.origine: The name Shelach comes from the Hebrew root שָׁלַח (shalach) which means "to send" or "to throw out," but in this genealogical context, it carries the meaning of "shoot" or "sprout," suggesting the idea of a descendant that is sent forth. This character appears in the genealogy established after the flood, highlighting the continuity of the human and divine lineage through the patriarchs.
H7974.emploi: Shelach is mentioned seven times in the Bible, exclusively in the genealogies of Genesis and 1 Chronicles. He first appears in Genesis 10:24 in the table of nations establishing the descendants of Shem after the flood. He reappears in detail in Genesis 11:12-15, where the text precisely provides the ages at which he fathered his son Eber and the duration of his remaining life. These passages constitute the only biblical testimonies of this patriarch; they firmly place him in the genealogical succession leading to Abraham and Israel, without reporting any particular event from his life.
H7974.portee: Shelach represents an essential link in the genealogical chain through which God has led humanity from Noah to Abraham, and then to Jesus Christ. His presence reminds the believer of God's faithfulness in maintaining His promise through generations, passing through ordinary men of whom we only know the names and dates. This genealogy anchors the Israelite faith in a real and verifiable history, showing that salvation does not occur suddenly but unfolds in a historical progression ordained by God.

sens: Freshwater spring near Jerusalem
Basin or reservoir fed by this spring
Symbol of God's living water
H7975A.detail:
1. Siloah is a natural freshwater spring located southeast of Jerusalem, at the lower part of the city. In Nehemiah 3:15, it is an important enough location to be designated as a geographical landmark during the reconstruction of the walls after the Babylonian exile.

2. Around this spring, the Israelites dug a basin or pond (the "Pool of Siloah") to store the water. Nehemiah 3:15 mentions this reservoir that Shallum built, connected to the king's garden: it was a strategically and agriculturally important installation for the city of David.
H7975A.origine: The name Siloah comes from the Hebrew שִׁלּוֹחַ (shilloach), which literally means "sent" or "the one who is sent." This image evokes the water that flows, which is "sent" from the source to the reservoir. The Gihon spring (which flows secretly to the east of Jerusalem) feeds Siloah through an underground channel dug under King Hezekiah, as reported in the Kings. The name thus reflects the idea of flow, of the movement of water sent from one place to another.
H7975A.emploi: Siloah is mentioned once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nehemiah 3:15, during the account of the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile. This passage situates Siloah near the king's garden, indicating that it was a fertile and well-irrigated area essential to the life of the capital. Elsewhere in the Bible, the word appears in other prophetic or symbolic contexts (notably in Isaiah), but the use in Nehemiah shows it as a concrete topographical landmark and a hydraulic project.
H7975A.portee: Siloah reminds the reader that God provides living water, which is essential for life.
