For the early Christians, the spring of Siloah became a symbol of the Holy Spirit and overflowing grace. In Isaiah 8:6, the "waters of Siloah that flow gently" contrast with the waters of enemy rivers, expressing trust in divine protection. This image of a faithful and gentle spring enriches meditation on the life-giving presence of God.

sens: Fountain near Jerusalem
Source of gentle and fresh water
Symbol of divine sweetness
H7975B.detail:
1. Siloah is a fountain located southeast of Jerusalem, a natural water source that supplied the city. Its name means "sent" or "that flows," as the water springs forth and continuously flows there.
2. The Bible describes it as flowing "gently" (Isaiah 8:6), which emphasizes its tranquil and steady nature, in contrast to the tumultuous waters of other rivers. It is a reliable and beneficial source for those who receive it.
3. In the passage from Isaiah, it becomes the image of the Lord's gentleness and goodness toward His people, in contrast to the proud human powers that some Judeans preferred to follow.
H7975B.origine: The name "Siloah" comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to send" or "to flow out" — the water is literally "sent" or "that flows" there. This fountain is also called Shelah (which also means "sent"). It was well-known in antiquity as one of the main sources of freshwater in Jerusalem.
H7975B.emploi: Siloah appears only once in the books we possess, in Isaiah 8:6. The prophet mentions it to encourage the people of Judah to accept the quiet protection that God offers, rather than seeking noisy alliances with foreign powers. This real fountain becomes in Isaiah a living parable: its gentle and constant waters represent God's peaceful grace, while the "tumultuous waters" of other rivers symbolize human plans filled with noise and fury.
H7975B.portee: Siloah reminds us that God's providence, though often discreet and humble, is constant and sufficient. It invites us to trust in God's gentleness and faithfulness rather than chasing after noisy and superficial solutions. It is a lesson in humility and trust for every believer.

sens: Shoot or branch of a plant, tree, or vine
Extension, prolongation of a plant that spreads far
H7976.detail:
1. A branch is a shoot or young sprout that grows on a tree or vine. It is the part that develops from the trunk or main branches. In Isaiah 16:8, the prophet speaks of the branches of the vine of Sibmah that "stretched out and went beyond the sea," imagining how this vine spread widely across the landscape.
2. The word can also refer to any extension or offshoot of a plant that branches out. The biblical image here is of a lush vine whose branches extend far, symbolizing prosperity and growth.
H7976.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of sending out or putting outside (the verb שׁלַח, "to send"). A branch is literally what is "sent" or "pushed out" by the plant — a natural extension that comes from the trunk or the main branch. This image of unfolding is fundamental to the meaning of the word.
H7976.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 16:8. The context is one of lamentation over Moab: the prophet uses the image of the vine of Sibmah and its extended branches to evoke the past splendor and the prosperity that was collapsing. The use remains focused and poetic, in a description of loss and desolation.
H7976.portee: This image of branches that extended far speaks to Christians of the natural growth of what is alive, and also of its fragility: the most beautiful extensions can be broken. It reminds us that earthly prosperity is subject to change and may invite us to seek a more lasting spiritual growth.

sens: Grandfather of King Jehoshaphat
Father of Azubah
H7977.detail: Schilchi is the father of Azubah (or Azubah), who was the mother of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is encountered in the royal genealogies twice (1 Kings 22:42 and 2 Chronicles 20:31) during the presentation of Jehoshaphat and his reign. His name appears only in this genealogical context, to establish the maternal lineage of the king.
H7977.origine: The name Schilchi means "armed" in Hebrew, formed from a root evoking weapon or military equipment. It is a typical name from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel.
H7977.emploi: Schilchi appears only twice in the Bible, in the two parallel passages presenting King Jehoshaphat: in 1 Kings 22:42 and in 2 Chronicles 20:31. In both cases, he is cited as the father of Azubah, mentioned to establish the maternal ancestry of King Jehoshaphat. He is a minor historical figure, known only through his daughter and his famous grandson.

sens: City in the southern region of Judah
H7978.detail: Schilhim is a city located in the southern region of the territory of Judah. It appears in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the land distribution (Joshua 15:32). The name literally means "fountains" in Hebrew, likely evoking the presence of water sources in this arid region of the Negev. It is also another name for Sharuhen, an important locality in the south of the country.
H7978.origine: The Hebrew name שִׁלְחִים (shil-chim) derives from a root meaning "fountain" or "source." This etymology reflects the vital importance of water in the desert of southern Judah. The name designates a place characterized by its springs, a precious element in a semi-arid region. Schilhim is identified as another name for Sharuhen.
H7978.emploi: Schilhim appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:32, in the context of the enumeration of cities in the southern territory of Judah. It is mentioned between Lebaoth and Ain, among twenty-nine localities assigned to this tribe. This unique appearance in the Bible suggests that it was a minor city, important mainly during the land distribution under Joshua, without being the site of major events reported later.

sens: Wood or stone furniture with a flat surface, generally elevated, used for placing objects or eating
Altar table where the consecrated bread and offerings are placed
Meal taken in common around a table
Provision of food, maintenance
Set of dishes served at a meal
H7979.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a simple piece of furniture: a flat surface supported by legs. For example, Exodus 25:23 describes the table of the Lord's sanctuary, made of acacia wood, two cubits long and a cubit and a half high.
2. In worship, the table takes on religious significance: it is the sacred piece of furniture in the tabernacle and the temple where the showbread — the blessed bread — and offerings intended for the Lord are placed. Ezekiel 41:22 speaks of it: "Such was the table that was before the Lord."
3. The word also designates the act of eating together, shared hospitality. In 1 Samuel 20:29, David explains: "He did not come to the king's table," meaning he did not participate in the royal meal.
4. "Table" can evoke the maintenance one receives, the sustenance provided by someone. Nehemiah 5:17 clearly shows this: "I had at my table one hundred fifty men" — meaning he fed them daily.
5. Finally, the word designates the set of dishes, the courses served at a feast. 1 Kings 10:5 states: "the dishes of his table," referring to the splendor of the king's food.
H7979.origine: The Hebrew word שֻׁלְחָן (shulchan) likely comes from a root meaning "to spread" or "to set up," evoking the action of preparing a flat surface. This term belongs to the family of words designating domestic and sacred utensils. The table was a symbolic piece of furniture in daily life and especially in worship: the tabernacle and the temple always contained one, sanctified and reserved for the bread and offerings.
H7979.emploi: The word שֻׁלְחָן appears sixty-two times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of Exodus and Ezekiel. Sacred uses dominate: descriptions of the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 25, 37; Ezekiel 40-44) enumerate the tables of gold or stone, their dimensions, their ritual destination. Alongside this cultic usage, the word appears in familial and royal contexts: Nehemiah speaks of his own table where he receives guests, 2 Samuel mentions the meals of King David. The psalms and the prophets also use it: Psalms 23:5 evokes the table prepared before the Lord for the faithful, while Malachi criticizes those who defile the Lord's table with their despised offerings.
H7979.portee: For the Christian, the word "table" evokes several truths. First, it reminds us that worship of the Lord requires order and beauty: the tabernacle was a place where every object, including the table, was measured and consecrated. Next, the table evokes hospitality and sharing: eating together binds people, and this reflects the communion that God wants to establish with His people. Finally, for those reading the New Testament, the image of the "Lord's table" — and that of the Last Supper — finds its roots here in the Old Testament: a set table, offered dishes, a covenant meeting.

sens: to exercise power over someone, to be the master
to oppress, to subdue by force
to have authority, control over something
H7980.detail:
1. To dominate means to have power over a person or group and to exercise it as a master. It is to be the one who commands and controls. In Esther 9:1, the Jews "dominated over their enemies": they took power over them and defeated them.
2. The word can take on a negative nuance when this power becomes oppression or crushing. In Nehemiah 5:15, the former governors "oppressed the people" with their unjust demands. It is the same root, but used to describe an abuse of power.
3. To dominate can also mean to have mastery or control over something: to be the master of a possession or situation. In Ecclesiastes 5:18, a man is "master" of eating and taking his share — he has the power to enjoy his goods. This is a beneficial control, a right of use.
H7980.origine: The Hebrew root שׁלט comes from an image of strength and domination. It is related to the idea of taking in hand, seizing power. In Aramaic, the close form שְׁלֵט (she.let) has the same meaning: "to reign" or "to dominate." This verb expresses the action of one who has a strong hand and imposes his will.
H7980.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical and poetic books. In Esther 9:1 and in the Psalms, to dominate evokes combat and victory: the one who dominates gains the advantage. In the laments of Ecclesiastes, the word takes on an existential hue: to be master of one's goods (5:18, 6:2) or to fear that sin may dominate over oneself (Psalms 119:133). The verb thus covers several nuances: to dominate militarily, to oppress economically, or to possess mastery over something. Its meaning oscillates between political power and personal possession.
H7980.portee: This word reminds us that all power and mastery come from God. For the Christian, it is a call to examine one's heart: over what does he exercise domination? Does he seek to oppress or to serve? Psalm 119:133 beautifully expresses this tension: to pray that sin does not dominate us is to acknowledge that we need God's strength to remain free.

sens: to exercise power over someone or something
to command a territory or a people
to establish someone in a position of authority
H7981.detail:
1. To exercise power over someone or something: this means having an authority that imposes itself, a concrete mastery. In Daniel 2:38, Nebuchadnezzar "dominates" over the children of men, the beasts, and the birds — a total and absolute domination.
2. To command a territory or a people: the verb describes one who reigns over an entire kingdom. In Daniel 2:39, the third kingdom "will dominate over all the earth," making it the undisputed master.
3. To establish someone in a position of authority: this means placing a person at the head, entrusting them with the "government" or "command." In Daniel 2:48, the king elevates Daniel and gives him command over Babylon — he constitutes him as chief.
H7981.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root that fundamentally means "to have power" or "to hold firmly." The verb appears in two main forms: a simple form (P'al) that emphasizes the act of dominating or reigning, and a causative form (Aphel) that means "to make reign" or "to establish in power." This root expresses the idea of seizing and maintaining control.
H7981.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears seven times in the book of Daniel, almost exclusively. It describes either the exercise of royal and political power (Nebuchadnezzar dominating over men and beasts, the kingdoms succeeding one another in world domination), or the establishment of a specific administrative charge (Daniel being appointed governor of Babylon). A particular occurrence in Daniel 3:27 uses the word to say that the fire "had no power" over the three men — the term denotes the absence of effect or domination. The context is always that of earthly power and the administration of human affairs.
H7981.portee: This word shows that all human power, even seemingly absolute — that of a Babylonian king over an empire — ultimately depends on God. In Daniel, it is God who elevates and establishes in command; the kingdoms that succeed one another in world domination are all subject to His plan. For the believer, this teaches that no authority can persist against the will of God, and that even the small — like the three young men — are protected beyond all earthly power.

sens: A piece of armor carried on the arm to protect against blows and arrows
A set of warrior equipment, combat weapons
Protection, covering that defends
H7982.detail: 1. The shield is the defensive weapon that the warrior carries to protect himself in battle. It is a solid object, often made of metal (gold, bronze) or wood covered with leather, held on the arm or in the hand. David reports gold shields from the servants of Hadadezer (2 Samuel 8:7), and the shields of King David are kept in the temple as treasures and war relics (2 Kings 11:10). 2. The word can also refer to the entire set of weapons and military equipment of a king or an army, the instruments of warrior power. It is in this sense that the shields "came from King David" and are stored in the house of God as symbols of His authority and past strength. 3. Figuratively, the shield becomes an image of protection and defense: the tower of David, adorned with a thousand shields hanging, evokes an impregnable and majestic fortress (Song of Solomon 4:4).
H7982.origine: The Hebrew word שֶׁלֶט (shelet) specifically denotes the shield, the defensive equipment of the warrior. Its exact etymology is obscure, but it belongs to the ancient vocabulary of war in Israel. The word is used throughout the Old Testament to speak of defensive weapons and, by extension, of protection in general.
H7982.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in biblical poetry. It always denotes a concrete element of armor or military equipment: the gold shields plundered by David (2 Samuel 8:7 and 1 Chronicles 18:7), those that the high priest gives to the captains of hundreds (2 Kings 11:10 and 2 Chronicles 23:9), the shields hanging on the tower of David as a sign of royal power (Song of Solomon 4:4), and finally those that soldiers seize at the moment of battle (Jeremiah 51:11). The context is always warrior, royal, or ritual.
H7982.portee: The shield reminds the believer that protection comes from God, even though the warriors of Israel bore material weapons. When the Bible speaks of the shields of King David kept in the temple, it shows how past victories and gifts received from God become monuments to His memory. This image of the equipped warrior also invites the reader to meditate on the "breastplate of righteousness" and the spiritual armor with which God clothes those who believe in Him.

sens: Force or authority that imposes itself
Ability to dominate, to master something
Power over life and death
H7983.detail:
1. The word denotes the power of a word or authority that imposes itself with force. In Ecclesiastes 8:4, the word of the king is "powerful" — it carries so much weight that no one dares to ask the king: "What are you doing?" It is a force that commands respect and obedience.
2. It is also the ability to master or dominate something: to have power over someone or something. The example in Ecclesiastes 8:8 shows that man has no "power" over the day of his death — he cannot hold it back or control it, even if he wanted to.
3. By extension, this power concerns the domains where life and death are decided — the breath, the fateful day — which exceeds human power and belongs solely to divine authority.
H7983.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of strength and domination. Aramaic uses the word "chésen" (authority) to express the same notion. This vocabulary is rooted in the experience of royal and political power: one who has power commands, decides, imposes his will.
H7983.emploi: The word appears only twice in biblical Hebrew, both in Ecclesiastes. First, it qualifies the word of the king: it is "powerful" because it engages royal authority and no one dares to openly contradict it. Secondly, it designates what man does not possess — no power over the moment of his death, no dominion over the breath that leaves the body. In these two uses, the word reveals the contrast between a real but limited human power (that of the king) and the radical impotence of any human before ultimate realities: death, fate.
H7983.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that all human power — even that of a king — is fragile and relative. Only God truly masters life, death, and fate. This invites us not to fear earthly authorities, but to recognize that all true authority comes from God and is accountable to Him. For the believer, it is an invitation to trust and humility.

sens: Official who exercises administrative or judicial authority under a king
Official responsible for the administration of a province or territory
Judge or person holding an official position
H7984.detail:
1. The word designates an official invested with authority, either in an administrative domain or in judicial matters. In Daniel 3:2, King Nebuchadnezzar summons the magistrates of the provinces to attend the dedication of his statue: these are officials appointed by the central power to govern the regions.
2. In an imperial context, the magistrate is often a functionary in the service of the king, who directs a province or city. The repetition in Daniel 3:2-3 ("all the magistrates of the provinces") emphasizes that these men form an official body, an administrative hierarchy placed under royal authority.
3. The term can also refer to a person who administers justice or holds an important judicial position, although the emphasis here is on their function as a representative of the king's power in conquered territories.
H7984.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁלְטוֹן (shilton) is derived from a root that expresses the idea of domination or power. It is related to the verb "to dominate" or "to reign." The term designates one who holds a share of royal authority, delegated to command a region or perform an official function.
H7984.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Daniel 3, in verses 2 and 3. It is used in the account of Nebuchadnezzar's statue, where the king gathers all the magistrates of his empire for an act of worship or allegiance. The context is that of a multicultural empire (Babylon) where power is delegated to officials tasked with governing on behalf of the king. These magistrates form a well-structured administrative class, hierarchically alongside other dignitaries (satraps, stewards, judges).
H7984.portee: This word reminds us that human authority, even when organized and official, remains subordinate to God. The spectacle of all these magistrates gathered shows the temporal power of kingdoms — but it is in this very context that God's judgment on Nebuchadnezzar's idolatry intervenes. For the Christian reader, this underscores the relativity of earthly powers and the importance of placing God above all political authority.

sens: The absolute power exercised by a king or an empire over a territory and its inhabitants
The extent of the territory subjected to this sovereign authority
The power and authority that allow for governance
The right to command and impose one's will
H7985.detail:
1. Domination primarily refers to the absolute power that a king exercises over his kingdom. When Daniel says that Nebuchadnezzar's domination "extends to the ends of the earth" (Daniel 4:22), he speaks of the king's political and military control over all the peoples subject to his empire. It is the power of one who reigns.
2. The word also describes the physical extent of this power — the territory itself over which this authority is exercised. When the king orders "throughout the extent of my kingdom" (Daniel 6:26), shol.tan refers to the entirety of the royal domain, from the center to the borders.
3. It is also the concrete power: the ability to act, to command, to make obey. When "domination" is given to an animal (Daniel 7:6), the text means that power to reign and dominate over other beasts is conferred to it.
4. Finally, it can designate the eternal authority of God himself. When Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges that divine domination "is an eternal domination" (Daniel 4:34), he affirms that only God possesses an authority that will never pass away, unlike the kingdoms of men.
H7985.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root related to the idea of mastery and control. In biblical Aramaic (the language of Daniel), shol.tan denotes the power of the sovereign, one who holds everything in his hand. This root evokes the image of a grip that tightens, of an authority that is not disputed. The word is closely linked to the idea of kingship and absolute governance.
H7985.emploi: The word shol.tan appears 9 times in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Daniel, which recounts the visions of successive kingdoms and their downfall. It is used first to describe the domination of earthly kings — especially that of Nebuchadnezzar, which extends far and lasts long (Daniel 4:3, 4:22, 7:6). But gradually, the word takes on a higher meaning: it designates the domination of God that lasts "from generation to generation" (Daniel 4:34) and that of the Son of Man in the eternal Kingdom (Daniel 7:14, 7:27). Thus, the text contrasts human dominations, limited and temporary — like that which is taken away from the animals (Daniel 7:12) — with the divine domination that alone is absolute and unshakeable.
H7985.portee: This distinction between ephemeral kingdoms and the eternal domination of God encourages the believer not to fear earthly powers, however impressive they may be. It reminds us that all human authority, even the largest empire, is limited and transient, while the Kingdom of God alone lasts forever. For the Christian, this affirms that history belongs only to God.

sens: Woman who dominates, who commands with authority
Woman who rules despotically, imposing her will without scruple
H7986.detail:
1. A woman who exercises dominant power, who takes charge and gives orders. It conveys the idea of asserted and tyrannical authority.
2. In Ezekiel 16:30, the word describes a prostitute who acts as an imperious mistress: she does not submit, she imposes, she reigns over her partners. The image underscores the cynical audacity of one who abuses her power of seduction.
H7986.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of dominating, reigning, imposing oneself forcefully. It designates one who masters, who has the reins in hand. The prophetic context of Ezekiel associates it with the image of a tyrannical sovereign.
H7986.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 16:30. Jeremiah reproaches Jerusalem, personified as an unfaithful woman, for behaving not as a submissive victim, but as an audacious and shameless mistress, one who reigns and imposes her law. It is a rare word, chosen for its dramatic weight.
H7986.portee: This term helps the reader understand the gravity of divine judgment: Jerusalem does not excuse herself, she does not groan under the yoke, she glorifies herself in her rebellion. She acts as an imperious mistress before her God. It is an image of pride and insolence that makes sin all the more grave.

sens: What is hidden, out of the sight of others
A conversation or action conducted out of the view or hearing of others
The discreet or private nature of a thing
H7987.detail:
1. The word designates what is withdrawn, hidden, away from sight. In 2 Samuel 3:27, Joab takes Abner "in secret" in the midst of the gate, meaning away, in a place where people cannot see, to strike him without a witness.
2. The meaning extends to the idea of tranquility or calm — what happens in private, away from public agitation. It is a place or moment of isolation, sheltered from view.
3. By extension, the word carries the idea of intimacy or discretion: what belongs to the private sphere rather than the public.
H7987.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of separation, of distancing. The word belongs to the family of terms that designate what is set apart, tranquil, private — the initial image is that of something or someone who moves away from the group, who withdraws. This notion of withdrawal and isolation also carries the idea of calm and tranquility.
H7987.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Hebrew, in 2 Samuel 3:27. It describes the moment when Joab leads Abner away, "in secret," to assassinate him away from witnesses. It is a concrete usage: not a secret kept, but a secret place, a situation conducted out of sight. The context shows the sinister use of the word: the secret becomes the means to commit a crime without a witness.
H7987.portee: This passage reminds us that darkness — secrecy, the absence of a witness — facilitates evil. For the Christian reader, this underscores the importance of living in the light, without fear of others' gaze, and refusing acts that must be hidden. God sees everything: no secret escapes Him.

sens: membrane and tissue expelled after the birth of the baby
last-resort food in case of extreme famine
H7988.detail:
1. The afterbirth is the envelope and tissue expelled from the mother's body after the birth of the child. It is a crude and anatomical term, referring to something that the Israelites knew from experience, related to every birth.
2. In Deuteronomy 28:57, Moses evokes a horrifying picture: a besieged and starving mother who will secretly eat even that tissue out of despair and hunger. It is the ultimate image of destitution and famine, an extreme example showing how God's curse would drive Israel to acts contrary to nature.
H7988.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁלְיָה comes from a root that denotes the back or what comes after. It is an anatomical and medical term related to childbirth. The word is rare in the Old Testament and refers to a well-known biological reality but rarely named so directly.
H7988.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 28:57. It is part of the list of curses that God promises to Israel if they disobey His covenant. This passage describes famine and siege so terrible that even a mother would lose all maternal instinct. The crude term underscores the unimaginable extent of the catastrophe: it indicates how far physical distress can lead a human being.
H7988.portee: This verse shocks because it names the unspeakable: it reveals what God sees as the consequences of sin and the rejection of His covenant. It is not a text of gratuitous threat, but a warning that takes human dignity and the horror of sin seriously. It calls for repentance and shows why obedience to God is inseparable from life, peace, and abundance.

sens: One who exercises power over others, who commands
One who has authority and dominion in a particular area
One who imposes his will imperiously or tyrannically
H7989.detail:
1. The master is one who holds power and commands: he is a sovereign or ruler. Joseph in Egypt is presented as master of the land, selling grain and receiving the submission of all (Genesis 42:6). It is recognized and established authority.
2. The master possesses dominion or mastery in a particular area. Wisdom, says Ecclesiastes, makes the wise more powerful than ten rulers of a city (Ecclesiastes 7:19): this is a form of power and influence. Man, on the other hand, is not master of his own breath and cannot retain his life (Ecclesiastes 8:8): here, "master" means having authority and control.
3. The word also designates one who governs imperiously, even tyrannically. Ecclesiastes reports errors committed by the one who governs (Ecclesiastes 10:5), highlighting how power can be exercised inappropriately. It conveys the idea of domination that sometimes imposes itself abusively.
H7989.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of dominating, reigning, or extending one's power over something or someone. This root evokes the action of holding something in hand, controlling it. The word also appears in Aramaic (shallit), where it carries the meaning of "one who reigns." It is a term that emphasizes less the legitimacy of power than its concrete and palpable exercise.
H7989.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in Ecclesiastes and Genesis. In Genesis 42:6, Joseph "commands" in Egypt: it is real and recognized power. In Ecclesiastes 7:19 and 8:8, the word designates either one who possesses public authority (the rulers) or the ability to dominate (mastering one's breath). In Ecclesiastes 10:5, it refers to the ruler and the errors he may commit. The context of Ecclesiastes often colors the word with a certain critique: human power is vanity or a source of disorder.
H7989.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the nature of power and authority. It is not absolute: a man is neither master of his breath, nor of death, nor truly of what he believes he dominates. Only God possesses true mastery. For the believer, it is a call to accept the limits of one's own power and not to place trust in human authority, which is fragile and often misused.

sens: To exercise power, mastery over someone or something
One who holds authority, power
To be authorized, permitted, legitimate
H7990.detail:
1. To exercise power, mastery over someone or something: it is the action of commanding, directing, controlling. It is the power that a king exercises over his kingdom or that a powerful person exerts over others. Daniel 4:17 expresses it clearly: "the Most High rules over the kingdom of men."
2. One who holds authority, power: it is the person who commands, who governs. Ezra 4:20 speaks of "mighty kings, masters of all the land." Daniel 2:15 designates Arjoc as "commander of the king."
3. To be authorized, permitted, legitimate: it is to have the right to do something, official authorization. Ezra 7:24 states that no tribute can be "levied" on the priests and servants of the Temple, in other words, no one has the legal authority to do so.
H7990.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of control and power. It appears in other forms to describe one who reigns or has authority. The basic meaning evokes the image of someone holding something in hand, dominating it.
H7990.emploi: This word appears about ten times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel. It is mainly used to speak of royal and divine power. In Ezra, it describes earthly kings who reign with authority (Ezra 4:20) and the legal authorization given by the king (Ezra 7:24). In Daniel, especially in chapters 4 and 5, it repeatedly asserts that it is God who truly rules over the kingdom of men (Daniel 4:17, 4:25), far beyond any human power. This is a central affirmation of the book of Daniel: despite the appearance of Babylonian power, it is the God of Israel who truly reigns.
H7990.portee: This word reminds the reader that all earthly power, even that of the most feared kings, is only apparent. It is God alone who truly and definitively dominates history and the kingdoms of men. For the Christian, it is a source of assurance and faith: whatever the events of the world, the ultimate dominion belongs to God.

sens: a portion of about one-third of a bucket or volume unit
a determined quantity used to proportion or distribute
a portion or share in a division
H7991A.detail:
1. The word designates a capacity measure, probably equivalent to about one-third of a larger unit (like a bucket or an ephah). It is a concrete unit for measuring liquids or solids. In Isaiah 40:12, the prophet speaks of God who "gathers the dust of the earth in a third of a measure," which shows the immensity of the Creator capable of holding in His hand a measure that, in reality, would be heavy.
2. More broadly, the word can refer to a portion, a share, or a quantity distributed according to a proportion. In Psalms 80:6, the text says that God quenches His people "with tears in full measure": this is an image of the abundance of sorrow poured out, as if the tears were distributed by this unit of measure, showing that the people receive it generously.
3. The meaning can be generalized to any portion or division in a sharing, without strict reference to a technical measure.
H7991A.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "three" (shalosh). A third is thus by nature a division into three equal parts. This root is found in the names of numbers and words related to tripartition. The starting image is simple: dividing a whole into three portions and taking one. The word then designated a standard unit of measure, probably because it represented a third of a larger measure.
H7991A.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 80:6, it describes how God quenches the people with tears: the "measure" evokes an abundance distributed, a kind of ration poured out generously. In Isaiah 40:12, in a context of grand cosmology, God gathers the dust of the earth "in a third of a measure," which emphasizes the contrast between the immensity of creation and the smallness of the divine measure. In both uses, the word is concrete (a unit of volume) but acquires a symbolic significance: it measures not only substances but also the extent of divine power.
H7991A.portee: This word reminds us that God controls everything with perfect precision and accuracy: He measures even the tears of the people and holds the entire universe within His reach. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize divine sovereignty over all things, from the smallest detail to the cosmos. The word transforms a simple unit of measure into a sign of God's providence.

sens: percussion musical instrument, probably triangular in shape or composed of three bars
symbol of rejoicing and gladness in public celebrations
H7991B.detail:
1. The triangle is a percussion musical instrument, likely triangular in shape or made up of three metallic elements. It was sounded by striking it, and its high, clear sound could be heard from afar. In 1 Samuel 18:6, the women of Israel play the triangle to celebrate David's return from victory against the Philistine, which shows that it accompanied joyful songs and dances.
2. By extension, the triangle is associated with festivity, dance, and the noisy expression of communal joy. The text of 1 Samuel 18:6 shows it used not as an instrument of solemn worship, but as an accessory of popular rejoicing: the women accompany it with singing and dancing to welcome their victorious king.
H7991B.origine: The word likely comes from a root meaning "three," either because the instrument had three strings, or because it was composed of three bars or had a triangular shape with three sides. This connection with the number three defines its distinct character among Israelite percussion instruments. Other instruments of the same group in the Bible include the tambourine and cymbals, all present in the same festive contexts.
H7991B.emploi: The triangle appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 18:6. This passage places it in a scene of military victory and solemn reception of the king: David returns victorious from the battle against Goliath, and all Israel comes out to meet him with music and dance. The triangle is among the instruments of the women expressing their joy. It is a popular, easily transportable instrument capable of producing a bright and noticeable sound, ideal for outdoor celebrations.
H7991B.portee: The triangle reminds us that joy and festivity are legitimate in the life of the believer, especially when they celebrate the works and victories of God. Its appearance alongside song and dance shows that praise to God can take joyful and communal forms, involving the body and the senses. For the Christian, this invites a whole, bodily, and expressive praise that expresses gratitude.

sens: Elite warrior or soldier attached to a chief or king
Military aide who fights alongside a commander
Administrative or military official in the palace or army
One who carries the shield or equipment of a superior
H7991C.detail: 1. The word primarily designates an elite warrior, often placed in the direct service of a king or military chief. In Exodus 14:7, the "fighters" of Egypt are these elite soldiers that Pharaoh places on his war chariots. 2. It is also a military officer who holds a rank of authority and can lead other men. The Tachmonite was "one of the chief officers" of David (2 Samuel 23:8), which shows his high rank among the king's warriors. 3. In the administrative context, it refers to a royal palace official who holds an official position. The "officer" on whose hand the king leaned (2 Kings 7:2) was a high-ranking official who had direct access to the sovereign and influenced his decisions. 4. Originally, the word evokes one who carries the shield or equipment of a chief, hence its meaning of aide or military assistant attached to a superior.
H7991C.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁלִישׁ comes from the root שָׁלוֹשׁ (three), hence its primary meaning: "the third" or "one who is a third." In the military context, it designates the third man of a chariot — after the driver and the main fighter — who carried the shield or the equipment of the chief. By extension, it became an honorific term to designate the trusted men of a king, his officers, and high-ranking military advisors.
H7991C.emploi: This word appears about fifteen times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and royal books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles). It always designates men of power: David's mighty men, the officers of the king of Israel, the Egyptian warriors in Pharaoh's service. In 2 Kings 10:25, the "officers" of Jehu are his trusted men who carry out his murderous orders. The word can also apply to the chief or commander himself, as in Proverbs where it appears in a context of royal wisdom. Its use always indicates a person of high rank, trustworthy and authoritative.
H7991C.portee: This word reminds us that in God's eyes, rank and position do not exempt one from moral judgment. The officer in 2 Kings 7:2 doubts the word of Elisha and pays for it with his life — his proximity to the king does not save him. For the Christian, this underscores that human responsibility and power are temporary: only faith in God and obedience to His word are enduring.

sens: The number three in an ordered series (first, second, third…)
An equal portion of one third (one out of three)
A day, a month, or a year that holds the rank of three
The third occurrence or repetition of an event
H7992.detail:
1. The most common meaning is ordinal: it is the number 3 when counting a sequence. Genesis 1:13 speaks of the "third day" of creation, the day when God caused vegetation to sprout. It is simply the position 3 in the order.

2. The word also designates a share: one third, meaning a division into three equal portions. Leviticus 7:18 concerns the meat of the sacrifice eaten on the "third day" — but when the text speaks of "the third part" (Joshua 19:10), it refers to the third of the lands, one share out of three assigned to Zebulun by lot.

3. Applied to calendars, "third" designates the month of rank three (Esther 8:9: "the third month, which is the month of Sivan") or a year counted from an event. In 1 Kings 18:1, the "third year" means three years after the beginning of the drought.

4. The word can also express a repetition. In 1 Samuel 3:8, when God calls Samuel "the third time," it shows a series of successive calls — God has already called twice, here is the third call.
H7992.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root שׁלשׁ (shalash), which expresses the idea of "three" or "to braid, triple." The adjective "third" naturally derives from it. In Hebrew, ordinal numbers (first, second, third…) are formed from cardinal numbers (one, two, three…) with appropriate suffixes. The word is very ancient and belongs to the fundamental numerical vocabulary of Semitic languages.
H7992.emploi: This word appears 93 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical, chronological, and legislative contexts. It is used to order the days of creation (Genesis 1:13), to count time in years and months (1 Kings 18:1, Esther 8:9), and to number divisions: the three tiers of an ark (Genesis 6:16), the three levels of objects of worship (1 Kings 6:6), the three sons of a character (2 Samuel 3:3). It also appears in genealogical lists and the organization of worship (1 Chronicles 24:8). Leviticus uses "third" for rules of sacrificial consumption: meat can only be eaten until the third day. Nowhere does it carry a figurative or mystical meaning: it is always an index of rank or number.
H7992.portee: This simple word reminds us that the Bible does not hesitate to report the temporal and practical details of ordinary life. The rules regarding the third day (as in Leviticus) show that the people of God honors order, the delimitation of time, and obeys concrete prescriptions. The counting of days and years also reveals the biblical importance of waiting and promise: the three days of fasting before the walls of Susa (Esther 5:1), the resurrection on the third day — all of this rests on a trustworthy measure of time.

sens: To project something violently away from oneself
To abandon or reject
To set aside, to get rid of
To pour, to spread or to scatter
To cast (a lot, a net) with a specific intention
To be thrown, to fall or to undergo expulsion
H7993.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to project an object with force. Moses throws the tablets of the Law against the rock (Exodus 32:19); the Egyptians are hurled into the Red Sea like stones to the bottom of the waters (Nehemiah 9:11). It is a violent, irrepressible gesture of rejection.
2. To abandon or reject someone: to reject a covenant (Psalms 50:17), to abandon a newborn child (Ezekiel 16:5: "cast into the fields"). The word designates the brutal gesture of getting rid of what one deems undesirable.
3. To set aside, to get rid of: to remove impure things from a temple (Nehemiah 13:8), to throw away garbage (Ecclesiastes 3:6). It is cleaning by expelling.
4. To pour, to spread or to scatter: Moses throws powder on the water to make it drinkable (Exodus 15:25); the fishermen cast the hook into the river (Isaiah 19:8), meaning they launch it to fish.
5. To cast (a lot): to cast lots with the Urim (Joshua 18:10) to seek God's will. It is a deliberate, ritual act.
6. To be thrown, to undergo expulsion: when one has a horror of someone, one throws them out. It is the passive form of violent rejection.
H7993.origine: The Hebrew verb shalakh comes from a root that evokes throwing, projecting with force. The form encountered in these usages is the "hiphil" (or causative), which makes the action transitive: "to cause to be thrown" or simply "to throw." The word carries a strong emotional charge: to throw means not only to move an object but to abandon it intentionally, often with anger or contempt. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), it is often translated by verbs like rhiptô (to throw), which retains this same idea of violence.
H7993.emploi: The verb throw appears 121 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is very frequent in narratives: throwing someone into a pit (Genesis 37:20-24: Joseph thrown by his brothers), throwing water in plagues (Exodus 7:9-10: staffs turned into serpents), throwing the golden calf into powder (Exodus 32:19-24: Moses). It is also found in a ritual context: casting lots to discern divine will. In the Psalms, "to throw" takes on a spiritual charge: God does not throw away his faithful (Psalms 71:9), but he throws away his enemies (Psalms 2:3). The meaning nuances between the concrete physical action and moral or divine rejection.
H7993.portee: This word speaks of the violence of rejection, but also of divine sovereignty. When the Lord "throws" a people out of their land (Deuteronomy 29:28), it signifies a radical rupture, an unappealable punishment. Conversely, when one prays to God not to cast us away from his presence (Psalms 71:9), one implores that he does not abandon us. The word also teaches the importance of what we reject: abandoning idols to powder (Exodus 32:20) or throwing away garbage (Ecclesiastes 3:6) is part of purification. For the believer, it is a reminder: what do you throw away from your life, and what do you ask God not to throw away from his?

sens: Diving aquatic bird mentioned in the lists of unclean animals
Bird of prey or carnivorous bird of the waters
H7994.detail:
1. The diver is an aquatic bird, meaning a bird that lives near water and dives to feed. In Leviticus 11:17 and Deuteronomy 14:17, it appears in the lists of animals that the Israelites were not to eat, classified among unclean birds alongside other fowl like the pelican and the cormorant.
2. It is a carnivorous bird or a bird of prey from the waters, which feeds by diving. Its predatory and aquatic nature made it an unclean animal according to Mosaic law, alongside other birds of prey.
H7994.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁלָךְ (shalakh) likely refers to the arctic diver or a similar bird. Although the exact etymology is uncertain, the word evokes the image of a bird that "dives" or "leaps" (the root may be related to rapid movement or immersion). The biblical context systematically places it among aquatic and carnivorous birds deemed unclean.
H7994.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the dietary codes of Leviticus and Deuteronomy. In Leviticus 11:17, it is listed among a series of birds forbidden for consumption: "the owl, the diver, and the hawk." In Deuteronomy 14:17, it reappears in a similar list alongside the pelican and the cormorant. Its usage is purely administrative and legislative: it serves to identify prohibited animals, without any other theological or narrative nuance.
H7994.portee: These lists of unclean animals teach the Israelites to maintain a ritual separation between the clean and the unclean. Although the prohibition of the diver is revoked by the Gospel (Acts 10:15), it reminds us that the Mosaic law guided the ancient people of God in the concrete practice of their holiness, distinguishing them from neighboring peoples.

sens: The part of a tree trunk that remains in the ground after cutting
What persists, survives, or continues despite destruction
A remnant, a seed that can be reborn or renewed
H7995.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the trunk or stump of a tree that remains embedded in the soil after the tree has been cut down. In Isaiah 6:13, the terebinth and the oak "retain their trunk when they are felled": even mutilated, the tree leaves a living remnant in the ground.
2. Figuratively, this represents what survives total destruction, what remains when everything seems lost. The stump symbolizes the hope of rebirth: as long as it exists, life can begin anew.
3. For Isaiah, it is the promise that even if the Jewish people are destroyed and scattered, a remnant will survive, a "holy offspring" that will rise from the ruins, just as a new tree sprouts from the old stump.
H7995.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root meaning "to leave, abandon," hence the idea of what "remains" or "subsists." It belongs to the family of words expressing the remnant, the relic, what remains when the rest disappears. This image of the persistent stump is found in biblical theology of the "remnant": even in the midst of judgment, God allows a living core to persist that guarantees continuity and hope.
H7995.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 6:13. The prophet uses it to announce to King Ahaz that, despite the invasion and devastation of the kingdom of Judah, a remnant will survive and give birth to a new faithful generation. The image of the persistent stump becomes a key to the theology of salvation: it expresses that God's judgment is never total and irrevocable, and that it always leaves room for restoration.
H7995.portee: This word speaks directly to the heart of the believer who is going through trials or living in a world of moral or spiritual ruins. It says that God never completely abandons His people, that a seed of life always remains, even in apparent destruction. It is a promise of hope: just as the stump can give rise to a vigorous tree, one who remains faithful to God can see new life sprout from their ruins.

sens: gate of the Jerusalem temple, located to the west
H7996.detail: Schalleketh is the name of a gate of the Jerusalem temple, placed on the west side of the building. Its Hebrew name evokes the idea of "overturning" or "destruction," probably due to its function: it was through this gate that debris and refuse were evacuated from the temple. It stood on the ascending path, and two guards faced each other to ensure its surveillance, one inside and the other outside (1 Chronicles 26:16).
H7996.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to overturn," "to throw out." This descriptive name clearly indicates the use of this gate: it served to evacuate what no longer had a place in the sanctuary. It is an example of the practical and meaningful names given to the various entrances of the temple.
H7996.emploi: Schalleketh appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:16, in the list of the temple gates and their guards established during the reign of King David. This passage enumerates the different entrances of the temple and assigns Levites to guard each one. Schalleketh, distinguished as the west gate on the ascending path, had a particular function in the sacred topography of the temple.
H7996.portee: This precise mention of Schalleketh recalls the meticulous order of worship in the temple and the importance given to every detail of the liturgical service, even to gates intended for the evacuation of debris. It shows that all functions of the temple, even the most mundane, fell within the sacred domain and required vigilant guarding.

sens: Take away, withdraw something from a place or situation
Extract, take out from
H7997A.detail:
1. Remove means to take something from its place or from where it is located. In Ruth 2:16, the harvesters must "remove" ears of grain from the sheaves so that Ruth can glean: it involves intentionally taking certain ears from the main lot to make them accessible to the gleaner.
2. The verb also evokes the idea of extracting or pulling something towards oneself, of making it come out from where it was. It is a movement that takes a part from a whole.
H7997A.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁלַל (shaláal) primarily expresses the action of pulling, removing, or taking. It belongs to the family of words that describe movements of separation and extraction. The root evokes the idea of detaching something from its context to take or remove it.
H7997A.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Ruth 2:16. It describes the concrete act of the harvesters who voluntarily remove ears of grain from the sheaves to allow Ruth to glean. It is an act of generosity and respect for the law of Leviticus: leaving the poor to glean the leftovers. The context shows that the removal is regulated, orderly, unlike simple looting.
H7997A.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of generosity towards the poor. Elimelech's harvesters do not merely tolerate gleaning: they actively facilitate Ruth's work by removing ears of grain for her, transforming a legal right into a fraternal act. This shows how God's law, when well applied, becomes an expression of charity.

sens: Take away by force the goods of a person or a city
Strip someone of what they possess
Seize, take as war booty
H7997B.detail: 1. Plunder means to take by violence and injustice what belongs to another: goods, wealth, merchandise. It is the act of the conqueror or the brigand who strips their victim. In Ezekiel 26:12, the riches of Tyre will be "taken away" and its goods will be "plundered": it is a systematic destruction of a defeated city. 2. To strip means to take away everything someone had, leaving them without resources. Psalm 76:6 describes warrior heroes "stripped" of their strength, unable to defend themselves. 3. The word can also describe one who suffers this violence: in Isaiah 59:15, one who turns away from evil is "stripped" by a world without justice. 4. To take booty means to gather for oneself the spoils of war: in Ezekiel 29:19, the army of King Nebuchadnezzar will "carry away the riches" and "take the spoils" of Egypt.
H7997B.origine: The Hebrew root sha.lal evokes the action of removing, seizing violently. It is linked to the idea of booty, prey torn away by force. The word appears in the context of war and divine judgment: God allows nations to plunder His enemies as an instrument of His justice.
H7997B.emploi: The verb plunder appears 11 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk). It always describes a violent warfare or judgment: the plundering of nations defeated by their conquerors, notably Babylon plundering Egypt. Sometimes God Himself declares that He will "deliver" a nation to plunder as punishment. The word can also be used in the passive to say that one is stripped, dispossessed of their goods.
H7997B.portee: This word reminds us that unjust violence against the weak is a crime in the eyes of God, and that plunder is among divine judgments. It invites the reader not to exploit others and to place their trust in God rather than in riches.

sens: What is taken from the enemy in battle: goods, livestock, money, precious items
What a wild beast catches and devours for nourishment
What is stolen or plundered during an ordinary crime
Any gain or acquisition
Figuratively: what is earned or obtained after a struggle
H7998.detail:
1. Spoil is primarily the right of the victor: after battle, Israel kept the herds and goods conquered (Joshua 8:27), and the leaders shared this spoil according to God's order, sometimes dedicating it to the Temple (1 Chronicles 26:27).
2. It is also the prey: Benjamin devours his prey in the morning and shares the spoil in the evening (Genesis 49:27), the image of the predator seizing its food.
3. Criminal plunder receives the same name: goods stolen through dishonesty.
4. The word extends to any gain: he who finds something great rejoices as over spoil (Psalms 119:162).
5. Figuratively, the Messiah on the cross shares the spoil with the mighty (Isaiah 53:12), not by stripping them, but by receiving his share of victory.
H7998.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to tear away," "to take by force." It primarily designates what is taken from someone by violence: in war, in combat, or by theft. The same root gives terms for "to plunder," "to strip away." It is a concrete word, rooted in the realities of combat and raid.
H7998.emploi: This word appears 64 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in war narratives (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings) and in the prophets. In the Pentateuch, God regulates the distribution of spoil (Numbers 31, Deuteronomy 20:14). The Psalms use it for the joy of one who discovers a treasure (Psalms 119:162). The prophets use it to describe future or past conquests. Isaiah 53:12 gives it a spiritual significance by applying it to Christ: it may be the only passage where spoil changes meaning, moving from the material to the spiritual.
H7998.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life is a struggle (Ephesians 6:12) where victories are won. The spoil shared with the victors (Isaiah 53:12) announces that Christ, through his cross, enters into glory and associates us with it. It is also an image of true gain: seeking the Word of God as one seeks great spoil (Psalms 119:162).

sens: To complete, finish, bring to an end
To restore, reimburse, pay what is owed
To recompense, reward, pay back
To punish, inflict deserved penalty
To satisfy, fulfill a vow or promise
To repair, restore, heal
H7999A.detail:
1. To complete, finish, bring to an end: the verb describes the action of completing something, finishing it. It is to finish what was started or unfinished. In Nehemiah 6:15, it is said that the wall of Jerusalem was "completed."

2. To restore, reimburse, pay what is owed: it is to return to someone what belongs to them or what has been taken from them, or to pay a debt. Exodus 22:15 speaks of "restitution" when a rented animal has died: the owner receives compensation.

3. To recompense, reward, pay back: to give someone what they deserve for good, to "render" back the good they have done. Psalms 22:26 says: "Those who seek the Lord will praise Him; your hearts will live forever"—that is, God "renders" life to those who seek Him.

4. To punish, inflict deserved penalty: to apply punishment to someone for their sin or crime. Deuteronomy 7:10 says that God "pays" (renders) to those who hate Him by sending destruction upon them.

5. To satisfy, fulfill a vow or promise: to carry out what one has promised to God. In 2 Samuel 15:7, Absalom asks the king for permission to "fulfill" a vow he had made to the Lord.

6. To repair, restore, heal: to make something or someone whole and healthy. Isaiah 57:18 speaks of God who "renders" health to the afflicted.
H7999A.origine: The verb comes from a Semitic root meaning "to be whole, complete, intact." It conveys the idea of totality and integrity: something complete is "whole." Hence, "to render" in the sense of "to make whole," "to reconstitute," but also "to recompense"—to give someone a reward or punishment that "completes" the cycle of merit. The name "Salem" (peace) comes from the same root: peace is the state where everything is in order, intact, reconciled. Aramaic uses the same word (שְׁלֵם).
H7999A.emploi: This verb appears 94 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy), the Psalms, and Proverbs. In the Law, it describes restitutions and compensations due in case of damage: if someone steals or breaks something, they must "render" compensation. In the Psalms, it often expresses the action of giving thanks to God and paying vows (Psalms 116:14). Proverbs uses it to show that everyone "receives back" what they have sown—good or evil (Proverbs 13:21). Job uses it to speak of divine retribution: God "pays" each according to their works. The word thus covers the entire spectrum: paying a debt, fulfilling a promise, receiving a reward or punishment, completing a task.
H7999A.portee: This word reveals that God is just and that every act has a consequence: nothing is forgotten, nothing is left unresolved. For the believer, "rendering" vows to God is to honor what one has promised, to fulfill one's word to Him. But it is also the promise that God will "render" justice, that He will reward faithfulness and punish evil. This justice is not vengeance, but restoration of integrity: God "renders" whole what was broken.

sens: To conclude a peace agreement with an enemy or adversary
To be at peace, live without conflict
A city or person who lives in tranquility and accepts peace
To put someone at peace with an enemy, reconcile
To approve someone and dispose others favorably towards them
H7999B.detail:
1. To make peace with someone is to conclude an agreement to stop a conflict or threat of war. Joshua 10:4 provides an example: Gibeon "made peace" with Joshua, meaning they accepted a treaty to avoid being attacked. It is a political and military act.
2. To be at peace means to live without conflict, in tranquility and security. As Proverbs 16:7 states, when God approves a man's ways, He causes his enemies to make peace with him—this is a restored harmony.
3. A "peaceful" city or people is one that chooses peace rather than revolt. In 2 Samuel 20:19, a city describes itself as "peaceful and faithful in Israel," meaning ready to live in accordance with the established authorities.
4. To put someone at peace with another means to reconcile them with him or place them under his protection. This is what "to make peace" means in an active sense: to establish agreement between two hostile parties.
5. More spiritually, to be at peace with God means to accept His authority and live in harmony with Him, as expressed in Job 22:21: "Submit to God, and you will have peace."
H7999B.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes integrity, wholeness, and the fulfillment of an agreement—the idea of being "whole" or "complete" by calming conflict. The peace (shalom) it denotes is not merely the absence of war, but the establishment of a stable and just bond. This root is found in the name "Solomon," which means "man of peace." The corresponding Greek word in the Septuagint is often eireneuo (to make peace).
H7999B.emploi: This verb appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives (Joshua, 1 and 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles) and in wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs). In contexts of war (Deuteronomy 20:12, Joshua 10:4, 1 Chronicles 19:19), it designates the political or military act of concluding a peace treaty with a defeated or threatening enemy. In wisdom and spiritual passages (Job 22:21, Proverbs 16:7), the verb extends beyond the political: it expresses inner peace and harmony with God or with others. Related Hebrew verbs (nominal peace = shalom) enrich this meaning by showing that biblical peace is always a fullness, a restored integrity, never a mere armistice.
H7999B.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that biblical peace is not merely the absence of conflict, but a state of harmony and integrity established by an agreement. It is also an invitation to seek reconciliation with those who threaten or contradict us—and especially with God. Job and Proverbs remind us: true peace comes from the covenant with God, from trusting in Him.

sens: To place the hands one over the other in a crossed position
To do something with thought and deliberate intention
H7919B.detail:
1. The literal meaning of the verb is to cross the hands, to place one over the other in a crossed position. This is what Israel does in Genesis 48:14: he intentionally stretches his right hand over the head of the younger Ephraim and his left hand over the elder Manasseh, crossing his hands voluntarily. This gesture is not random: it expresses an intention.
2. By extension, the verb means to act with intention, with thought, or to show wisdom and discernment in what one does. The crossing of the hands evokes the conscious, deliberate attention of one who "knows what he is doing." This is why the text emphasizes: Israel placed his hands "intentionally" — he acts voluntarily, not by clumsiness or by chance.
H7919B.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the crossing, intertwining of hands or arms. The basic image — crossed hands — suggests a conscious, thoughtful, controlled action, hence the meaning of "doing with intention" or "acting wisely." This root belongs to a family of words that revolve around the idea of prudence and discernment.
H7919B.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 48:14. Israel the patriarch, at the moment of blessing his grandsons, intentionally crosses his hands: he places his right hand on the younger (Ephraim) and his left hand on the elder (Manasseh), in a conscious and voluntary action. This gesture expresses his deliberate intention to bless Ephraim before Manasseh, despite the order of birth. The context reveals that this measured and thoughtful action extends the divine wisdom that Israel recognizes in Ephraim.
H7919B.portee: This passage shows that Israel acts with full knowledge, with a clear intention. For the reader, this reminds us of the importance of acting consciously, with discernment, rather than by routine or chance. Israel's gesture also foreshadows how God sometimes overturns human orders by His wisdom: the younger is blessed before the elder, as is the case in the history of salvation.

sens: Descendant of Zerubbabel who returned from exile with Ezra
Man from the family of Elam who had married a foreign woman during Ezra's time
Father of Shemaiah, who repaired a part of the wall of Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time
Son of Arah, father-in-law of Tobiah who opposed Nehemiah
Priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
Priest during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah
H7935J.detail: The name Shecaniah refers to several men in Israel's history between the exile and the restoration of Jerusalem. 1. A descendant of Zerubbabel whose descendants returned from Babylon with the priest Ezra, as indicated in Ezra 8:3, thus participating in the reconstruction of the people after the exile. 2. A son of Jehiel among the sons of Elam who had married a foreign woman, which was contrary to the Law at the time of the people's return. 3. The father of Shemaiah, who contributed to the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. 4. A son of Arah who became the father-in-law of Tobiah, the Ammonite who opposed Nehemiah's restoration efforts. 5. A priest counted among those who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel and Joshua. 6. A priest active during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, several centuries earlier than the others.
H7935J.origine: The Hebrew name Shecaniah literally means "dwelling with the Lord" or "inhabiting with God" (from שכן "to dwell" and יה "the Lord"). It expresses the proximity and communion of the bearer of the name with God, a hope characteristic of pious Hebrew names. The name appears several times in genealogies and accounts of the return from exile, testifying to its common use among the restored people.
H7935J.emploi: Shecaniah is a name that designates at least six distinct characters in the Old Testament, all living between the time of the Babylonian exile (6th century) and the reign of Hezekiah (8th century for the latter). Most of them are mentioned in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which recount the restoration of Jerusalem and the Temple after the return from exile. Ezra 8:3 specifically attests to a Shecaniah whose descendants returned with Ezra. These various Shecaniah figures are discreet yet real actors in the religious and civil life of the people: priests, family elders, builders of the wall, men with complex genealogies where alliances with neighboring peoples and faithfulness to the Law intersected.
H7935J.portee: These men named Shecaniah remind us that the restoration of Israel after the exile was the work of many obscure generations, not just great names like Ezra and Nehemiah. Their very name, "dwelling with God," suggests the hope that animated the restored people: despite exile and dispersion, God remained with His people. This is a lesson for the believer: in difficult times, God remains faithful, and those who return to Him, even obscurely, participate in His restoration plan.

sens: Descendant de Zorobabel dont les descendants revinrent de l'exil avec Esdras
Fils de Jehiel, parmi les fils d'Élam, qui avait pris une femme étrangère au temps d'Esdras
Père de Schemaeja, qui répara une partie du mur de Jérusalem au temps de Néhémie
H7935L.detail: 1. Shecaniah is primarily a descendant of Zerubbabel (the leader of the exile upon return) whose lineage returned from captivity with Ezra around 458 B.C. 2. He is also the son of Jehiel, among the sons of Elam, who had united with a foreign woman, which was contrary to the law of Moses. In Ezra 10:2, Shecaniah speaks before Ezra and acknowledges the sin: "We have sinned against our God by marrying foreign women." He thus shows the repentance of the returned exiles. 3. He is also the father of Shemaiah, who worked on the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:29): his son guarded the eastern gate.
H7935L.origine: The name Shecaniah comes from the Hebrew שְׁכַנְיָהוּ (Shekhanyahu), which literally means "he who dwells with Jehovah" or "inhabiting with the Lord." It is composed of two elements: שׁכַן (shakan), meaning "to dwell, to inhabit," and יָה (Yah), an abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah. This name expresses the confidence that God dwells with those who belong to Him, even in the midst of exile and dispersion.
H7935L.emploi: Shecaniah appears by name twice in the accounts of the exile and return (Ezra 10:2 and Nehemiah 3:29). In Ezra 10:2, he plays an important spiritual role by speaking up and acknowledging the people's sin regarding mixed marriages, thus encouraging collective repentance. In Nehemiah 3:29, his son Shemaiah participates in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem, showing that the family remains faithful to the work of restoring the city. These two passages illustrate the role of Jewish families returned from exile: some acknowledge their faults, while others work to rebuild the city and the temple.
H7935L.portee: Shecaniah embodies authentic repentance at the time of the return from exile. His public confession of the sin of mixed marriages (Ezra 10:2) shows that there is no shame in admitting one's faults before God and the community, but rather strength and a path toward restoration. His name, "he who dwells with Jehovah," reminds us that even in disaster and captivity, God never leaves His own. For the Christian, this speaks to the courage of sincere confession and the certainty that God remains with those who repent.
